News.title: Wet wipes urgently recalled over contamination fears — 'stop using immediately'
News.content:
Wet wipes urgently recalled over contamination fears — 'stop using immediately'

A popular brand of wet wipes has been pulled from shelves due to a health risk

View 2 Images A brand of wet wipes has been recalled (Image: wing-wing/Getty)

A brand of wet wipes has been urgently recalled from customers over contamination risks. The wipes may be microbiologically contaminated, meaning they could cause adverse skin reactions.

‌



The FreshWipes Intimate Unscented Wipes were sold on the FreshWipes website, Amazon UK, TG Jones (formerly WH Smith), TikTok Shop and QVC. It is described as a 10-pack of moist wipes, which are also sold in multipacks and in self-care bundles.

‌



The Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) issued a recall notice warning customers of the risk. It said: "It has been identified that affected batches may be microbiologically contaminated, with the preservative system not performing as required.

‌



"This could result in users experiencing adverse skin reactions. The affected batches do not meet the requirements of Regulation (EC) 1223/2009 (the ‘Cosmetics Regulation’)."

View 2 Images Some packets of Fresh Wipes Intimate Unscented Wipes have been recalled (Image: OPSS)

The OPSS added: "The product has been recalled from end users by FreshWipes. Consumers in possession of an affected batch should stop using the product immediately.

‌



"Contact your place of purchase for instructions on return or disposal of product and refund/redress."

Affected wet wipes

FreshWipes Intimate Unscented Wipes

LOT 0926 and 0515

‌



FreshWipes has also shared its own recall notice, as it said no other wipes are affected. In its guidance to customers, it said: "Check the batch number printed on the back of the pack. If it reads LOT 0926 or LOT 0515 the product is part of this recall.

"What to do: Please stop using the affected product immediately. If you have purchased Freshwipes Intimate Wipes from Batch LOT 0926 or LOT 0515, please contact our customer support team at Sales@freshwipes.co.uk with a photo of your remaining packs clearly showing the LOT number.

"We apologise for any inconvenience caused and remain committed to the safety and quality of our products."

‌



FreshWipes will offer a free replacement or store credit. It added: "If you bought your products from another retailer, please contact them directly and say you wish to return the product."

This week, B&Q also issued a recall notice for an electric fan. The White 9 Inch Table Fan was sold between March and July this year, but has been recalled as it poses a fire risk.

In its notice about the 30W fan, B&Q said: "A potential safety issue has been identified in relation to the White 9 Inch Table Fan sold between March 2026 and July 2026. In some cases, an electrical component may overheat leading to a fire or electric shock risk.

Article continues below

"If you think you have this product, please stop using it immediately and return to your nearest B&Q store for a refund."

News.title: Royal Mail customers will notice new delivery change from August
News.content:
Royal Mail customers will notice new delivery change from August

The British delivery company confirmed the update in a recent social media announcement

View Image The Royal Mail has shared the news with customers online (stock image) (Image: Getty)

The Royal Mail has confirmed a new change to how it makes deliveries across parts of the UK. Customers in certain areas of the country will likely notice the update this month as they go about their day.

‌



Taking to social media to share the news, Royal Mail uploaded a video to let Brits know about its new Electric Cargo Cycles. The delivery company announced it is deploying the environmentally-friendly vehicles as part of its Net-Zero goals. Royal Mail customers in a handful of UK cities will spot the newly launched cargo cycles from August - a change from the usual Royal Mail vans.

‌



In the caption of the video Royal Mail shared recently, it said: "We’ve launched our first Electric Cargo Cycles, expanding what is already the UK’s largest electric delivery fleet. The first 20 Minimal Pedal 4 Cycles will be deployed this month in cities including London, Brighton and Cambridge, with plans to roll out to further locations in the future."

‌



The Royal said the cycles are manufactured at Minimal’s microfactory in West London. It adds: "Their introduction marks another step towards our target of achieving Net-Zero by 2040."

In the video, a Royal Mail staff member explained: "The new pedal 4 cycles can travel up to 37 miles on a single charge, and charge from a standard plug socket. They'll help reduce emissions and improve air quality in the communities we serve, while creating new opportunities for people to join Royal Mail."

‌



The cargo cycles are expected to also help speed up deliveries. As postal workers won't need to share vans and can have their own cargo cycles, it is hoped this will streamline their day-to-day duties.

The cargo cycles can be used on roads with a speed limit of 30mph or lower, as well as on bike lanes, paths, and greenways. Postal workers won't need a driving license to operate one, making Royal Mail jobs accessible to a wider range of people.

According to Mark Riley, Delivery Design Manager at Royal Mail, the introduction of electric cargo cycles is a key milestone in the company's efforts to achieve net zero emissions by 2040. These vehicles are expected to enhance delivery efficiency, reduce emissions, and improve local air quality, while also creating employment opportunities for those without a driver's license.

Article continues below

The new cargo cycles come as the Royal Mail announced a "major milestone" on Thursday (August 6). In a post shared on social media, the delivery company said: "Our 9,000th electric van has officially joined the fleet, helping us deliver letters and parcels with fewer emissions.

"With nearly a third of our delivery routes now zero-emission and 44 delivery offices operating fully electric fleets, we're continuing to invest in a more sustainable future. 9,000 electric vans. UK's largest electric delivery fleet. Working towards Net-Zero by 2040."

News.title: Influencers avoid jail over death of man 'tortured and humiliated' on livestream
News.content:
Influencers avoid jail over death of man 'tortured and humiliated' on livestream

Raphael Graven, 46, also known as Jean Pormanove, was found unconscious by fellow streamers in France after having been live online for more than 298 hours

View 2 Images Raphael Graven died after livestreaming a challenge (Image: Instagram)

Two influencers have been convicted after "torturing and humiliating" a French streamer who died while livestreaming an extreme challenge.

‌



A broadcast by Raphael Graven, 46, also known as Jean Pormanove, was interrupted soon after his co-streamers found him unconscious and lying on a bed in August last year in a village near Nice.

‌



His livestream on the Kick platform had been been running for more than 298 hours.

‌



And now Safine Hamadi and Owen Cenazandotti have been convicted of aggravated violence following his death after an investigation found he was regularly subjected to humiliation and abuse in his content.

View 2 Images Raphael Graven was better known online as Jean Pormanove (Image: Instagram)

A Nice court has handed down suspended prison sentences to the pair, who claimed that the abuse took place with the consent of Graven.

‌



Pormanove had more than 500,000 social media followers.

Several internet users noticed a sudden end to the livestream on Kick. He reportedly endured “10 days and nights of torture” which included sleep deprivation, extreme physical violence and the “ingestion of toxic products”.

Pormanove caused controversy for his live antics, with fellow content creators Naruto and Safine in particular. He was seen in clips having food pushed into his mouth while he was restrained, being tackled in a room that appeared to be a basement and having objects thrown at him.

‌



Hamadi, who expressed remorse during the trial, was given an 18-month suspended prison sentence while Cenazandotti was handed down a two-year prison sentence which was also suspended.

Hamadi and Cenazandotti have also been ordered to pay fines of €5,000 (£4283) and €15,000 (£12,848) respectively. While they have been banned from posting online for six months.

Neither man was charged with the manslaughter of Graven, after the prosecution said probable causes of death appeared to be related to his poor health and fragile heart.

‌



And the pair were also acquitted of abusing Graven's psychological frailty, with the influencer previously telling police that he had consented to the extreme challenges.

Damien Martinelli, the prosecutor in Nice, said the autopsy showed the death was not caused by a trauma and “not related” to the intervention of any third party.

It was claimed by French investigative website Mediapart that co-streamers were mistreating Pormanove in live broadcasts, sometimes encouraged by payments from viewers, to generate more subscriptions and money.

‌



The criminal investigation was looking into “deliberate violence against vulnerable persons” and “spreading recordings of images related to offenses involving deliberate violations of physical integrity,” Martinelli’s statement said.

The Nice prosecutor also told last August how investigators had previously interviewed Pormanove and one of his co-streamers who both appeared to be victims of violence and humiliation. But they “strongly denied being victims of violence, stating that the events were staged in order to ‘generate a buzz’ and make money,” he added.

Kick, the streaming platform, remains part of an investigation by French authorities, and it told the New York Times it was not involved in the proceedings against Hamadi and Cenazandotti.

Article continues below

It added: "The ruling relates solely to two individual content creators."

The Mirror has contacted Kick for comment.

News.title: 'I used to weigh 24st - now I'm training for the Marathon des Sables'
News.content:
'I used to weigh 24st - now I'm training for the Marathon des Sables'

Geoff Stockley used to munch on pastries, baguettes, fish and chips, foot-long Subways and KFC during lunch breaks, until a sobering visit to his GP

View 5 Images Geoff Stockley before his weight loss (Image: SWNS)

A bus driver whose weight ballooned to 24st thanks to daily bacon rolls and pasties on his lunch breaks shed 9st after a blood pressure scare. Geoff Stockley, 39, was always larger than friends growing up - and gained more weight when he became a bus driver due to long, tiring days where he was mostly sat down.

‌



The dad-of-two munched on pastries, baguettes, fish and chips, foot-long Subways and KFC when on his lunch breaks at work, as they were conveniently located within the bus station. But this led to Geoff ballooning further to 24st and having to order XXXL shirts online because such large sizes were rarely available in-store.

‌



Geoff, from Poole, Dorset, never stuck to any diets when he tried to lose weight - thinking he would be okay because he was young. But after a doctor's appointment for a different issue flagged he had a very high blood pressure, he realised how serious a problem his weight was.

‌



Geoff started a Couch to 5k plan and started learning more about healthy nutrition so he could eat healthier foods that would still keep him full on his long shifts instead of eating convenience foods. Not only did he start to see the weight coming off but found he had more energy, could walk longer distances and be more active with children Elliot, 10, and Georgia, 16.

View 5 Images Geoff ballooned to 24st (Image: SWNS)

After around two years Geoff had shed a third of his body weight - slimming down to 15st 10lbs from over 24st - and swapping his XXXL shirts for a large. Alongside improving his blood pressure, he has started strength training and has signed up to run Marathon des Sables 2027.

‌



Geoff said: "I never prioritised being active and I was always overweight. I've been a bus driver 18 years - there's easy access to bad food at the station, and the weight kept coming on without me realising.

"I kept thinking to myself I'd do better but by my lunch break I'd have bought a bacon baguette, something from the bakery, chip shop chips or a KFC.

"So when the doctor flagged high blood pressure at a younger age than I expected, it was a bit of an eye opener. I think I'd been aware I should live a healthier life, but I didn't realise how significant that was until then.

‌



"Now I'm here, I have no intention of going back to that weight. I can show other people who do shift work that it is possible to do these things, even if it's not easy.

"Some people have to do a double take because they don't recognise me now. And my very supportive wife, Sian Stockley, 40, says I can't go back to that size again."

View 5 Images Geoff Stockley doing the Southampton marathon in 2023 (Image: SWNS)

‌



Geoff had gained weight after 15 years working as a bus driver prior to his GP's warning about his elevated blood pressure in 2023. He said: "There were bakeries around the station. Alongside the takeaways, I loved all things savoury, like sausage rolls, bacon and cheese turnovers and pasties."

His weight had increased over the years but he always made excuses to do something about it - until his blood pressure forced him to confront it head-on. He started running and began educating himself on healthier food options, meaning he could still feel full on his long shifts.

He said: "I started to lose weight when I combined the running with the nutrition - leaning how to eat better, cooking food to keep me full that wasn't so calorie-dense.

‌



"Simple things like just putting your trainers on and going out walking for 10 minutes. Instead of going to the bakery, I'd walk round the corner to Aldi and pick up some sliced chicken and fruit.

"People noticed relatively quickly that I was more active - my children noticed I could keep up with them more when they were running around."

View 5 Images Geoff Stockley after his weight loss (Image: SWNS)

‌



He completed his weight loss in early 2025 and has since maintained the weight loss after joining a strength training gym, and continuing his running. Geoff said: "It has led to me feeling a lot more confident in myself and a lot more aware of the choices I make."

In order to challenge himself, Geoff is looking to take on the Marathon des Sables 2027. The iconic six-day ultramarathon through the Sahara Desert in Morocco sees runners battle temperatures regularly above 40°C. in what is one of the toughest races in the world.

View 5 Images Bus driver Geoff is looking to take on the Marathon des Sables 2027 (Image: SWNS)

‌



Geoff is now raising money to fund the challenge, which will likely cost around £5,000 in total, including his travel and supplies. He said: "I want to show my family that something which doesn't feel possible, is possible if you work at it.

"It feels enlightening now to be able to go into a shop and buy a t-shirt or pair of shorts, now I'm a size large. Being where I am now would have seemed impossible 10 years ago. I've set myself a big challenge and it does feel overwhelming but I'm excited to get out there."

DIET BEFORE WEIGHT LOSS

‌



BREAKFAST: bacon baguette

SNACKS: chocolate bar

LUNCH: foot long Subway

‌



SNACKS: crisps

DINNER: large Dominos

SNACKS: ice cream

‌



DRINKS: full sugar Monster

DIET AFTER WEIGHT LOSS

BREAKFAST: scrambled eggs

‌



LUNCH: cooked chicken and lots of fruit

DINNER: chicken fajitas with lots of veg

SNACKS: fruit, Greek yogurt, protein powder and chia seeds

Article continues below

DRINKS: water, black coffee, sugar-free Monster

News.title: Couple left £973 out of pocket after confusing rule blocks them from dream holiday
News.content:
Couple left £973 out of pocket after confusing rule blocks them from dream holiday

Peter Wiles and his wife Rogelyn Caresosa had been planning to go on a holiday to Cappadocia in Turkey, but their holiday ended at Manchester Airport where Turkish Airlines stopped them from boarding

View 2 Images Peter Wiles and Rogelyn Caresosa were unable to go on their holiday

A man was left 'questioning his sanity' after he and his wife missed a Turkish Airlines flight .

‌



Peter Wiles and Rogelyn Caresosa had been looking forward to a romantic getaway in Cappadocia, a region of Turkey famous for its colourful hot air balloons and multi-level subterranean cities carved out of soft volcanic ash stone over thousands of years.

‌



The couple married in 2024, paving the way for Rogelyn to move to the UK on a spouse visa and live with her factory worker husband. Having saved up the cash for the May 2025 getaway, Peter splashed out £973.30 for flights from Manchester Airport.

‌



Both Peter and Rogelyn were distraught when their dream getaway ended at the airport.

"My wife was devastated, we had to get a taxi home as it was late on a Sunday and the trains had finished," Peter told the Mirror. "This whole debacle has honestly had me questioning my sanity at times!"

View 2 Images The couple only made it as far as Manchester Airport (Image: Kenny Brown | Manchester Evening News)

‌



Peter had booked and paid for two Turkish Airlines return flights to Turkey for himself and his Filipino wife, as part of a single booking in his name, using his Tesco Bank credit card.

They encountered a small difficulty in booking. Because Rogelyn holds a UK spouse visa, her old Biometric Residence Permit (BRP) card had technically expired at the end of 2024 under the UK's switch to digital eVisas, although her actual immigration status remains valid until 2027.

Before applying for Turkey's eVisa, Rogelyn called the Turkish Consulate, which advised her to use her BRP number rather than her UK "share code" as the "additional visa number" on the form.

‌



However, once at Manchester Airport, a Turkish Airlines gate agent rejected this, insisting the share code should have been used instead. This is despite the eVisa printout they presented, which stated that "eVisas of other countries are NOT accepted as supporting documents."

Ultimately, Rogelyn was denied boarding and so the couple were left at the airport, their plane leaving without them.

Peter has now been left fighting to get his money back, attempting to claim it back via his bank and Turkish Airlines. So far, he has been unsuccessful. He claims that Turkish Airlines refused to give a clear written explanation for the refusal, at various points citing a vague "issue" with the visa, then claiming the couple were a "no show".

‌



Following a request from Peter, Tesco Bank raised a chargeback, which the airline contested twice, before Tesco Bank ultimately dropped it. The bank accepted the airline's "flight operated as scheduled" explanation, despite that not addressing why boarding was denied.

Peter would go on to report the incident to the Ombudsman, but she ruled against him on technical grounds: no valid Debtor-Creditor-Supplier agreement existed for the wife's ticket because she, not Peter, was the one denied boarding.

The lengthy and frustrating process has left Peter doubting himself. "I've developed a complex about being misunderstood and feel I have to explain everything in detail," he added.

Article continues below

A Tesco Bank spokesperson said: "We were sorry to hear about the experience Mr Wiles had when attempting to travel with his wife. After careful consideration, we concluded that his case didn't meet the criteria for a successful Section 75 claim. He referred his claim to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which upheld our decision."

Turkish Airlines did not respond to a request for comment.

News.title: Illegal working arrests soar as top Reform figure Zia Yusuf branded 'pillock' over migration plan
News.content:
Illegal working arrests soar as top Reform figure Zia Yusuf branded 'pillock' over migration plan

Latest figures show 17,000 people have been arrested over illegal working since the general election - as Reform's Zia Yusuf was mocked after announcing a 'Deliveroo Law'

View 3 Images Reform's Zia Yusuf has been mocked after his latest migration announcement (Image: Maja Smiejkowska/PA Wire)

Illegal working arrests have more than doubled in two years, the government has announced - after a Reform UK chief was branded a "pillock" following another botched migration announcement.

‌



Figures released by the Home Office on Friday show 17,000 people have been arrested since July 2024 - up 122% on the previous two years. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood claimed rogue employees and people with no right to work in the UK have "nowhere to hide".

‌



On Thursday Reform's Zia Yusuf was accused of trying to divert attention from sleaze allegations by announcing a 'Deliveroo law' to target illegal working. He was mocked when it was pointed out that company chiefs already face jail terms, as Mr Yusuf had demanded.

‌



Terrorism referrals rocket as children account for one in three cases READ MORE :

Alarming stats show children under 5 suffer from food poverty as families forced to skip meals READ MORE :

View 3 Images Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said illegal workers and law-breaking bosses will have nowhere to hide (Image: Getty Images)

New data shows a 50% rise in people being returned to their homeland after being arrested for illegal working, with 2,357 deported since the general election. It comes after a week-long crackdown which saw over 900 visited by Immigration Enforcement, with 269 arrests, including 57 linked to small boat arrivals.

Ms Mahmood said: "This government has put more resources into Immigration Enforcement to crack down on it. This surge in enforcement activity takes us to the highest level in British history. Illegal workers and rogue employers have nowhere to hide.”

‌



Mr Yusuf, the party's home affairs spokesman, said bosses at firms that employ people with no right to work in the UK would face jail if his party gets into power. But he was swiftly reminded that such laws are already in place.

Lib Dem home affairs chief Max Wilkinson posted on X: "Oh dear Zia Yusuf. It’s already illegal and the offence carries a prison sentence of up to five years. What a pillock!"

Ms Mahmood has pledged to clamp down on the 'gig economy', including the delivery sector. From October these firms, including Deliveroo, will be legally required to check everyone working in their name is eligible to work in the UK.

‌



Failure to do so will incur fines of up to £60,000 per person, director disqualifications and potential prison sentences of up to five years. The Home Secretary has also announced plans to double the Immigration Enforcement budget by 2029, with a 60% staf increase.

The Home Office said this would lead to tens of thousands of raids. Reform have been accused of trying to grab attention with headline-grabbing migration announcements.

On Monday Nigel Farage and Mr Yusuf said they would use the Royal Navy to intercept and return people on small boats. But that idea was swiftly torpedoed by the French government, which branded the idea a violation of France's sovereignty.

‌



And on Thursday Mr Yusuf vowed to create a "tip line" for people to report illegal working or gang activity on their high street - with the potential for a cash reward. He said: ""Under a Reform government, Britain will have the harshest penalties in the world for those employing illegal migrants.

"Bosses of companies employing illegal migrants will be sent to prison, and their companies fined 10% of their global revenues. We will introduce the toughest penalties anywhere in the world for illegal working."

View 3 Images Bridget Phillipson said Reform tried to deflect attention (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock)

‌



A Deliveroo spokesperson said: "Illegal working should absolutely be addressed, and that's why we've led the industry in cracking down on the sophisticated, organised criminals who attempt to abuse our platform. We run right to work checks on all riders, conduct multiple daily identity checks and use cutting-edge fraud-detection technology, and we'd encourage other industries affected by illegal working to do the same."

And Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "This is Reform’s latest desperate attempt to deflect attention from the ever-growing catalogue of scandals engulfing Nigel Farage and his party.

“This Labour government is already cracking down on illegal working. Since July 2024, illegal working enforcement activity has reached record levels, with arrests up 83% and raids up 77%."

Article continues below

Mr Farage is currently fighting a by-election in Clacton after resigning amid a Parliamentary standards probe into a £5million 'gift' that he did not declare. And last month it emerged that the Met Police is investigating donations to the party amid questions about the original source of the money.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
In a statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Stuart Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, Blaik pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
Policing powers were stepped up in Thetford on Thursday evening following the disorder earlier in the week.

Norfolk's chief constable Paul Sanford told the BBC: "We have moved asylum seekers away from properties in the town, that's absolutely correct."

He urged the public not to make assumptions and said there were Thetford residents now "concerned for their own safety".

"This is people's lives we're talking about, this is human beings we're talking about and we ask the public that are protesting just to think about that for a moment."

Amid the disorder, pictures appeared to show a heavy police presence in the residential area of Canterbury Way on Thursday night.

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

Norfolk Police has imposed public safety measures in the town, including requiring people to remove face coverings if asked to do so or face arrest.

Officers will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or who they suspect may commit, anti-social behaviour, to leave the area.

The measures were put in place from 18:00 BST on Thursday and remain until 07:00 on Friday.

News.title: How a diary entry solved the murder of a missing man
News.content:
When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had disappeared six years earlier.

Richard Dyson vanished without trace in November 2019. He was last seen alive on 17 November that year and was reported missing eight days later when he failed to meet his daughter, Bethany.

"He was by all accounts a very good father, and he was regularly in contact with his daughter Bethany who was, I believe, 19 at the time of his disappearance. It was totally out of character," Ryan recalled.

"It was clear that he had disappeared off the face of the Earth."

Richard, who was 55 at the time, had been living in his car at Parkside Cottage on Christopher Wright's farm on Sheffield Road in Barnsley, helping with small jobs around the farm.

The farm was searched, but other than a collection of illegal weapons belonging to Wright, nothing more unusual was found and there was no sign of Richard.

His phone, however, showed it had never left the farm.

Police believed from the outset that Richard had been killed and that Wright and his childhood friend, Karl Schwalbe, were responsible, according to Ryan.

"We very much suspected their involvement, but without a body it's very difficult to prove murder," he said.

On 28 July, Wright, 73, and Schwalbe, 72, were convicted for their roles in Richard's disappearance and murder, ending a six-year wait for answers for Richard's family.

At a sentencing hearing at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday, Wright was jailed for 35 years for murder and Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

But how did police finally catch them?

News.title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
News.content:
Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cellsâ¦ this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

News.title: Wildfire-ravaged habitats in Wales could take centuries to recover, environmentalists say
News.content:
It could be hundreds of years before habitats destroyed by wildfires in Wales recover, an environment watchdog has said.

Nick Thomas, from Natural Resources Wales (NRW), said if soil had been incinerated in upland areas rich in peat, which grows at about a millimetre a year, it could take centuries for the vegetation to come back.

He called 2026 the worst year Wales had ever experienced.

As well as damage to natural habitats and animal life, Thomas warned loss of soil could increase flood risks, because it no longer acted as a "sponge" holding water on high ground.

Wales has witnessed huge wildfires this summer, including one major incident and the evacuation of a village in Conwy county.

In the Rhinogydd mountain range in Gwynedd, which is home to a National Nature Reserve and a Special Area of Conservation, a blaze burned for nearly two weeks and affected over 2,000 acres.

Both fires were visible from space.

Meanwhile, a fire in Blaenavon, Torfaen, could be smelt as far away as Cardiff.

Although fewer wildfires were reported in the second half of July in England and Wales compared with 2025, Thomas said: "This year seems to have been worse, I would say, than any of the ones I can remember.

"I would expect this to probably be the worst year for wildfires perhaps we've ever had."

While some areas will recover quite quickly - potentially within a couple of years - he said: "It all depends on how deep the fire goes.

"If a fire burns into the soil and incinerates the soil... then you've lost hundreds of years worth of soil.

"So it's going to take hundreds of years really for that vegetation to come back in a similar way to what it was."

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
News.content:
Do you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?

The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.

But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.

Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago.

But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?

News.title: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details some may find distressing

A 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future.

"This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC.

Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan.

She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023.

El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October.

For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare â with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food.

In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area.

But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive.

"They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voice

After weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick.

Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured.

It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help.

Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps.

There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada).

The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge.

It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth.

"Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father.

Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity.

"I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says.

"I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again."

According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan.

News.title: Boxer charged with killing aid worker in Athens after his wife gave police 'key' details
News.content:
Appearing in court earlier, Ahmadzai asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.

His lawyer, Christos Erdas, said his client had exercised his right to remain silent, and that his rights had been "violated" through leaks of evidence and documents from the case file - including his right to the presumption of innocence.

The lawyer said that when Ross was found, she had no injuries and any apparent cause of death was "entirely absent".

He said his client wanted the forensic medical report and the "toxicological and histological examinations of the deceased" to be included in the case file.

Erdas added: "His [Ahmadzai's] stance towards the prosecuting and investigating authorities did not constitute a stance of denial but, on the contrary, one of reservation, so that he may present his defence in full once the case file has been completed with the above essential documents â which were not sought by the preliminary investigating authorities â with the sole aim of establishing the substantive truth for both sides."

Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months.

News.title: Amanda Knox defends Fringe comedy show after claims it will 'trivialise violence'
News.content:
Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has defended her solo comedy show following calls for it to be cancelled.

The sold-out show called Cartwheel, which Knox will perform at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, discusses motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter.

Knox told the BBC she is not the first person to use comedy to talk about traumatic events and said her material focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women".

But Stephanie Kercher, the victim's sister, said she is concerned it will "normalise and trivialise" violence against women, and Meredith, in particular.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Stephanie Kercher, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Responding to the comments, Knox said: "The interesting irony of that is that my daughter is a huge motivation for me doing this show.

"It's about how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women and what it means to raise a daughter in that world, knowing how bad it can be.

"If they [Kercher's family] saw my show, they would recognise that."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by nearly 5,000 people.

It states the show disrespects her memory and risks making light of such a harrowing event.

News.title: Firearms officers called to violent disorder that left two men in critical conditions
News.content:
Two men are in a critical condition after violence broke out in a village in Torfaen.

Firearms officers from Gwent Police were called to the incident happened near Hospital Road and Mill Road in Pontnewynydd, near Pontypool, on Thursday.

Four men were arrested, and police say while two remain in custody, another is in hospital.

Officers have appealed for anyone with information, CCTV or dashcam footage from the area between 19:00 and 19:30 BST to contact them.

The National Police Air Service also attended the scene, alongside paramedics.

Det Ch Supt Anne-Marie Salwey said: "Violence in any form is completely unacceptable and anyone who is found to be involved in this disorder will be dealt as we will not accept this behaviour in our communities.

"We recognise that reports of this nature will prompt concern from our residents and it is likely that you will see officers in and around the area conducting enquiries as part of this investigation," she said.

The road between Mill Road and Hospital Road remains closed in both directions.

News.title: Police to end review into siblings who died in farmhouse 'bloodbath'
News.content:
A forensic review into the deaths of a brother and sister 50 years ago will end almost four years after it began, despite not delivering any new conclusions.

The bodies of Martha and Griff Thomas were found at a farmhouse in Llangolman, Pembrokeshire in 1976, originally prompting a double murder investigation.

Family member Huw Gibby, 79, said he was left "shell-shocked" that the investigation had failed to find any new answers, and described crime scene photos as a "bloodbath".

Dyfed-Powys Police said a "significant amount of complex work" had been undertaken, and "the family has been updated on the limitations faced in reviewing an incident that took place 50 years ago".

On a chilly Saturday morning in December 1976, postman Nigel Rossiter pulled up outside the isolated Ffynon Samson farmhouse in west Wales.

It was his first week in the job, and he spotted a couple of letters still lying on the floor of the porch where he had delivered them days before.

Smelling burning inside, he raised the alarm. This led to the discovery of two bodies â Griff, 73, who was badly burnt, and Martha, 70, who had severe injuries.

Police were called and found Martha - known as Patti - lying slumped on a magazine rack in the corner of the living room, with severe head injuries.

Chairs had been knocked over, and an overturned television lay at her feet. It was still switched on, with the sound of static filling the room.

News.title: Veteran camps in woods for months waiting for home
News.content:
An Army veteran has spent the last 15 weeks camping in woods while waiting for his social housing application to be processed.

Blair Murray, 44, served more than a decade in the Royal Logistics Corps up to 2010, but was made homeless by a landlord last year and spent months staying with friends before setting up camp in woodland near Crook in County Durham.

Murray said he had lined up a job and arranged to start counselling sessions, but both were being held up by his lack of a home.

Since the BBC got in touch with Durham County Council, homeless prevention manager Christopher Hepworth said the authority had worked with the Armed Forces Outreach Service and booked him into a Travelodge.

Hepworth said: "We will continue to work with him to secure suitable, stable, long-term accommodation."

In the most recent survey carried out by the Office for Veterans' Affairs, one in 400 ex-service personnel reported they were homeless or sleeping rough.

News.title: Man wrongly jailed for murdering man wants to restore his 'forgotten' grave
News.content:
A man who was wrongly jailed for 11 years for murder is raising money to restore the grave of the man he was accused of killing.

Michael O'Brien was one of three men wrongly convicted of the 1987 murder of Cardiff newsagent Philip Saunders.

O'Brien, along with Darren Hall and Ellis Sherwood, became known as the Cardiff Newsagent Three. They were eventually cleared in 1999, in what became one of Wales' worst miscarriages of justice.

He said he recently visited Saunders' grave and was "sad" to see there was no longer a headstone there and the area was "unkempt."

"It just sort of hit home that one, the killer was still at large, and two, this man has largely been forgotten about," O'Brien said.

Saunders was killed with a shovel in his backyard. It seemed the ambush and brutal attack was an attempt to steal his day's takings.

In June, nearly 40 years on from the original crime, South Wales Police said they were launching a review of the evidence in the case, "in the hope advances in forensic science will provide the breakthrough needed".

News.title: All schools in England to get pupil attendance targets, government says
News.content:
Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve pupil attendance, the government has confirmed.

Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

It comes as official attendance data, published on Thursday, suggested school absence rates in England remained above pre-pandemic levels, with nearly one in five pupils missing at least 10% of school in the 2025/26 academic year.

Education minister Paul Waugh said the new attendance targets would take each school's local challenges into account, but that "every school has a role to play to improve attendance".

Before the Covid pandemic, when many schools closed to pupils for significant periods of time, attendance rates at English mainstream state schools regularly stayed above 95%, but schools have struggled to get back to those rates in the years since.

Thursday's figures, external suggested an overall attendance rate of 93% for 2025/26, a slight decrease on the previous year. That includes both authorised absences, such as illness, and unauthorised absences, which is when pupils miss school without permission or a valid reason.

The rates of persistent absence have doubled since the pandemic. A pupil is described as persistently absent if they miss at least 10% of school sessions.

In 2018/19, persistent absence rates for England state schools were around 10%, while the most recent data showed it was at 19% in 2025/26.

Pupils on free school meals and those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) were also still more likely to be absent from school than their peers.

News.title: Met Police boss admits mistake over plagiarism row
News.content:
Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Grove said he had been investigating allegations Arday had plagiarised parts of his PhD, and contacted him in 2025 to offer him the right of reply.

"In early February I received a call from a Met police officer saying that a complaint had been raised against me by someone and Professor Arday was very distressed and I shouldn't contact him again," Grove told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was a complete shock. Apparently it was for harassment but I hadn't contacted him for four months and then maybe I think I've only sent three or four emails to him in total."

The Met closed its inquiries into the case.

Sir Mark told LBC: "We dropped the ball on that one, let's not beat around the bush.

"A report came in of harassment or some crime like that, it should have been screened out as not requiring investigation...

"We shouldn't have made that call to him [Grove] and said that."

The University of Cambridge said on Tuesday it had begun an investigation into Arday, who became the institution's youngest black professor in 2023, following "new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

In a statement published by campaign group Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said the "relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love".

"I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement," he said.

Speaking of his decision to step down he added it should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

His resignation followed a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis completed at Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) and other research.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, but did not uphold the charges.

The Times reported Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

In an interview with the Times, Arday said that he could not afford a proofreader to catch mistakes when he started out in academia.

Further questions were raised in the press about the truth of other claims, including Arday saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he raised Â£5.5m for charity.

News.title: Instagram’s new book feature totally misses the point of reading
News.content:

In the Roman Empire, owning a vast and extravagant library was a status symbol. The elite would amass mountains of scrolls and piles of books not only to read but to display as a signifier of wealth and intellect, and wealth of intellect. Lucian of Samosata, the satirical writer of the second century AD, compared folk who did so to “an ass listening to a lyre” in his essay Adversus Indoctum or The Ignorant Book Collector. Oh, what Lucian would have made of Instagram…

The social media platform has long served as an exercise in personal branding, where what you’re reading is part and parcel of who you are – or want to be perceived as. In recent weeks, Instagram has rolled out a feature that makes it more visible than ever: a banner that allows users to display a book title at the top of their profile (albeit with a 20-character limit.) Telling people you read Ulysses just got that much easier.

Book-signalling is nothing new – just look at the Romans. But its current iteration as we know it dates back to the days of yore and by that I mean the 2010s, when literary tote bags had a chokehold on anyone who had ever read The Catcher in the Rye and thought, ‘Wow, that Holden Caulfield guys seems cool.’ Instead of being emblazoned with any specific title, the literary tote tended to cast its net wider. It told passersby not what was on its owner’s nightstand but that its owner shops at independent bookstores like Daunt Books and has a subscription to The New Yorker…

open image in gallery Is social media shifting the focus from enjoying books to performing as a reader? ( Warner Bros )

Books have also become commodities unto themselves. This happens with buzzy releases like Yesteryear or Famesick, whereby the reading of them signals to everyone else on the tube that you too are part of the zeitgeisty in-crowd. But it is perhaps nowhere more apparent than in the case of the prize-winning publisher Fitzcarraldo Editions, whose stark white and cobalt blue covers are conveniently visible from a mile away meaning anyone within a five mile radius will know you to be a serious reader of serious books, the kind that win Nobel Prizes. Not to mention, there is also the use of books as aesthetic objects, with #BookshelfWealth taking over TikTok and the emergence of Book Stylist as a profession and the dawn of the celebrity book club.

The fashion world is reading up on the trend too, from the book bag charms launched earlier this year as a collaboration between Coach and Penguin Random House (Bleak House too big to fit in your clutch? Here’s a mini Sense and Sensibility) to the literary-focused events hosted by Prada and Miu Miu in recent years. Lucian is surely rolling in his grave.

All of which is to say that Instagram adding this “what are you reading” banner to user profiles is far from surprising. But while it feels like a natural extension of the above, it also feels more dubious in nature. While these other means of book-signalling are certainly in service to digital platforms – did you really read The White Album by Joan Didion if you didn’t post about it on Instagram? – they are, in fact, material. In order to carry a Daunt Books tote bag, you would have to actually patronise Daunt Books. Likewise, in order to bask in the clout of owning a Fitzcarraldo Editions book, you must buy, if not read, a Fitzcarraldo Editions book and in doing so support an independent press. And if, say, you wish to seem like the type of intellectual socialite who attends the sort of chic book readings that have sprung up as of late, well, you have to attend them.

By comparison, the new Instagram update is excruciatingly online – it asks us to log on to prove that we’re doing something that requires, by nature, logging off. It perhaps also misses the point that one of the reasons that reading has become so aspirational is because having a rich offline life has become so aspirational. Is it not just another way of making reading feel like a competition, shifting the focus from enjoying books to performing as a reader?

Still, it is worth noting that the appeal of appearing bookish is underpinned by a frankly optimistic belief: that books matter and reading is cool. At a time when more than a third of UK adults have given up reading for pleasure, that’s nothing to shirk at, I suppose. And so with that, I’ll sign off here: “READING: The Life of M by Rachel Cusk.”

Rail passengers are facing travel chaos for a second day after a widespread power failure affecting a large section of the UK’s rail network continues to cancel and delay services.

Passengers in Greater Manchester, the Midlands, and the northwest of England face severe delays, alongside numerous cancellations.

Delays and cancellations are expected until midday on Friday, with passengers advised to check National Rail Enquiries and operators’ websites for updates.

open image in gallery National Rail are advising passengers to expect disruption until midday ( National Rail )

The train line operators currently experiencing disruption include:

East Midlands Railway

Northern

TransPennine Express

Transport for Wales

Travellers for all operators are advised that they are able to use their ticket dated 6 August on any valid route on Friday.

National Rail said: “There was a failure of the electricity supply at a communications centre yesterday afternoon that caused severe disruption to trains across the Greater Manchester area and the north west of England.

“Although trains are now able to operate, the severity of the disruption that occurred on the network yesterday means that a number of trains and crew are now in the wrong locations for the start of service today.”

Electricity distribution company SP Electricity North West’s website states that a power cut in Harpurhey, which is north-east of the city centre, affected more than 400 postcodes, including that of the Manchester Rail Operating Centre.

It said: “The power cut in your area caused by an unexpected incident on our high voltage cable has now been resolved.”

open image in gallery Further major disruption was announced in Wales on Friday – several routes travelling between Cardiff Central and Newport are affected ( National Rail )

Manchester's Bee Network continues to accept tickets from affected rail passengers during the second day of disruption. Rail ticket acceptance is in place across all Metrolink lines and Bee Network bus services in Greater Manchester.

Chris Wright, Network Rail’s North West route director, said: “I’d like to thank passengers for their patience following yesterday’s power outage and the disruption it caused across the North West.

“Our engineers worked through the night to restore signalling systems and recover the railway, and I’m pleased that most services are now running this morning.

“While some passengers may still experience disruption, we’re continuing to work closely with train operators to return services to normal as quickly as possible.”

Further major disruption was announced in Wales on Friday, as a fire on the track near Cardiff affects signalling and overhead electricity power.

Any passengers planning to travel with CrossCountry, Great Western Railway and Transport for Wales on a route between these stations can expect severe delays or cancellations until the end of the day, National Rail has said.

News.title: No jobs for the next generation: Young workers struggle in Trump’s cooling economy
News.content:

The U.S. job market presents a perplexing picture this year, appearing stable with consistent, if not spectacular, hiring following a sluggish 2025.

Yet, beneath these headline figures, a complex, contradictory reality emerges. While some sectors grapple with severe labor shortages, forcing premium wages, others leverage technology so effectively their need for new hires has diminished.

This creates an unusual scenario where the American labor market, typically either robust or struggling, is currently experiencing a blend of both.

open image in gallery Hiring sign for sales professionals is displayed at a store, in Vernon Hills, Illinois ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

For those employed, job security remains unusually high, with layoffs at historically low levels. Companies, still mindful of past labor shortages, are reluctant to shed staff.

This trend was underscored in July when unemployment benefit claims reached their lowest point in over 50 years; the jobless rate dipped to a one-year low of 4.2% in June, a figure expected to hold steady.

However, the landscape is tougher for jobseekers. In May, 27.5% of the unemployed had been out of work for six months or more, the highest proportion in four and a half years. Economists term this "no hire, no fire."

open image in gallery A job seeker waits to talk to a recruiter at a job fair in Sunrise, Florida ( Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All Rights Reserved. )

The Labor Department is set to release July employment figures this Friday, with expectations of nearly 98,000 jobs added by companies, government agencies, and nonprofits. This would represent a notable improvement over June's disappointing 57,000 positions and mark a continued recovery from 2025.

That year saw anemic job creation, with fewer than 10,000 jobs monthly – the weakest hiring outside a recession since 2002. High interest rates and uncertainty surrounding President Donald Trump’s economic policies were cited as factors discouraging companies from expanding their workforces then.

So far in 2026, employers have averaged 92,000 jobs per month. While historically unimpressive, the US now requires fewer jobs to prevent unemployment from rising. Factors like immigration crackdowns and baby boomer retirements mean a smaller pool of individuals competing for work.

open image in gallery High interest rates and uncertainty surrounding President Donald Trump’s economic policies were cited as factors discouraging companies from expanding their workforces then ( AP )

The "break-even" rate of monthly hiring, 155,000 between 2023 and 2024, has plummeted, potentially nearing zero, according to a Federal Reserve study. Sal Guatieri, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets, observed, "There are just fewer people available to hire."

This scarcity has led to higher wages for job changers, who saw a 7% raise last month, significantly outpacing the 4.4% increase for those who remained in their roles.

Simultaneously, businesses have become increasingly productive, leveraging technology to automate tasks. "We are seeing companies produce more with their current staff," Guatieri explained, "So there’s less need to take on new workers."

open image in gallery The Federal Reserve headquarters, where construction continues, is reflected in a mirror in Washington ( Reuters )

He concluded that worker shortages and rising productivity "will keep the lid on the rate of hiring and monthly job growth."

The broader outlook is further complicated by global events, including the Persian Gulf conflict driving up energy costs, and the burgeoning influence of artificial intelligence, which could either enhance worker efficiency or displace jobs entirely.

The June jobs report revealed a peculiar anomaly: 720,000 people exited the labor force, with a striking 700,000 (97%) aged 25 to 34. A shrinking labor force typically reduces competition and can artificially lower the unemployment rate.

open image in gallery The broader outlook is further complicated by global events, including the Persian Gulf conflict driving up energy costs

Should this June drop prove a statistical quirk, and the labor force rebound, the unemployment rate could unexpectedly tick upwards. Furthermore, a report by Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco researchers highlighted a surprising increase in the difficulty of securing employment.

Contrary to typical economic expansions, this recovery is not reaching workers at the margins. "Instead of being pulled in, the pipeline into employment is shrinking such that the recovery is no longer reaching workers at the margins," they noted.

Even those typically quickest to re-enter the workforce – prime working-age individuals (25 to 54) with college degrees – are struggling to find new positions.

San Francisco Fed researchers are still investigating the precise reasons for this challenging job search, speculating on factors such as immigration crackdowns, tech and government contractor slowdowns, policy uncertainty, or "early signals of broader labor market deterioration."

Cameron Norrie produced a remarkable turnaround to down third seed Alex de Minaur after he saved one match point on his way victory in the third round of the National Bank Open in Montreal.

Norrie won 5-7 7-6 (5) 6-1 against the Australian to continue his hot streak, with the British No 2 hoping to go even better than his semi-final run in Mexico, eyeing a shot at his first Masters title since his sole triumph at Indian Wells in 2021.

The pattern for the last-32 contest in Canada started with De Minaur able to break Norrie immediately before the Brit raced into a 4-1 lead.

World No 7 De Minaur stayed calm and after he broke back, the Australian edged a hard-fought first after 62 minutes.

open image in gallery Cameron Norrie saved a match point in his comeback win over Alex De Minaur ( Reuters )

Norrie was staring down the barrel when De Minaur broke twice in the second to establish a 5-2 advantage, but the former Wimbledon semi-finalist saved match point before he hit back instantly and took the tie-break to force a decider.

With De Minaur’s resistance broken, Norrie cruised home with three more breaks in the third set to win after two hours and 53 minutes and continue his excellent form with a sixth victory in seven matches since a first-round exit at Wimbledon.

Norrie now faces the challenge of Frenchman Arthur Fils in the round of 16, but feels his resilient mentality could be key to overcoming yet another stern test.

"Everyone is so tough,” he said. “I'm playing the next highest guy Fils - he's one of the best players in the world when he's confident and playing well but I'm just so happy.

"I've got some time to rest, happy with my attitude. I played every single point and that's what I came to do and it was the icing on the cake to win the match."

Additional reporting from PA

Ukraine has hit a major logistics hub of Russian online retailer Wildberries in Yekaterinburg, east of Moscow, continuing its three-week campaign of near-nightly strikes.

At least 20 Wildberries warehouses have been attacked since July 18, sparking major fires, destroying entire warehouses of stock, and disrupting its vast logistics network across the world's largest country. A Reuters review of satellite imagery shows at least 1.18 million square metres of storage space - more than a fifth of the company's capacity - has been damaged or destroyed.

The strikes are part of a campaign by Ukraine to "bring the war home" to ordinary Russians and raise the cost to Russia of continuing the conflict that Moscow launched in February 2022.

Wildberries, whose vast product range includes items such as night-vision goggles, ammunition pouches and helmets, alongside regular clothing, cosmetics and electronics, is a linchpin of the consumer economy and is often described as Russia's answer to Amazon.

Kyiv accused the firm of helping to bolster Vladimir Putin’s war machine. The company and the Kremlin say it does not supply to the army.

According to Data Insight analyst Sergei Semko, goods destroyed by strikes on Wildberries warehouses in Moscow and Tambov regions alone were worth up to an estimated $2.9 billion.

The company, with a few of its warehouses hit as recently as Thursday, said on Telegram it had paid a second tranche of financial ‌support to nearly 100,000 sellers whose ​goods were damaged.

Mapped: Where has Ukraine hit Wildberries sites?

open image in gallery Ukraine strikes Wildberries sites in Russia and annexed Crimea ( AP )

What is Wildberries?

Wildberries is Russia's largest online marketplace. It has been called the country's equivalent of Amazon, as its business model resembles a mix of Amazon Marketplace, eBay, and Temu.

Founded in 2004 by Tatyana Kim, who is now Russia's richest woman, the company has since become the dominant e-commerce platform in Russia and several neighbouring countries.

Hosting millions of third-party sellers, the platform sells almost everything, from electronics to groceries. The marketplace features clothes, books, cosmetics, toys, appliances, household items, sports gear and much more. There’s an “E-Pharmacy” page and a travel section for booking plane tickets or hotels.

open image in gallery A woman walks past Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries' logo in downtown Moscow on 27 July 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

It operates a vast network of warehouses, sorting centres, and logistics hubs across Russia.

In 2021, Kim acquired a small bank and turned it into what is now Wildberries Bank, but that institution has since come under sanctions by the U.K. and the European Union.

Now, its facilities are being deliberately targeted by Ukrainian drones.

Wildberries, together with other e-commerce platforms, handles goods and services worth the equivalent of 8.5 per cent of Russia's economy.

Why is Ukraine attacking Wildberries?

Kyiv’s reasons for attacking Wildberries appear to be two-fold.

Ukrainian officials say that the company's warehouses and transport network are actively involved in storing or transporting goods that ultimately support the Russian military, a claim Moscow denies. Because Kyiv alleges that the company is part of Russia's wartime logistics and economic infrastructure, they insist Wildberries’ infrastructure is a legitimate target.

However, the attacks also appear to be part of an attempt to increase economic pressure on Russia.

An ‌executive at Ukraine’s leading arms producer, ​Fire Point, emphasised that Wildberries is being targeted partly because of ​its partnership with state-controlled bank VTB.

open image in gallery The four-year war in Ukraine continues to slow the Russian economy ( (Iryna Rybakova/Ukraine’s 93rd Mechanized Brigade via AP) )

In an interview posted on Monday, Denys Shtilerman, Fire Point’s co-founder and chief designer, described Wildberries as the largest borrower in Russia and said its demise would lead to the collapse of a large number of banks, including VTB.

Described as the “backbone” of what the Kremlin calls the Russian “platform economy,” Wildberries has been considered central to plans for economic growth after the government purchased a 5 per cent stake in the company earlier this year.

Together, Wildberries and competitor Ozon account for economic activity worth around 8.5 per cent of Russia's GDP.

They support around four million jobs, or more than five per cent of Russia's workforce.

As the country continues to face a steadily-weakening rouble, and a steadily-increasing inflation rate, the central bank has cut its key interest rate to 14 per cent, highlighting the growing strain on Russia's wartime economy.

Continued Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries are set to further add to this pressure.

How has Russia responded?

For Russia, the attacks on Wildberries mark another severe economic blow amidst the increasing cost of sustaining its war in Ukraine.

The Kremlin has acknowledged it may have to financially prop up Wildberries, which has lost 10 per cent of its warehousing capacity and a huge amount of stock as a result of Ukrainian attacks.

open image in gallery Zelensky met with congress on Tuesday to discuss further sanctions on Russian oil ( AFP/Getty )

Meanwhile, the US Senate took the first steps toward passage of a sweeping Russian sanctions bill.

After meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky, the bipartisan procedural vote secured an 86-12 majority.

News.title: Wine experts reveal the 9 best supermarket rosés perfect for sunny summer days
News.content:
Over the last few years, rosé has enjoyed a transformation from a summer staple to a year-round vino. Driven in part by celebrity brands (think Brad Pitt’s Miravel or Kylie Minogue Wines), the Provençal giant Whispering Angel has been cited as boosting the worldwide rosé market.

The wine has a loyal legion of sippers, thanks to attractive marketing, subtle flavouring and A-lister approval – Adele told US Vogue: “Whispering Angel turned me into a barking dog. It did not make me whisper.” A blend of cinsault, grenache and vermentino grapes, the wine is loved for being very pale and very dry, with subtle flavours of orange, red fruits and a little dried herbs and spice.

But with a price tag of £25, it’s little surprise supermarkets have rushed to offer more affordable alternatives. Aldi and Asda, in particular, have leaned heavily into the trend, producing bottles that don’t just take inspiration from the original but are near-identical – right down to design cues and playful naming (see Asda’s Screaming Devil).

“Yes, the classic pale Provençal styles are still everywhere – light, easy, and made for sunny afternoons – but there’s also a more interesting mix creeping in,” Candace Bugden, expert wine taster and TikToker, says. “Think rosés with a bit more flavour, a bit more texture... darker in colour, deeper in texture and complexity. Interesting and versatile.”

Be it a Nerello Mascalese grown on Mount Etna’s slopes in Sicily or a rich Arbousset Tavel plonk from Tesco, “these are bottles you can happily drink in the garden but also take to the table with food and not feel like you’re compromising,” Bugden says.



Supermarket shelves are now filled with convincing rivals to rosé’s like Whispering Angel, with sommeliers often highlighting bottles such as Leoube, which costs less than £18. Meanwhile, wine enthusiasts on TikTok love M&S’s la balconne and Lidl's breath of paradise bottle.

“Whispering Angel is a great wine, as is its more refined offering,” says wine writer Katie Brook. “But are we paying for quality or a name?” In a bid to help you keep costs down ahead of your next springtime soirée, I asked experts to share their favourite supermarket rosé and affordable Whispering Angel alternatives.



What to look for in a supermarket rosé

"I always recommend looking to the regions in and around Whispering Angel’s home, the southern French Mediterranean region of Provence – so look for labels that say Languedoc, Pays D'Oc, IGP Méditerranée or Corsica,” says The Independent's wine columnist, Rosamund Hall.

By looking in these regions, “you'll find wines made using similar grapes. They'll have a familiar appearance and taste: delicate pale dusty-pinks with aromas of fresh summer berried fruits, hints of orange zest, and of course a beautiful, uplifting acidity”, she explains.

Lucy Hitchcock, the wine enthusiast behind the @Partnerinwineuk social media account, explains: “The peculiar thing is, a lot of the Whispering Angel ‘dupes’ that are popping up now, are actually Sainte Victoire Cotes du Provence rosés.” This region has recently become the first ‘cru’ of Côtes de Provence, noted for its distinctive terroir. “Sainte Victoire is a very specific quality area of Côtes de Provence, with a specific microclimate producing beautifully balanced grapes,” Hitchcock adds.

For those looking for a swap-out Provencial rosé, Emilee Tombs, wine writer and assistant travel editor at The Independent, suggests the Loire Valley. “While it might not offer better value, rosé wines from this area of northwest France have a similar dry, crisp style with red fruit and citrus notes.”

Meet the experts

From left to right, Candace Bugden and Katie Brook ( Candace Bugden/Katie Brook )

Katie Brook is a journalist with a specialism in wine and a decade of experience as a wine reviewer. She is the founder of Run To Wine, a London- and Surrey-based running club that ends its sessions with a wine tasting.

Candace Bugden, otherwise known as @this.wine.woman, is a TikToker with more than 50,000 followers. As well as sharing excellent bottles of wine online, she is assistant manager of tours and tastings at the Wiston Estate in West Sussex.

Lucy Hitchcock is the wine enthusiast behind the @Partnerinwineuk social media account. She has nearly 100k on Instagram and 65k on TikTok, with her reviews of Aldi or M&S bottles regularly going viral.

( Emilee Tombs/Rosamund Hall )

Emilee Tombs is assistant travel editor at The Independent and holds a WSET Level 3 Award in Wines from the Wine and Spirits Education Trust. She has written for a number of wine publications, from Noble Rot to Ocado Life magazine.

Rosamund Hall is a writer, presenter and columnist specialising in wine and spirits. She is The Independent's weekly wine columnist with 'The Wine Down' and writer of the best rosé wines.

Tom Gilbey started winemaking at age 23, then became an importer, wine merchant, and advisor. He shares his recommendations on his website, as well as to his 666k followers on Instagram and 218k on TikTok, aiming to demystify the world of wine.
