World.title: Govt. approves grant program for Romanians living abroad who want to invest in the country
World.content:
Romania’s government approved in its Thursday, August 6 meeting the decision to launch the program Diaspora Invests at Home, aimed at Romanians living abroad who want to set up businesses in the country.

The program has a total budget of EUR 100 million, with grants to be managed by the Development and Investment Bank (BID) on behalf of the Finance Ministry.

The grants can cover up to 60% of the investment loan, capped at EUR 200,000 per eligible beneficiary, the Finance Ministry explained.

The grants will be awarded between 2026 and 2029, subject to the available budget.

The investment loans intended to finance business capitalization can range from EUR 5,000 to EUR 500,000, with a maximum loan term of 10 years and a final maturity date no later than December 31, 2037.

The program is open to newly established companies whose share capital is majority-owned by Romanian citizens who have resided abroad for at least 12 consecutive months during the past 18 months. Applicants must provide evidence of at least one year of relevant professional experience or studies in the field for which funding is requested and must maintain the investment and ownership structure for at least three years after the completion of the project. Beneficiaries must also provide a minimum own contribution of 10% of the investment project's value, reduced to 5% for entrepreneurs younger than 35.

“With the mandate granted today, we are ensuring that the EUR 100 million in funds will be managed transparently and efficiently, reaching those who dare to start new businesses in Romania. In this way, we are offering Romanians in the diaspora not only an invitation to return, but also concrete financial support and a strong institutional partnership to bring back the experience, capital and professional skills they have acquired abroad,” Finance Minister Alexandru Nazare said.

(Photo: Dreamstime)

simona@romania-insider.com

World.title: Democracy Digest: Study Finds Slovakia Has Europe’s Weakest Spy Agency
World.content:
Police investigate Czech MP over car crash; countdown to municipal elections; Havel human rights award to be preserved

Czech police this week launched an investigation into MP and government commissioner for the Green Deal Filip Turek on suspicion of bodily harm through negligence over a car crash last month, which saw the honorary president of the Motorist Party – a ruling coalition junior partner – collide with an ambulance at a busy thoroughfare in Prague’s city centre. Caught on CCTV, the traffic accident led to the ambulance’s driver being injured and incapacitated for several days, sparking calls from opposition parties as well as President Petr Pavel for Turek to step down from both his parliamentary and government positions – although experts remain divided on who precisely was to blame for the collision. Turek has since temporarily vacated his position as the government’s plenipotentiary for climate change and the Green Deal pending the results of the investigation and vowed not to use his parliamentary immunity should the police file criminal charges against him. “I think the investigation will go well for me because I kind of know the regulations,” he told TV Nova, also suggesting the injured ambulance driver was “talked into” staying under hospital care longer than necessary for the optics.

This week was the deadline for political parties, movements and coalitions to officially register for the upcoming municipal elections, scheduled to be held across Czechia on October 9-10. Candidacies will now be reviewed by state electoral authorities by August 22. In the capital Prague, two dozen political groupings will take part in the race to win the big and hotly contested prize, a couple more than four years ago, on top of electoral fights for the city’s 57 local districts. In addition to electing their political representatives in the Czech Republic’s more than 6,000 towns, cities and municipalities, voters will also vote for a third of the Senate’s seats. About 155 candidates have registered to run for this year’s partial Senate race, less than the last ballot, mainly a result of pre-election agreements and joint candidates put forward by opposition parties.

Dagmar Havlova, the widow of the former dissident and president, along with the Vize 97 foundation confirmed this week that the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prize will be preserved and continue to be awarded every year. This follows a previous announcement by the Vaclav Havel Library – which has faced an exodus of staff, sponsors and funding in recent months – that it would no longer participate in the annual award ceremony after Havlova withdrew her consent for the NGO to use the former playwright’s name. Coming with a cheque of 60,000 euros, the award was established shortly after Havel’s death in 2011 to recognise outstanding achievements in the field of human rights and has been awarded by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe since 2013 together with the Vaclav Havel Library and the Charter 77 Foundation. Past laureates include Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, Russian journalist Vladimir Kara-Murza and Belarusian activist Maria Kalesnikava.

World.title: Lands in Limbo: Danube ‘Microstates’ Dream Big Despite Lack of Recognition
World.content:
From the village of Batina in Croatia's far northeast, the only land route leads to the Free Republic of Liberland, a self-proclaimed microstate on the banks of the Danube River.

A bicycle is the only practical means of transport. The journey begins on an asphalt road before continuing onto gravel and then a dirt track, until the road disappears altogether.

The final kilometre must be covered on foot, across the dried-up bed of a Danube backwater. In summer, it feels more like walking across desert sand before reaching the dense forest that forms the "centre" of Liberland.

World.title: Letter from Brussels: Ceuta Migrant Panic Casts Shadow Over EU’s Summer
World.content:
The weeks that bridge July and August are a period when the EU buildings around Schuman here in Brussels grow quiet, and correspondents’ group chats go mute.

But this year the last week of July was far from quiet. While EU spokespersons were cycling through out-of-office messages and the unlucky ones were covering for absent colleagues, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - the largest single-day surge in irregular arrivals ever recorded on EU territory.

Dozens died. Within two days, the story had stopped being about victims. It had become a story about Europe’s political nerves.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Sweltering Capital Needs Green Fixes for ‘Urban Heat Islands’
World.content:
As another intense heatwave sweeps across the region, millions of people have discovered that if they live in a heavily-urbanised part of a city, it can have a major impact on temperature levels.

Concrete, asphalt and densely-packed buildings trap heat long after the sunset, creating so-called “urban heat islands” that make temperatures several degrees higher than in nearby greener areas.

Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia, offers a striking example. BIRN compared temperatures in sunny and shaded locations across the city. While not a scientific experiment, the readings highlight how trees and parks can reduce the heat.

A measurement taken at noon on one of the busiest boulevards in the city, Partizanski Odredi, showed 33 degrees celsius in the tree shade and 40 degrees in direct sunlight. The results were similar on St. Clement of Ohrid Boulevard in the city centre. Around noon, the thermometer read 34 degrees in the shade and 44 degrees in the sun.

World.title: Kosovo Serb Businessman and Politician Radoicic Indicted for War Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip



Milan Radoicic. Photo courtesy of N1.

Kosovo’s Special Prosecution on Thursday said it has filed an indictment charging 20 people it suspects of committing war crimes against civilians in the western town of Gjakove/Djakovica during 1999.

BIRN has learned that Milan Radoicic, a well-known Kosovo Serb businessman and politician, is among the suspects.

The prosecution said that, according to the indictment, during the 1998-1999 war in Kosovo, the suspects, operating in different capacities of the Serbian Interior Ministry, “are accused of participating in the killing of 107 civilians during a large-scale military-police operation.

“During this operation … the defendants initially separated the women and children from the men. The women were robbed, taking their gold jewellery, money and other valuables, while the men were executed, some in their homes and yards, some at a location known as ‘Taliqi Bridge’. The houses were also burned,” the Prosecution added.

It proposed a trial in absentia for the defendants since they are all out of reach of Kosovo’s authorities.

In April 2025, the Pristina Basic Court issued an arrest warrant for Radoicic and 19 others suspected of war crimes in May 1999 in Gjakova/Djakovica.

The court said the Special Prosecution was investigating suspicions that from May 7 to May 10, 1999, the suspects were among uniformed Serbian military and police forces who “entered houses and using force and threats took everyone present out of their homes and separated the men from women and children. Later they killed 106 civilians of Albanian nationality.

“After the war, their bodies were found in a mass grave in Batajnica in Serbia,” the court added.

The court said it suspected that Radoicic and the 19 others “arrested and imprisoned 300 other civilians from the Albanian community and other ethnic communities, who were first kept in improvised prisons” and treated inhumanely.

Many of these prisoners were transferred to prisons in Kosovo and eventually to Serbia, to be released after June 1999 with the assistance of the international community, the arrest warrant notes.

“All the Albanian civilians and civilians and of other nationalities who lived in Gjakova were barred from their home via force and threats. First, all the houses of Albanians in Gjakova were robbed and then burned, causing material damage,” it added.

The court noted that the suspects do not have addresses in Kosovo and are not accessible to the Kosovo authorities.

Charged multiple times

Radoicic is well known to the Kosovo authorities. They have charged him with multiple crimes, or listed him as the main suspect a number of times, but have not so far been able to bring him to court.

Together with 42 individuals, he was charged with terrorism and endangering the constitutional order of Kosovo over the attack by armed Serbs on a police patrol in the Kosovo village of Banjska in September 2023, which left one police officer dead.

Only three Kosovo Serbs have been arrested related to the attack. They have pleaded not guilty. Radoicic, who since fled to Serbia, took responsibility for leading the assault but insisted he did so without informing the authorities in Belgrade.

At the time of the attack, Radoicic was deputy leader of Srpska Lista, the main Serb party in Kosovo, which operates closely in line with Serbia’s government,

Serbia launched an investigation into Radoicic in September 2023, when the Belgrade Higher Prosecutor’s Office said it was probing him for organising an armed group, the unauthorised amassing of a large cache of weapons, which he transported to Kosovo, and for “serious crimes against general security”.

Belgrade prosecutors questioned him in October 2023, when he reportedly claimed innocence.

In April 2024, the Kosovo authorities seized most of Radoicic’s property in the country.

Prosecutors there also implicated him in a corruption scam in Brezovica in the Sharr Mountains National Park. He narrowly avoided arrest in 2022 when he tried to cross from Serbia into Kosovo, but turned back at the last second.

Commenting at the time on the warrant issued against him, Radoicic suggested he was a victim of a campaign against Serbs in Kosovo.

Radoicic was earlier named as the main leader of the criminal group that organised the murder of the Kosovo Serb politician Oliver Ivanovic, in 2018, together with businessman Zvonko Veselinovic. The men were never charged.

In an interview with BIRN a few months before his murder, Ivanovic named Radoicic as the real power-holder in the Serb-majority north of Kosovo.

World.title: Bulgarian Man Killed After Being Lured to Meet Teenager, Police Say
World.content:
Plovdiv’s historic old town area. Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Klearchos Kapoutsis.

Police in Bulgaria’s second biggest city, Plovdiv, said on Thursday that they have made eight arrests over the death of a man who was lured by teenagers to a meeting with “a 17-year-old girl, posing as a 15-year-old” and then severely beaten up.

Police told a press conference that the teenagers had concocted a scheme to track, lure and then attack alleged paedophiles, and then livestream the beatings.

Their victim, who was assaulted on Tuesday at a site near Youth Hill, a location near many of the tourist sights close to the centre of Plovdiv, has been named as Georgi Kuzev.

After being assaulted, Kuzev was discovered by passers-by and taken to hospital. Nova TV said he had suffered a severe brain injury and various fractures. He died several hours later.

The incident was initially reported by media as having potentially been a homophobic attack, after other such attacks in Plovdiv in 2020, sparking outrage from LGBTQ+ rights groups.

But the announcement at Thursday’s police press conference caused a U-turn in speculation around the case.

Atanas Kalchev, mayor of Krichim, a small town near Plovdiv, said the victim was originally from Krichim.

“The case is extremely serious and is characterised by a high degree of public danger due to the cruelty of the crime committed,” Kalchev said in a statement on Wednesday before the police announced the circumstances of the attack.

“Even if the initial theories [about a homophobic attack] don’t get confirmed, this doesn’t take away from the weight of the crime,” Kalchev added.

World.title: Romanians Urged to Use Less Electricity in Heatwave as Danube Levels Drop
World.content:
The Romanian government on Thursday urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption between 7 p.m. and 11 p.m. until the end of the month, to ease pressure on the power system during the ongoing heatwave.

“Keeping electricity consumption as low as possible during the evening hours will not affect essential services, such as healthcare,” Romania’s interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said.

“We are going through a difficult period that could last another one to two weeks, and we are compelled to take these measures,” he added.

The capital, Bucharest, has already reduced street lighting by one-third in the evenings and switched off illumination at landmark buildings and museums overnight to save electricity. Other cities have introduced similar measures.

Earlier this week, the country’s largest energy-intensive companies, including car manufacturers, steel producers, fertilizer plants and other major industrial consumers, suspended operations or scaled back production to reduce pressure on the power grid.

A prolonged heatwave and record-low water levels on the Danube have forced Romania to restrict water use for agricultural irrigation, disrupting river transport, tourism and the energy sector. The authorities have also shut down one reactor at the country’s only nuclear power plant, at Cernavoda, which relies on Danube water for cooling.

Low water levels on the Danube are expected to continue affecting operations at the Cernavoda nuclear plant at least until mid-August. The government declared a nationwide energy alert on July 31, which will remain in force throughout August.

World.title: Kosovo Delays Speaker’s Election Amid Coalition Talks Uncertainty
World.content:
Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti addresses Kosovo’s parliament in its inaugural session, August 6, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

The leader of Kosovo’s ruling party, Vetevendosje, Albin Kurti, on Thursday asked parliament for more time before proposing a name for the new speaker, after MPs elected in the June 7 polls took their oath at the assembly’s inaugural session.

Kurti, who is also caretaker Prime Minister, had been expected to submit a name for the proposed speaker, but instead called for more time “to give the talks for an agreement on a new president a chance”.

Kurti is in the midst of negotiations to form a coalition government, which also involve deciding on a name to put forward to parliament as Kosovo’s next president. If no president is installed by MPs, the country will have to hold general elections yet again, according to the constitution.

“The inauguration of parliament this time should not be [a step] towards another dissolution and snap elections, which are unjustifiable and unnecessary for citizens and harmful for the economy,” Kurti said in a short speech.

However, his announcement sparked angry reactions from opposition MPs in the chamber.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje Movement won 53 of the 120 seats, down four from the last December 2025 election, but well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22 seats. The Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, which is Kurti’s most likely coalition partner, won 18 seats.

A repeat of the parliamentary deadlock that paralysed the country for much of 2025, when no party had enough seats to elect parliamentary officials and form a government, has likely been avoided – but only when it comes to the election of a speaker and a government, for which the winning party needs only a bare minimum of 61 votes.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority to form the next government by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 snap elections has not been solved; the parties still need to come to an agreement to elect a new President. Failure to do this within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament would trigger another election.

The opposition PDK in a statement criticised the latest development as “a continuation of the institutional blockade by Kurti, in contradiction with the obligation set by the Constitutional Court” – which set a 30-day deadline for the election of a parliamentary leadership from certification of the election results on July 8.

“This is a sign of the lack of seriousness and responsibility from the biggest party [Vetevendosje],” Bedri Hamza, head of the PDK, said.

As his only potential partner for a coalition, Kurti has so far twice met LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku – but without managing to get a deal on a new President.

Kurti insists the new President should be unaffiliated with any party. Abdixhiku, however, maintains that the post of head of state belongs to the LDK.

“I hope and trust that we can have a positive move during the day but it remains to be seen,” Armend Zemaj, an LDK MP, said on Thursday, after the interruption of session.

He voiced concerns about constitutional deadlines for the parliament, which cannot be considered inaugurated until the speaker and five deputies are elected.

World.title: Croatian Mountain Rescue Service Rescues Another Foreign National on Biokovo
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – The Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS) has had to rescue yet another foreign national stuck on Biokovo.

As Index reports, the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service (HGSS) has reported a night-time rescue of a foreign national who got lost last night in the area of Sutvid above Živogošće near Makarska, at around 1,050 metres above sea level on the southeastern part of Biokovo. HGSS received the call on Wednesday at around 18:30.

The man reported that due to high temperatures and lack of water he had become severely dehydrated, felt extreme weakness and was no longer able to safely continue moving or find the way. Four rescuers from the HGSS Makarska Station immediately set out into the field, and due to the demanding terrain they were soon joined by another four.

“After several hours of night ascent, the rescuers reached the injured person at 22:50. First aid was provided at the scene and after a rest and rehydration, accompanied by the rescuers, he began the descent towards the vehicle,” the HGSS Makarska Station announced.

The operation was successfully completed at 02:50. Photos published by HGSS show that the man had set out on the ascent in sandals. HGSS once again warns everyone not to go into the mountains without appropriate equipment and a sufficient amount of fluids.

“We’d once again like to appeal to all visitors to Biokovo to please, please carefully plan their trip before going into the mountains. During the summer months it is absolutely paramount that you bring a sufficient amount of water, avoid the hottest part of the day and use appropriate hiking footwear,” HGSS said.

World.title: This Croatian Island is Closer to Italy Than to the Mainland of its Own Country
World.content:
August the 7th, 2026 – There’s a far-flung Croatian island that is closer to neighbouring Italy than to the Croatian mainland. Only a lighthouse keeper lives there, and he’d be able to arrive on Italian shores much more quickly than he’d manage to arrive in Croatia.

Far out in the Adriatic Sea sits an isolated island from which, on a clear day, both shores of the Adriatic are clearly visible. Putni kofer writes that only a lighthouse keeper lives there, and day-trippers rarely stop by.

If you look at a map of the Adriatic and study the area from Split towards the shores of Italy, you will see the islands of Brač, then Hvar, then the more distant Vis and Korčula, followed by the open-sea island of Biševo… After that long stretch there is nothing, only deep blue emptiness, and then, almost in the middle of the open sea, another “little dot”. That’s Vela Palagruža, Croatia’s most remote island of all. It’s a narrow rocky islet barely a kilometre and a half long. From here to the Italian coast, you’ll cover just 68 kilometres, while to Split it is more than 120. In other words, this piece of Croatia is almost twice as close to foreign land as to its own.

this position made the island so important

It is precisely this position that for centuries gave Palagruža an importance out of all proportion to its size. It is the only point on the Adriatic from which, in clear weather, both the Italian and Croatian coasts can be made out, so for thousands of years the island served as a landmark and resting place on the long voyages between the Italian shore and Dalmatia.

Archaeologists have been confirming this for decades. At the Salamandrija site, on the plateau right next to the lighthouse, traces of human presence going deep into prehistory have been found, and in later periods the island became a sanctuary for seafarers. Finds of pottery inscribed with the name of Diomedes, the hero from the Iliad, confirmed that Palagruža was a place where sailors paid homage to him before setting out onto the open sea.

it remained under italian control until 1860

Until 1860, Palagruža was under Italian administration. When the Austrian authorities took it over, a lookout service was established on the island, and then in 1875 the lighthouse was built. Twenty years later a meteorological station was added. Since then Palagruža has never been without people.

The stone lighthouse stands in the middle of the island at 90 metres above sea level; with its lantern it rises to about 126 metres above the sea. A steep path about 700 metres long leads up to it – a real mountaineering stretch on which donkeys once helped the lighthouse keepers. About ten years ago they were replaced by a cable winch built specifically for this purpose.

the lighthouse keeper welcomes guests… but rarely

Today only the lighthouse keeper lives on Palagruža all year round; in the past entire lighthouse families – more than ten people – used to stay there. It is he who, during the summer, welcomes the guests who manage to reach this little piece of paradise.

And for those rare visitors that means exactly what it sounds like. There is no shop, restaurant, bar or pharmacy. There is not even the possibility of quickly buying something extra. Plovput looks after the lighthouse, and through them one can arrange summer accommodation in one of the two four-bed apartments, with a minimum stay of seven days. The building stands high on the island’s ridge, so a stay is not recommended for people in poorer health. What you get in return is hard to compare with anything else on the Adriatic: silence, the sea on all sides, and the feeling that you are on a planet of your own.

the highest number of endemic plants in all of southern dalmatia

Vela Palagruža is 1,400 metres long and only 300 metres wide, with gentler slopes on one side and vertical cliffs on the other. The climate is exceptionally mild and rainfall is scarce, so vegetation is lush in spring, autumn and winter, while in summer the coast is almost bare. Among the islands of southern Dalmatia, Palagruža has the most endemic plants. Here grow the Palagruža cabbage, Palagruža centaury, Palagruža horsetail, open-sea spurge and other species you will not find elsewhere. The archipelago around the main island also includes Mala Palagruža and a series of rocks and reefs. To the south-east lies the islet of Galijula, officially the southernmost land point of Croatia.

the former home of the richest fishing grounds in the entire adriatic

The waters around Palagruža were once one of the richest fishing grounds in the Adriatic. Today lobster and white fish are mainly caught here, and the area remains primarily a fishing zone. Visits have to be arranged with the lighthouse keepers or with one of the fishermen from Komiža; organised group excursions practically do not exist. For a place of this kind, that is probably not bad news.

World.title: Hajduk Stun Žalgiris 5-2 Away in Conference League Qualifier
World.content:
Hajduk beat Žalgiris 5-2 away from home in the first leg of the third qualifying round for the Conference League. The Split side celebrated in Vilnius thanks to goals from Michele Šego (5′, 44′), Adrion Pajaziti (56′), Dalisson (73′) and Rokas Pukštas (75′). Nikola Petković (35′) and former Hajduk man Marko Capan (86′) scored for the hosts. The return leg is in a week, on August 13, kicking off at 9 pm at Poljud.

This is Hajduk’s first away win in Europe in almost six years, since a 1-0 triumph at Renova in the second qualifying round of the Europa League. The winner of the Hajduk–Žalgiris tie will face the winner of the clash between Raków and Hammarby in the next qualifying round; their first meeting finished goalless.

Two goals from Šego put Hajduk ahead at the break

Hajduk took the lead as early as the fifth minute. Pajaziti played in Marin Šotiček, who squared the ball back from the edge of the box. Šego ran onto it, and Žalgiris captain Yuri Kendysh brought him down, conceding a penalty and picking up a yellow card in the process. Šego made no mistake from the spot, sending the keeper the wrong way to make it 1-0.

Just four minutes later, Hajduk squandered a big chance to extend their lead. Goalkeeper Vincentas Šarkauskas spilled the ball, and Pukštas crossed from the right for Šotiček, who volleyed wide from close range.

Hajduk won another penalty in the 13th minute. Šotiček again broke through on the left and entered the box, where he was brought down by Deividas Šešplaukis. Šego stepped up again, but this time Šarkauskas got down to save his effort, which was heading into the left corner.

Žalgiris pulled level in the 35th minute. Bilenkyi played in Nikola Petković, who slipped away from the attention of Hajduk’s defense unnoticed. Goalkeeper Silić misjudged the flight of the ball and pushed it into the path of the Žalgiris forward, who made it 1-1.

Hajduk still went into the break in front, however. In the 44th minute, following a foul on Pukštas, Šego produced a phenomenal strike straight from a free kick from around twenty meters to make it 2-1.

Hajduk seal the win in the second half

The second half began with a forced change for Hajduk, as center-back Alec van Hoorenbeeck was forced off through injury and replaced by Ron Raci. Hajduk continued to press forward and extended their lead in the 56th minute. After a short combination from a corner, Pajaziti got into the box and finished precisely from an angle to make it 3-1.

Hajduk then settled the tie with two quick goals. The first came in the 73rd minute, when a long ball from goalkeeper Toni Silić set up Anđelo Šutalo to assist Dalisson, who finished from the right to make it 4-1. Just two minutes later, Rokas Pukštas cut out a pass from the home side’s defense, went past his marker and scored from five meters to make it 5-1.

Žalgiris did manage to pull one back before the end. Former Hajduk player Marko Capan, who had come on in the second half, scored from a free kick from around twenty meters in the 86th minute. In stoppage time, Hajduk also had a goal disallowed, as Šotiček’s effort was ruled out for offside.

World.title: Serbian Historian: “Croatians Have Reason to Celebrate, They Got What Historically Belongs to Them”
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Serbian historian Milan St. Protić has openly stated that Croatians have a reason to celebrate Operation Storm (Oluja), and that “they got what historically belongs to them” in a recent interview for N1 Serbia.

Index reports that the historian assessed that there’s no way out of the state the entire region has been in since the 1990s without confronting one’s own responsibility. According to him, in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina the same rhetoric is still used, and all sides avoid responsibility while waiting for the other to first admit their own crimes. Protić notes that Operation Storm is rightly celebrated on the Croatian side and mourned on the Serbian side, and that this pattern has been repeating for decades now, and will likely continue to do so.

“Honestly, yes, the Croatians absolutely have something to celebrate. They got the result they wanted and which, historically speaking, belongs to them. Dirty things happened on both sides – that’s just what war is. There are no clean wars or ones like we watch in partisan films. Wars are horrendous, inhuman and no one can come out of them with clean hands and a totally clear conscience,” Protić said, recalling that the insane policies of Slobodan Milošević ended catastrophically for the Serbs themselves as well.

“And now the Serbs are marking the anniversary of Operation Storm, whether that be in Belgrade or in Mrkonjić Grad, it’s all being done with false pathos and crocodile tears. That emotion is, of course, fake. They don’t care about the people who suffered. If they’d cared, they would have pursued a different policy at the time or opposed it entirely. Today’s authorities in Serbia are the direct successors of those back then; they like to justify and support everything Milošević did, so it’s clear what this is really all about,” he stated.

the price of war

Protić posed the question of who “sold the Serbs in Croatia down the river” after first stirring them up, arming them and inciting them. Asked about the 200,000 people who were left with nothing and about the fact that the case still has no legal epilogue after three decades, he replied with a counter-question: which war ends in court?

“The winner has always imposed their own legal solution. War is settled on the battlefield, not in court. You lost there, and in the meantime you also sinned. The fact that others also sinned is on their conscience and their issue to deal with. The issues of the other side cannot be a justification for the things we committed,” he emphasised.

serbia’s need to finally look in the mirror

The prominent Serbian historian believes that in Serbia, people lack examination of their own actions.

“We’ve never had the courage, wisdom or will to realistically and soberly examine the responsibility, the policy and the consequences of the 1990s. We haven’t admitted to ourselves how disastrous that policy was, and we still feel its consequences of it all today,” he said, adding that this discussion must be opened if there is a desire to move forward into the future.

“If we want to step out of this swamp, then we’ll actually have to do it. We should have done it a long time ago, but we didn’t, I’d say out of weakness, despair and a sense of defeat. Of course, people will play that card. Such a wounded people as we became then is easy to manipulate,” he said. That manipulation, he added, continues. “When the Serbs beat their chests and swear that Kosovo will ‘forever’ be Serbian, deep down they know the truth. When they forge Serbian history, whether to deny Serbdom or to glorify it, they do it exclusively in their own interests,” Protić noted.

the end of yugoslavia and the birth of mature nation states

“It was clear that the Yugoslav peoples no longer wanted to live together. No one can force anyone to stay where they do not want to be. Why did our former brothers want to leave Yugoslavia? That is a question both for them and for historians. The moment someone decided to prevent that by war, the gates of hell opened,” Protić described. According to him, the solution could have been a peaceful and friendly separation. For the situation to be resolved, he believes, every nation must examine itself rather than constantly looking at what the other side did wrong.

“One must not live in the conviction that everything done in our name was ‘right’ and ‘clean’, while everything foreign was ‘dirty’ and ‘evil’. That is proof that none of these nations has matured and that they still feed on that kind of infantilism which often brings unimaginable horrors,” he said. He observed that the same rhetoric and refusal to look at the other side is used in Croatia, Bosnia and Serbia, only with different signs.

“I try my best to simply avoid talking about others; someone of their own should tell them that. That’s why I appeal that Serbs take a long, hard look in the mirror. A person, and a nation, confronts their own responsibility independently of the other. That confrontation is not mutually conditioned. Whenever it is conditioned, both on their side and on ours, it is actually just an excuse to avoid responsibility,” he said.

belgrade was the one to sell its own people down the river

Protić also stated that the expelled people from Knin served the Belgrade authorities only for political score-settling and that there was no real desire to help them. “Belgrade rejected everything that could have led to a compromise – both Rašković’s attempt with Boljkovac, and the Z4 Plan, and the opinion of the Badinter Commission. In the end they left those people high and dry, unprotected, to suffer such a miserable fate,” he said. He noted that even after 30 years there is money for EXPO, Belgrade Waterfront and various investments, but none for the refugees. He also recalled that everything possible was done to conceal their arrival in Serbia. “How can one justify that in such a large Republic of Serbian Krajina the Croatian army swept everything away in four days?” he asked.

even the “mourning” is disrespectful in serbia

Regarding the commemorations for Operation Storm in Mrkonjić Grad, Protić wondered about the appropriateness of such events.

“Is that how one mourns for any sort of victims? Heavy drinking before and after? Is that how it’s done? Or do you raise a monument to those who did unfortunately suffer, hold a memorial service and go home to grieve? What kind of paganism is this? Do Serbs do it this way?” he asked, before assessing that it is all simply abuse and that absolutely nothing of it is remotely sincere.

“They really don’t care about those who suffered. They don’t care how many young men died under their command in Republika Srpska… They don’t give a damn about those unfortunate refugees from Croatia, except for those who sided with them in order to achieve some ridiculous interests in Serbia,” he said.

World.title: Danube Recedes, Shipping Stopped: “Water Level Has Never Been This Low”
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – The Danube has receded so much that shipping has had to be stopped, with experts claiming that the river’s water level has never been this low.

An extremely low water level on the Danube has seriously hindered navigation near Vukovar in recent days. Some ships can no longer continue their journey, cargo vessels are stranded, and Croatia’s largest river port has had almost no traffic for ten days. Index reports that the water level of the Danube near Vukovar has dropped to minus 60 centimetres. In some sections of the fairway the river is only about 1.2 metres deep, forcing ships to reduce their cargo or stop sailing altogether.

The low water has exposed sandbanks, rocks and other underwater obstacles that are normally hidden at usual river levels. “We’ve now got to watch out for all the sandbanks, for the rocks – for all the underwater obstacles that until now were under water and inaccessible. Now, unfortunately, we keep having problems with them,” said Saša Piljaš, president of the Dunav Vukovar Sport Fishing Association, as reported by HRT.

two cargo vessels are stranded not far from erdut

The problems first affected smaller boats and are now making navigation difficult even for the largest vessels. “The fairway should be at least two metres deep for it to be worthwhile for shippers to transport cargo. Anything below that means sailing at reduced capacity, so profitability becomes questionable,” said Borna Čerina, head of the Navigation Safety Service at the Vukovar Port Authority. A cruise ship has been moored in Vukovar for a week, while two cargo ships are stranded near Erdut.

“In the fairway near the village of Erdut we have two cargo ships that ran aground a few days ago and are still sitting there. They will either have to lighten their load or wait for the water level to rise,” Čerina said.

no navigation at the port of vukovar for ten days

The consequences of the low water level are also being felt by the Port of Vukovar. In recent weeks shippers were still arriving with almost half the usual cargo, but even that traffic has now stopped.

“Over the last ten days we’ve had no navigability at all. All the barges are anchored either in their ports or in certain areas, waiting for a better draught,” said Marijan Kuprešak, director of the Port of Vukovar. If the water level does not rise soon, the port could lose a large part of its contracted traffic. “Partners who signed contracts with us were supposed to move around 200,000 tonnes of goods through the Port of Vukovar over the next three months – a significant tonnage for the port and significant revenue. It is now questionable whether the partners will organise some other form of transport, by cargo or by truck,” Kuprešak emphasised.

“I’ve never seen anything like this”

Retired port captain Ivan Barović, who worked on the Danube for more than 20 years, said he had never experienced a situation like this before. “There have been ice blockages around Dalj, and there have been high water levels when we had flooding at this spot. But the water level has never been this low,” Barović said.

The Danube is navigable almost all year round, and interruptions until now have mostly been caused by ice or floods. Such a prolonged suspension of navigation near Vukovar, according to Barović, has not been recorded before. “Captains have to use all their knowledge to bring ships safely into port. It’s another matter how profitable it is to load a ship to only 50 percent of its draught so it can pass certain sections,” he said. He warned that conditions like these may not remain an isolated case.

“I’m afraid we can’t be too optimistic, but we have to take certain steps. This is a situation where we have drought here and floods in some other area,” he stressed. The lowest water level ever measured on the Danube closr to Vukovar was recorded about a hundred years ago and stood at minus 110 centimetres.

World.title: Will Croatia Have Enough Electricity and Water?
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Prolonged drought, the absence of heavier rainfall and high temperatures have seriously affected Croatian rivers, springs and pumping stations. Will Croatia actually have enough electricity and water?

As Domagoj Puljizovic reports for Poslovni, the Danube and Drava have dropped to record low levels, inflows on the coast and islands have decreased significantly, and electricity production in hydropower plants has weakened.

Despite the challenges, the director-general of Croatian Waters (Hrvatske vode), Zoran Đuroković, says that the water supply for the population is not currently under threat. The water level of the Sava has fallen to –298 cm, while historical minima have been broken on the Danube and Drava. Due to unfavourable hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava, the Krško Nuclear Power Plant (NEK) will gradually reduce reactor power to 80 percent during the night of 6 August.

This is a planned measure to ensure that the average daily temperature of the Sava does not exceed 28 °C and that the average daily temperature rise remains within three degrees. NEK has been operating continuously for 280 days since its overhaul in November 2025; if conditions worsen, power will be reduced further. The last time NEK operated at reduced power because of Sava temperature and flow was in 2003.

recovery won’t happen quickly

“There is no doubt that Croatia will have enough electricity,” Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said on Tuesday, adding that there is “no threat whatsoever” regarding NEK. Turning back to water supply:

“The situation is quite serious. This is already a prolonged low-water period,” Đuroković told HRT, warning that a rapid recovery cannot be expected. The Danube at Batina has fallen to –144 cm, surpassing the minimum recorded as far back as 1909. A historically low level has also been measured on the Drava, where the previous record of –172 cm has been exceeded with a drop to –192 cm. High water temperatures are also a problem.

The situation is even more sensitive on the coast, islands and karst areas. The long period without rain has reduced the yield of springs and pumping stations, prompting many water utilities to call on citizens and businesses to use water rationally.

“Inflows there are already greatly reduced, so capacities are being cut,” Đuroković said. In some areas pressure drops in the network are being recorded, but water supply remains stable. Conservation measures are being introduced and the use of water for irrigation, filling swimming pools and other non-essential purposes is being restricted, but the basic needs of the population are not currently threatened.

In Lika the situation is relatively stable, although the yield of some springs has decreased, particularly in the Brinje area. Đuroković warned that the disappearance of the snow cover has eliminated an important natural water-storage source for Lika watercourses.

Continental Croatia is currently in a more favourable position thanks to groundwater and large river systems. “There will be no shortages on the continent. The situation is quite good,” he said. Zagreb’s Water Supply and Sewerage company (ViO) also says there is no cause for concern, stating that water extraction in the city area is proceeding without difficulty.

“In the City of Zagreb, water extraction is taking place smoothly and there are currently no indications of possible disruptions in water supply,” ViO emphasised. The city company stresses that it continuously invests in the new network and maintenance of existing infrastructure and is implementing an action plan to reduce water losses, which last year amounted to 55 percent. They add that their water inspection service checks cases of illegal connections, and citizens can report suspicions of unauthorised water use to vodno.redarstvo@zgh.hr.

Croatian Waters has intensified monitoring and sent water-warden services into the field. Special attention is focused on smaller watercourses, which become sensitive to pollution due to low flow and high temperatures.

“Any inflow of pollution into these small rivers can cause ecological incidents,” Đuroković warned, calling on cities, municipal companies and economic entities to carefully treat wastewater. Recovery of water levels is not expected in the next five to seven days. The drought is already affecting hydropower plants, especially those on the Drava, where production has been reduced due to weaker inflows.

Croatian Waters and HEP are coordinating the use of available water so as not to endanger the biological minimum in the rivers. In Istria the key role is played by the Butoniga reservoir, which is currently sufficiently full. Larger restrictions are not expected there, but citizens are still being urged to use water rationally.

no reductions… for now, anyway

Istrian Water Supply and Sewerage Buzet has warned users in the areas of Vižinada, Kaštelir-Labinci, Višnjan, Tinjan and parts of Poreč and Kanfanar to immediately limit irrigation of green areas and washing of yards, and that if consumption is not reduced the first degree of restriction could be introduced. Vodovod Pula-Labin, which supplies the Pula and Labin areas and part of central Istria, says that water supply is regular and that reductions are not currently planned.

HEP: We’ll secure electricity from our own sources and by purchasing

In the event of a halt in production from the Krško Nuclear Power Plant (NEK), Hrvatska elektroprivreda (HEP) would secure the necessary quantities of electricity through production from its own available generation sources and by purchasing the remaining quantities on the wholesale market, HEP told Hina on Wednesday.

“In the event of a halt in production from NE Krško, HEP would secure the necessary quantities of electricity by engaging production from other available own generation sources and by purchasing the remaining quantities of electricity on the wholesale market,” HEP stated.

The Ministry of Economy, responsible for energy, says that the Croatian and Slovenian governments are taking all necessary activities to ensure that the Krško Nuclear Power Plant continues to operate stably and safely even under conditions of high Sava River temperatures.

“We are in constant communication with the Slovenian side and jointly monitoring the development of the situation, with the aim of preserving the security of electricity production and supply,” the ministry told Hina. NEK reported on Wednesday that due to the continuation of exceptional hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava, it will begin operating at 80 percent reactor power during the night of Thursday, 6 August 2026, and will announce a return to full power when conditions allow.

“Due to the continuation of exceptional hydrological and meteorological conditions on the Sava River, NEK will, as announced, begin a gradual reduction of reactor power during the night of Thursday, 6 August 2026. In the first step, power will be reduced to 80 percent,” NEK reported on Wednesday.

This is a planned and controlled temporary measure necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Environmental Consent (OVS), according to which the daily average temperature of the Sava River at the point of complete mixing downstream of the Brežice Hydropower Plant must not exceed 28 degrees Celsius, and the average daily temperature rise must not be greater than three degrees.

World.title: Đurđenovac: The Small Croatian Town That Was Once a European Industrial Giant
World.content:
August the 6th, 2026 – Đurđenovac is a small, overlooked Croatian town that not only used to have almost 600 kilometres of railway tracks, but was once a European industrial giant.

Situated far from anywhere that often ever gets a mention, Đurđenovac isn’t somewhere splashed across the glossy pages of travel mags. Turning the pages of the history book back, however, we’ll see that it was once booming. It actually grew alongside a sawmill and a tannin factory, gained workers’ colonies, schools and a kindergarten, and became the first electrified place in all of Slavonia.

If you walk through Đurđenovac today, Putni kofer reveals that you’ll mostly hear little else other than birdsong and the occasional passing car. About a hundred years ago, however, the sounds there were completely different. Through the dense old forests around the town, locomotives rumbled day and night, hauling logs to a factory that was one of the strongest industrial hearts of this part of Europe. According to publicly available data from the Croatian Technical Encyclopaedia, in 1929 the factory in Đurđenovac operated a narrow-gauge forest railway an astonishing 582 kilometres long. To put that in perspective, it is roughly the same as the straight-line distance from Zagreb to Sarajevo and back. Along that network ran a whole small army of trains, and the local company’s rolling stock numbered 61 locomotives and as many as 2,800 wagons.

it all began with a businessman from austria…

To understand all this better, we have to go back to the distant year of 1866, when the Viennese entrepreneur Josip Pfeiffer, after reaching an agreement with the landowner Ladislav Pejačević on the exploitation of the forests, built a steam sawmill in Đurđenovac. Over several decades and several changes of ownership, a tannin factory (a substance essential for leather processing) was added to the sawmill in 1889. From 1895 the company operated as Neuschloß’s Našice Tannin Factory and Steam Sawmill, later known simply as Našička.

As the factory eventually grew, so did the town around it. Đurđenovac developed into a purpose-built industrial town with workers’ colonies, schools, a post office, a kindergarten and a workers’ club. It was so far ahead of its time that it became the first electrified place in Slavonia. In as early as 1891, the factory received electric lighting, and by 1917, electricity had reached every apartment in the town.

Hundreds of kilometres of track led deep into Papuk and Krndija

All of this needed to be fed with wood, almost constantly, and in enormous quantities. That’s why, in parallel with the factory, a narrow-gauge railway developed that pushed out from Đurđenovac deep into the surrounding forests of Papuk, Krndija and beyond. The little trains climbed the slopes, hauled logs to the sawmill and tannin works, and then returned empty for a new load. Year after year the network was extended until by 1929 it had grown to the aforementioned 582 kilometres.

At that time the company was part of a holding with its headquarters in Geneva, with branches in Romania, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Austria, and offices in Belgrade, Sombor, Rijeka, Zurich and Milan. In its best days, up to the Second World War, more than 10,000 people worked for the firm as a whole, of whom around 1,400 were in Đurđenovac itself. For a Slavonia town, those numbers sound almost unreal today.

an entire railway system simply vanished…

“Everything that grows must one day stop,” says an old folk saying. In the middle of the twentieth century, trucks increasingly took over the transport of wood from the forests; they were faster and cheaper than tracks that needed constant maintenance. Forest railways thus gradually lost their purpose, and those in and around Đurđenovac were dismantled during the 1960s. Rails and sleepers were pulled out of the ground, and many of the old alignments were turned into the roads we drive on today, often without realising that a locomotive once ran there.

After the Second World War the company operated under various names, first as the Tannin Factory and Steam Sawmill, then as DIP, and finally as DIK Đurđenovac. It ran into business difficulties at the beginning of the 1990s, and bankruptcy was declared back in 1994. DIK ceased operations in 2007, although some successors continued wood processing in parts of the former facilities. The cultural-historical complex of Đurđenovac is today protected and entered in the Register of Cultural Goods of the Republic of Croatia.

World.title: Veteran Recalls the Moment Operation Storm Began
World.content:
August the 5th, 2026 – On the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, Croatian veteran Ivan Mikulić recalls the moments when he and his fellow soldiers realised that a major operation was about to begin – even before they knew its name.

Mikulić, a member of the 3rd Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade, spoke about the days that changed the course of the war and the emotions surrounding Croatia’s advance toward Knin. At the time, soldiers on the ground had not been officially told that Operation Storm was beginning, but many sensed that something extremely significant was approaching.

“Our unit was in Donji Kazanci, on the Livno–Grahovo route. On August the 3rd, we were moved to Pržine, near Grahovo, to a peat factory. At that point, we concluded that an operation could begin in the morning, even though we knew nothing about Storm. But as soon as we were moved there, we knew we were going forward in the morning,” Mikulić recalled.

When artillery fire began around 05:00 on August the 4th, the uncertainty entirely disappeared. “There was a sense of anxiety and excitement among the soldiers. People had already heard that the operation was definitely starting. When the artillery barrage began, there was an explosion of sheer joy. Some even raised a toast,” he said.

The long Road to Knin

Mikulić also remembers the moment his unit entered Knin and moved toward the city’s famous fortress. The soldiers did not immediately enter the fortress area, as security positions had already been established ahead of them and some units encountered delays along the way. “We reached the fortress and stopped there. We sat down on the wall,” he recalled.

Soon, local residents began approaching the soldiers and offering them refreshments.

“The beer had already arrived, Karlovačko had already reached the fortress. However, it was no longer possible to actually enter the fortress,” Mikulić said. At that moment, the Croatian flag had not yet been raised on the fortress, but the approach had already been secured.

A Victory Marked by Sacrifice

Despite the intense heat and the expectation of heavy fighting, the battle in Knin did not unfold as many soldiers had anticipated.

“We expected a fight, but there wasn’t one because they had all fled. It was complete and utter chaos. There were civilians hanging around in the city itself as well, but overall everything went well,” Mikulić said. However, victory came with a heavy price. He noted that the 4th Guards Brigade lost four soldiers in Knin itself.

memories that will remain forever

Over three decades later, Mikulić says the memories of those days remain vivid and clear.

During the war, he served on many fronts, from Kruševo and Zadar to Dubrovnik and Mostar. “I lost many friends, and that cannot be forgotten. It really wasn’t that long ago,” he said. As Croatia remembers Operation Storm, stories from veterans like Mikulić serve as a reminder that behind the historic images of victory were the experiences, sacrifices, and personal memories of the people who lived through those defining moments.

World.title: Rait Kallus: Is Estonia planning future traffic based on the past?
World.content:
If autonomous vehicles become widespread at the pace currently forecast, today's decisions in city planning may prove inadequate within just a few decades, writes Rait Kallus.

The world is on the brink of the biggest transformation in transportation since the invention of the internal combustion engine. Self-driving cars are no longer the stuff of science fiction but a rapidly advancing technology whose impact on cities may be greater than we can currently imagine.

According to forecasts generated by various artificial intelligence models and transportation analyses, the widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could increase traffic volumes on city streets by roughly 30 to 50 percent. If that scenario materializes, a four-lane road may no longer be sufficient in the future, with capacity needing to expand to the equivalent of six lanes. Likewise, a major highway that now has three lanes in each direction may eventually require five lanes in each direction.

The reasons are straightforward. A self-driving car no longer has to wait in a parking lot or driveway. It can drive to pick up its owner, take the children to school, then head to pick up another family member or travel on its own to its next assignment. Every such empty trip adds more vehicle miles traveled. Even if the total number of cars does not increase significantly, the burden on city streets could grow substantially.

The largest share of public transit users consists of people who rely on it out of necessity rather than preference, such as young people who do not yet have a driver's license. This group stands to benefit the most from autonomous vehicles, since they would be able to travel independently and safely without a license. It is reasonable to assume that a large share of them — estimated at more than 70 percent — would choose personal transportation over public transit under those circumstances.

Another major user group consists of older adults, for whom convenient door-to-door travel is the highest priority. If autonomous transportation becomes significantly cheaper than taxi service, a substantial share of this group as well — estimated at 50 to 60 percent — could prefer self-driving vehicles to conventional public transit.

If these developments occur, public transit in Estonia could lose more than half of its current ridership. That would fundamentally alter the traffic models and assumptions on which cities and transportation infrastructure are currently planned.

Unfortunately, urban planning in Estonia is often moving in the opposite direction. Instead of preparing for future traffic volumes, many places are reducing the capacity available for automobile traffic. If autonomous vehicles become widespread at the pace currently forecast, today's decisions could prove inadequate within just a few decades.

If traffic volumes increase to the extent projected by multiple forecasts, rebuilding individual intersections or optimizing traffic signal timing will no longer be enough.

Self-driving Tesla vehicle. Source: ERR

Tallinn needs strong transportation arteries — fast primary connections that function like the arteries of the human body. The heart could not supply the body if its arteries were replaced with veins, and the same principle applies to urban traffic. If the main transportation corridors become slow, fragmented or too limited in capacity, the city itself begins to suffer and decline.

Whether these transportation arteries follow existing major roads, pass through neighborhoods or are built partly along new routes is ultimately a matter of planning. What matters is that they provide enough capacity to meet future transportation needs.

At the same time, not every mode of transportation has to share the same street space. Pedestrians, cyclists and green spaces also need uninterrupted networks of their own, which do not have to run alongside roadways. When every mode of transportation is given space suited to its purpose, mobility, safety and the overall quality of the urban environment all improve simultaneously.

Urban planning and street network design are investments that last at least half a century. New buildings are designed with a 50-year service life, but they often remain in use much longer. The same is true of streets, intersections, bridges and the urban environment as a whole. That means every decision made today will shape how people move around cities well into the middle of the next century.

If we design cities around yesterday's traffic model, we may discover that the infrastructure we build no longer meets society's actual needs. The purpose of urban planning is not to react to change after the fact, but to anticipate it.

World.title: Mia Mireia Uusorg takes U20 World Athletics Championships silver
World.content:
Uusorg scored 5,961 points across the seven events: 100-meter hurdles, high jump, shot put, 200-meter sprint, long jump, javelin throw, 800 meters.

This tally was just 138 points short of her U20 PB, also a domestic record, placing her second behind Finland's Enni Virjonen (6,214 points) in Oregon. Switzerland's Anna Pfister took bronze.

"The emotions are still at their peak! I was afraid after the high jump that everything was lost, but I made a comeback," Uusorg said of her performance. "I came to the competitions with expectations and hopes that I would do all my things. It didn't go as planned, but in the end all the cards played in my favor."

On day one, Uusorg set a 100-meter hurdles PB of 13.71, put in a high jump of 1.63, improved her personal best in the shot put to 11.33, and ran the 200 meters in 24.27.

On day two she clocked 6.23 in the long jump, threw the javelin 45.30, and improved her PB in the 800 meters to a time of 2:13.90, clinching silver.

"I'm definitely pleased with the shot put. I've struggled with it a lot in various multi-events that I've done before. The high jump was definitely below any expectations, but sometimes it's like that. That's how multi-events are. I'm also extremely pleased with the 800-meter run. Running a personal best in these conditions was the biggest success," Uusorg added.

From the other Estonian competitors, Annika Põlluaas finished 21st with a total of 4,616 points after failing to post a score in the long jump.

In the boys' categories, Henri Apri advanced to the pole vault final, having cleared his qualifying height of 5.25 on his third attempt. Martin Plak finished 17th with a vault of 4.95.

The Estonian foursome of Tristan Konso, Pia Lauren Matsalu, Dmitri Petrogradov, and Miia Ott failed to make the mixed relay finals, finishing 18th in the heats with a time of 43.69.

Petrogradov had set a new U20 domestic 100-meter record earlier in the meeting.

The U20 World Athletics Championships run to Sunday.

World.title: Entomologist: several new insect species reach Estonia annually
World.content:
University of Tartu entomologist Mati Martin says that the numbers of lice and fleas have decreased significantly, but every year several new insect species arrive in Estonia. The sea buckthorn fruit fly, for example, has made growing sea buckthorn pointless in many places.

"Once we carried out a small study — it was more than ten years ago — and at that time we found that about 15,000 insect species could be identified in Estonia. Looking at studies done in neighboring countries, one could assume that Estonia has 24,000 insect species or even more," Martin said.

The abundance of human parasites such as lice and fleas has decreased considerably. "With the expansion of trade, insects living on food products move very often and very quickly together with goods," Martin noted. "Right now it is very fashionable to install stone paving around houses and on many courtyards. But stone paving is a very good habitat for soil‑dwelling ants, which are tiny black ants. There have been enormous numbers of them lately."

Mati Martin. Source: ERR

Martin has noticed that because lawns are mowed very frequently nowadays, and when dandelions start growing there, for some reason ants like them very much. "I did research in my own garden, and of ten dandelions growing in the lawn, nine had ant nests in the soil around them," Martin said.

There are also large differences between the insect communities of western and eastern Estonia. "Insects have divided up the vegetation period — from early spring until almost the arrival of snow, some insect species are active, and some species are active even under the snow."

"Insect allergies are a serious problem; Estonia has even had fatal cases, and everything happens quite quickly," the insect scientist pointed out.

"Blackflies bite very painfully; they last throughout the summer, and even in September one can still fall victim to them," Martin noted.

Insects develop in cycles. Three to four years is a normal cycle; in the fifth, sixth and seventh years, for some reason, their numbers become very high and then we see them everywhere. "If they develop according to a normal cycle, we do not see them much," Martin explained, referring to why ladybirds are scarce this year. "For example, right now there are relatively many webbing moths. Even under normal conditions, insect abundance fluctuates from year to year."

Every year, according to Martin, several new insect species arrive in Estonia. "The sea buckthorn fruit fly is one of the latest to reach us, and it eats sea buckthorn berries with great appetite. In some places, growing sea buckthorn has already become pointless," the scientist said.

World.title: Estonian police and ISS say most health data queries are lawful
World.content:
An internal review by the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) and the Internal Security Service (ISS) found that most health data queries made by officials were justified, but the thousands of checks raise concerns from attorney-at-law Carri Ginter about eroding trust between patients and doctors.

Interior Minister Igor Taro instructed the heads of the PPA and ISS in early June to review all queries their officials made about people's health data.

"Queries are made because of work-related needs," Taro said about the main results of the review.

ISS Director Margo Palloson. Source: ERR

ISS Director General Margo Palloson said the ISS made health data queries about roughly 13,000 people over 13 months. The review confirmed that the queries were made on a legal basis and for duties assigned to the ISS by law. 80 percent of the queries were related to security and background checks, including checks on ISS officials, candidates and service providers. 20 percent were made as part of intelligence gathering and criminal proceedings.

2 percent of all queries were incorrectly labeled but were lawful and justified in substance. One violation was found in which an official made queries about a close relative, and supervisory proceedings were launched.

Police reviewed all health data queries made this year. The review covered queries made to The Health and Welfare Information Systems Centre (TEHIK), the Health Insurance Fund's information system via X-Road, and directly to healthcare institutions, totaling 2,139. The review confirmed that all queries were related to police duties or proceedings and that a technical trace exists for each query. The vast majority were lawful and justified. There were 135 cases that were not assessed as correct or lawful or that require further review.

Kristi Mäe and Carri Ginter. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

PPA Deputy Director General Kristi Mäe said police must always weigh any infringement of people's fundamental rights, and the reliability of sensitive data is especially important.

The PPA's most serious critical finding concerned the use of prescription data — retrieving information through X‑Road about purchased medication to determine a person's possible location. Using prescription data for searches in this way is not seen as proportionate, and the PPA instructed investigators to immediately stop the practice.

Minister Taro said oversight of state databases is reliable and citizens' information is secure. He said legislation on data protection needs updating, but the audit results from the PPA and ISS show that agencies' daily internal controls work effectively.

"Queries are not made only because of crime. For example, when the ISS makes queries, they carry the responsibility of conducting background checks on everyone who deals with state secrets or applies for a state secrets permit. There are also certain sensitive positions, such as structures of vital service providers that handle sensitive information. For example, the Defense Forces are a major requester because we must know that these people do not have drug addictions," Taro said.

Eesti 200 general assembly on March 29, 2026. Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Attorney-at-law Carri Ginter said officials' overly free access to sensitive data undermines trust between doctors and patients and urgently requires a stricter legal framework and judicial oversight.

"When it comes to health data, the most important thing is that I must be able to tell my doctor the truth. I must be able to trust that information with my doctor without police getting it through email," Ginter said. "The functioning of internal audits has been confirmed, which is great. But what we learned is that a thousand people a month are queried, and I refuse to believe that Estonia has a thousand potential criminals whose health data must be checked monthly — meaning 13,000 queries. It comes to about a thousand queries a month. This system clearly needs clearer regulation and much stricter oversight."

World.title: Katarina Papp: Donating food should become standard practice
World.content:
It is important to prevent edible food from ending up as waste simply because its further use was not properly planned or because no suitable partner was available at the necessary moment, Katarina Papp writes.

Estonians have long been smart consumers and throwing away edible food was simply unthinkable just a few decades ago. As a consumer society, however, we have reached a point where everything is available everywhere and in abundance. We have more choices than we need and that has led to a growing problem: edible food is ending up in the trash.

Around 167,000 metric tons of food waste are generated in Estonia each year. About half of that — more than 80,000 metric tons — is food loss, meaning food that was still fit for human consumption. That amount would have been enough to meet the annual food needs of roughly 100,000 people.

Food loss occurs throughout the food supply chain, from primary production and the food industry to wholesale and retail trade, food service and households. In addition to its economic costs, food loss also has significant environmental impacts. Producing food requires land, water, energy and human labor. When edible food becomes waste, all of the resources used to produce it are wasted as well.

At the same time, there are people in Estonia who struggle to put food on the table every day. The number of people in need of food assistance has not gone away, yet the Estonian Food Bank's warehouses are often empty.

Unfortunately, these two problems — food waste and access to food — exist side by side in Estonia.

Food may be left over even with good planning

Companies put considerable effort into planning production, inventory and food preparation as accurately as possible. No business wastes food intentionally — it simply would not make economic sense. At the same time, it is impossible to eliminate surplus food entirely. When producers, retailers, caterers or event organizers plan quantities, they have to account for the possibility that actual consumption will differ from forecasts, and no business wants to run out of food that people need.

For example, organizers of last year's Song and Dance Celebration could not risk having any choir or dance group go without soup. Even with highly experienced caterers and careful planning, it is difficult to estimate quantities precisely for an event of that scale, and some food was left over.

Because the possibility of donating surplus food had been anticipated in advance and the entire process had been planned, the donation effort went smoothly. A total of 8,700 liters of leftover soup was distributed to people in need through various organizations. Careful event planning is certainly important, but it is equally important to have a plan for what happens when edible food is left over.

Estonia has the necessary capacity for food redistribution

Estonia has effective systems in place for rescuing and redistributing edible food. Both nationwide and community-based initiatives have emerged to help reduce food loss and ensure that surplus food reaches people who can use it.

The Estonian Food Bank is the country's longest-running and largest food redistribution organization. Its mission is to reduce food loss while helping people who struggle to afford enough food. Every week, food assistance reaches more than 15,000 people through the Food Bank's network. In 2025, the Estonian Food Bank distributed approximately 4 million kilograms of edible food to people in need.

Volunteer helping in food distribution at Estonia's Food Bank. Source: Katrin Press/Food Bank

In addition to the Estonian Food Bank, a number of community-based initiatives across the country help reduce food waste and make food sharing a normal part of everyday community life. For example, community food cabinets (such as Foodsharing and Toiduringlus), maintained by local volunteers, operate in many parts of Estonia. People can leave food they are unable to use, and anyone who wants it is free to take it. Other initiatives, such as Fudloop, allow people to purchase food rescued from stores and wholesale warehouses for a nominal fee. At daycare centers, parents and staff can also take home leftover edible food from food cabinets at the end of the day.

The work of all organizations involved in food redistribution is important not only because they reduce food loss, but also because they help reinforce the understanding that edible food belongs on people's tables — not in the trash.

Food donation needs to be systematic

The Ministry of Climate has circulated for interagency review a bill to amend the Waste Act with the aim of reducing food loss and increasing the donation and redistribution of edible food. Under the proposal, by 2030 food waste must be reduced by at least 10 percent in the food industry and by at least 30 percent in retail, food service and households, compared with the average for 2021–2023.

The bill does not require companies to donate food. Instead, it seeks to establish a system in which businesses have a clear plan for ensuring that edible food reaches people when surplus remains despite careful planning.

The Food Bank supports the proposal and considers one of its most important changes to be the requirement that larger retail and food manufacturing companies disclose on their websites what share of the edible food they write off is donated. This will make it possible to assess whether a company has organized its operations so that as much edible food as possible reaches people rather than becoming waste. It will also help reduce the risk of greenwashing — that is, companies highlighting partnerships with food redistribution organizations even though the actual share of donated food from their total surplus is very small or nonexistent.

Another important change is the requirement that larger retailers and food producers offer to enter into a cooperation agreement with the Food Bank or another food redistribution organization. Such an agreement does not obligate companies to donate all surplus food. Instead, it helps them establish an effective system for situations in which edible food is left over.

At present, food donation often depends on whether a company has an employee who considers it important and takes the initiative. It is possible that a company's management is not even aware that donations are taking place or to what extent. This approach is neither sustainable nor conducive to organizing food rescue in a systematic way.

A cooperation agreement helps establish how the surplus food donation process will work: who is responsible, when and how the food will be transferred and what food handling requirements must be met. This gives both the donating company and the receiving organization confidence that the entire process has been carefully planned.

It is important to prevent edible food from ending up as waste simply because its further use was not properly planned or because no suitable partner was available at the necessary moment.

For companies, it is important that their food donation partner be a trustworthy organization capable of accepting food quickly, maintaining the required cold chain and distributing it to people in need.

Responsibility shared by entire food supply chain

According to a 2020 study by the Stockholm Environment Institute's Tallinn Center (SEI Tallinn), more than half of all food loss occurs in households. This shows that raising public awareness about how to plan food purchases more effectively and make better use of leftovers is essential to reducing waste. The national government and local governments have gradually been working to increase that awareness.

Although households account for a large share of food loss, that is no reason to overlook the rest of the food supply chain. Reducing food loss is not the responsibility of any one group — every link in the chain must do what it can. For businesses, that primarily means improving planning, tracking food loss and establishing systems for redistributing edible surplus food.

Carts filled with bags of food aid at the Food Bank. Source: Anna Pavlenko/Raadio 4

Many companies in Estonia's food manufacturing, wholesale, retail and food service sectors have already made food donation and redistribution a routine part of their operations. However, there are still businesses where edible food continues to end up as waste. The proposed legislative changes are intended primarily to help those companies that have not yet adopted a systematic approach to reducing food loss.

Neither the Food Bank nor other food redistribution organizations want to reduce companies' revenue or impose unreasonable obligations on them. Instead, we want to follow the food waste hierarchy, under which food that can no longer be sold but is still safe for human consumption should first be directed to people, then to animal feed and only as a last resort to biogas production or composting.

Edible food is not waste. Estonia has the people, expertise and infrastructure needed to reduce food loss and ensure that edible food is consumed rather than discarded. The goal of the proposed amendments to the Waste Act is to help make surplus food donation a standard practice throughout Estonia.
