World.title: Thai teen kills 8 in rampage at home and school before shooting himself
World.content:
SCHOOL VIOLENCE. A student reacts with a relative after being evacuated from Debsirin Nonthaburi School, following a shooting incident at the school, in Bang Kruai district in Nonthaburi province on the outskirts of Bangkok, Thailand, August 7, 2026.

(2nd UPDATE) Police say the shooter, who was 14 years old, fired at least 26 bullets, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds. The gun had belonged to his grandfather.

BANG KRUAI, Thailand – A Thai teenager killed at least six people and himself at a school outside Bangkok on Friday after fatally shooting his grandparents, police said, in the Southeast Asian nation’s worst mass killing since 2022.

Students streamed out of the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, on the capital’s northwestern outskirts, as the wounded were loaded on to ambulances and teachers hugged each other and cried. In photos circulated by emergency workers, one person is seen lying down on a stretcher outside an ambulance, while another is attended to by a medic.

Police said the shooter, who was 14 years old, fired at least 26 bullets, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds. The gun had belonged to his grandfather, police said.

One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought there were firecrackers going off or someone banging an object.

“I didn’t think it was a gun at first,” he said. “There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again.”

Lieutenant Colonel Trirong Phophan, a spokesman for the National Police, told Reuters the suspected shooter was among the seven people killed. Fifteen people were injured, he added.

Second school shooting

Education Minister Prasert Jantararuangtong told Reuters that both teachers and students were among those reported dead. Police identified the perpetrator as a student.

It is the second school shooting in Thailand this year after a teacher died and a student was injured in the south of the country in February.

Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, described arriving as the shooting was ongoing and his team treated students with injuries in the back, chest and arms. They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds in her chest and arm.

“We gave CPR for about 30 minutes and rushed her to the hospital as we could not get her heart rate up, but we tried our best,” he said.

In the 2025 academic year, the school had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers, according to district authorities.

Deputy Education Minister Akkharanan Kannakittinan said in a statement he was coordinating to provide assistance.

History of shootings

Gun ownership and gun violence are not uncommon in Thailand, which has seen a series of deadly shootings in the past six years, with children among the victims.

Thailand’s worst mass killing by a single perpetrator in its recent history took place in 2022, when a former policeman ran amok in a three-hour gun-and-knife attack in the northeast that killed 36 people including 22 children stabbed as they slept at a daycare centre.

A gunman killed five people including security guards and a vendor at a Bangkok market in July 2025 before turning the gun on himself, while a teacher died in the southern city of Hat Yai in February this year when a shooter opened fire at a school where she worked.

In 2020, a soldier killed 29 people in a shooting rampage in Nakhon Ratchasima. And in 2023, a 14-year-old used a modified handgun to kill two people and wound five others at a luxury Bangkok shopping centre.

After the 2023 shooting, Anutin, who was then serving as interior minister, ordered a raft of gun control measures, including a short-term ban on new licenses, import restrictions, and banning of people under 20 years from shooting ranges.

Longer-term measures also included a medical certificate assessing the mental health and psychological condition of gun owners as well as a specified validity period for some gun licenses.

Thailand had an estimated 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, equating to around 15 guns per 100 residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey. – Rappler.com

World.title: Loren Legarda, Leandro Leviste out of the country – immigration bureau
World.content:
WINNER. Businessman Leandro Leviste is proclaimed winner of the congressional race in Batangas 1st District on May 13, 2025.

Legarda and Leviste left the country days after the Ombudsman announced the plunder and graft complaints against them

MANILA, Philippines – The Bureau of Immigration confirmed on Friday, August 7, that Senator Loren Legarda and her son Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste have left the country on August 2, days after the Office of the Ombudsman announced the plunder and graft complaints against them.

“The office confirms the departure of [Senator] Loren Legarda and [Representative] Leandro Leviste in separate flights last August 2. Both had no derogatory records at the time of departure,” BI spokesperson Dana Sandoval told Rappler.

On July 31, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla announced that plunder and graft complaints are currently pending against Legarda and Leviste over the latter’s solar energy projects.

The Ombudsman also included Duterte-time energy secretary Alfonso Cusi in the pending complaints over the alleged conspiracy “to secure exclusive government rights over the country’s solar energy resources through legislative and regulatory actions.”

According to the Ombudsman, investigation also revealed that some service contracts were transferred to Leviste’s affiliated corporations that only exist on paper, but had not started operations.

“All indicators point to the fact that they had no intention to fulfill contracts that they had garnered. The terminated contracts resulted in more than ₱10.44 billion in unpaid financial obligations to the government,” the Ombudsman said.

Complaints are not enough to bar Legarda and Leviste from leaving the country.

The Ombudsman, however, could ask for a precautionary hold-departure order (PHDO) against the two since the complaints are already at the preliminary investigation level or one step before becoming actual cases. The investigator may file this with a court and the latter will issue a PHDO as needed.

On Friday, the Senate confirmed that Legarda is currently on medical leave.

“Last August 3, the [chief of staff] of the Office of Senator Legarda sent a letter informing the Office of the Secretary that ‘Senator Loren Legarda will be on medical leave from 3 to 5 August 2026’,” Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. told Rappler on Friday, August 7.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Senator Erwin Tulfo also confirmed that Legarda filed for a medical leave, adding that this was the reason for her absence during the Senate impeachment hearings.

“Wala naman ho binanggit kung ano’ng klase. Basta sinabi lang ho, medical need (It was not specified which type of medical leave. She just said it’s for medical need,” Tulfo said.

Legarda has skipped the impeachment trial from August 3 to 5. – With a report from Patrick Cruz/Rappler.com

World.title: How Maria de Leon’s guilty plea strengthened US case vs Quiboloy
World.content:
Los Angeles-based Maria de Leon is sentenced for her involvement in an immigration fraud scheme that aided members of Quiboloy's group in staying in the US

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – Who is Maria de Leon, the septuagenarian who was sentenced for her role in an immigration fraud scheme that helped members of doomsday preacher Apollo Quiboloy‘s group remain in the United States?

On Tuesday, August 4, a US federal judge sentenced the 77-year-old Los Angeles-based paralegal to time she already served, crediting the roughly four months she spent in custody after her 2021 arrest. She posted bail after her arrest.

It was her guilty plea that gave US prosecutors a vital insider’s account of how followers of Quiboloy allegedly manipulated the American immigration system.

For years, De Leon’s work unfolded not from the pulpit of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) but through paperwork.

A former Quiboloy follower told Rappler on Friday, August 7, that De Leon was an “outsider” to the KOJC and that her dealings with the detained preacher’s group were limited to handling its immigration paperwork. She is known in the KOJC as “Liberty,” the name of her firm.

Through her firm, Liberty Legal Document Services, prosecutors said she prepared immigration filings that helped KOJC members stay in the US, allowing them to continue soliciting donations for what authorities described as a bogus charity.

Her admissions would later substantiate one of the central mechanisms of the US government’s case against Quiboloy.

In 2022, De Leon agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy, admitting she knowingly prepared and filed immigration petitions based on sham marriages, arranged solely to obtain legal status for KOJC members.

According to court records, the paralegal participated in an eight-year conspiracy with Quiboloy’s subordinates to secure permanent residency and, ultimately, US citizenship for church workers who otherwise could not lawfully remain in the country.

In her plea agreement, she acknowledged that the immigration applications were “based upon false representations of the bona fides of the underlying marriages.”

Federal prosecutors said the immigration scheme supported a wider trafficking operation detailed in a 74-page indictment unsealed in November 2021. Weeks later, Quiboloy and two other of his associates were placed in the US Federal Bureau of Investigation’s list of wanted people.

The Quiboloy church workers brought to the US on fraudulently obtained visas were allegedly dispatched across the country to solicit donations for the Children’s Joy Foundation, which authorities described as a bogus charity used to finance KOJC operations and the lavish lifestyles of its leaders.

The same indictment charged Quiboloy and seven associates in an alleged sex trafficking conspiracy, accusing KOJC leaders of coercing girls and young women into sexual relationships with the Davao-based religious leader through threats of “eternal damnation” and other forms of psychological coercion.

De Leon was not accused of participating in the alleged sexual abuse but was charged as part of the broader conspiracy.

Quiboloy and several of his associates have been detained in the Philippines due of a trafficking case before a Pasig City court and child sexual abuse cases before a Quezon City court.

The US has sought Quiboloy’s extradition, and the Philippine foreign affairs department said it endorsed the request to the justice department.

Quiboloy is closely associated with detained former president Rodrigo Duterte — they are known to be close friends and the preacher served as presidential adviser during the previous administration. – Rappler.com

World.title: SC latest ruling: Bad news for Duterte’s impeachment battle
World.content:
ARRIVED. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Senate on July 7, 2026, to meet with her lawyers but did not attend the impeachment trial.

The Supreme Court recently junked Duterte's petition questioning the initial process of her impeachment at the House level

Vice President Sara Duterte suffered a defeat at the Supreme Court (SC) filled by appointees of her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Via a unanimous decision on Wednesday, August 5, the High Court junked the two petitions — including the one filed by the Vice President herself — questioning her impeachment proceedings.

The petition questioned the validity of the hearings on the impeachment complaints conducted by the House committee on justice. In other words, the Vice President was challenging the early stages of her impeachment proceedings that are currently in full-blown trial at the Senate impeachment court.

Should the petitions have been granted, they might have had an adverse effect on the ongoing trial.

The SC dismissed the consolidated petitions GR No. E-05546 (filed by lawyer Israelito Torreon, et al.) and GR No. E-05667 (filed by Duterte) for being moot, or no longer being in need of resolution. It explained that this was so because the House already approved and transmitted the articles of impeachment to the Senate.

The impeachment articles — in this case, four — refer to the list of impeachable allegations against Duterte. They include Duterte’s alleged misuse of her confidential funds and threats to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

By constitutional design, it’s the House of Representatives that has the mandate to assess if an impeachment complaint against an impeachable official is substantial. The House committee on justice is supposed to hold hearings, and the House plenary could later decide whether or not to approve the articles of impeachment.

On May 11, a total of 257 lawmakers voted to approve the articles, impeaching Duterte for a second time.

After the approval, the articles are now with the Senate which is in the middle of the impeachment trial.

At the trial’s end, the senator-judges will vote to either convict or acquit Duterte. If convicted, the Vice President will be removed from her position and will be barred from holding government office perpetually. She can no longer run for president in 2028.

In its briefer, the SC explained that the House’s transmittal of the articles marked the end of the lower chamber’s role in the impeachment process, and the initiation of an impeachment case. The actions Duterte and Torreon wanted to stop had already been completed, said the High Court.

“The SC further held that the impeachment process had already moved to the Senate, which had convened as an impeachment court and had begun proceedings…. Any ruling on the validity of the actions taken by the House and its Committee on Justice would no longer affect the controversy,” said the High Court.

Settle the debate?

Duterte’s 2025 impeachment was stopped by an SC decision that found that the articles of impeachment were unconstitutional, therefore voiding them, and stopping the trial at the Senate before it could even go full-blown.

The decision penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen said the 2025 impeachment proceedings violated Duterte’s right to due process and the one-year bar rule. This rule prohibits the initiation of more than one impeachment proceeding against an impeachable official within a year.

For 2026, Duterte wanted to replicate the same feat.

She argued before the SC that the 2026 impeachment complaints violated the one-year bar rule and that their referral was invalid. The Vice President also questioned the public hearing held by the committee on justice which evaluated the evidence and witnesses against her.

Some called the committee hearings a “mini-trial,” but Duterte called it a “fishing expedition.” University of the Philippines College of Law associate dean and constitutional law professor Paolo Tamase explained that a fishing expedition means that a party is using an existing legal proceeding to dig deeper into another offense.

Its purpose is to look for things against a person using evidence that can be found only through another legal proceeding, he added.

For the House prosecution, the latest SC ruling settled the debate on this so-called fishing expedition.

Play Video

“This means that all the talks about the mini-trial fishing expedition that we saw earlier, repeated by the defense, are now coming to an end. This means that the launch of the fight is no longer at the Supreme Court, but here in the Senate Impeachment Court. And we have high confidence that at the end of this process, the truth will prevail,” House prosecutor Terry Ridon said in Filipino.

“They’re questioning the proceedings at the House, including the decision to transmit to the Senate. And therefore, they hope that if the House is junked, this process will also be junked. That will not happen because the petition has already been trashed,” he added.

Senate: Independent, jurisdiction absolute

The Senate impeachment court, speaking through its spokesperson Reginald Tongol, said the SC ruling confirmed that the job of the House in initiating the impeachment had already been accomplished.

According to Tongol, the ruling also affirmed that the Senate, as the impeachment court, has exclusive jurisdiction over the impeachment trial as stated in Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution.

“Like what’s stated in the Supreme Court resolution, the transmittal of the articles of impeachment activated the Senate’s power to convene into an impeachment court. The jurisdiction of the Impeachment Court is now absolute,” the spokesperson said in Filipino.

Tongol explained that the Senate was never a party to the SC petitions and is operating “entirely distinct” from the House prosecutors. That being said, the spokesperson said that the procedural history, evidentiary gathering, as well as the House’s internal findings prior to the transmittal of the articles are within the House’s jurisdiction.

“The Impeachment Court does not inherit their legal disputes, nor will the Court litigate them in the adjudicatory phase of the process,” Tongol said.

“Because the impeachment court is fully insulated from whatever happened at the House of Representatives, the impeachment court begins with a blank slate in this adjudicatory phase,” he added.

This exclusive jurisdiction of the Senate could have been put to a test if the SC ruled the other way.

When the SC decided that the 2025 impeachment against Duterte was unconstitutional, the Senate archived the articles of impeachment. But that was a different instance — a full-blown trial had yet to commence at the time.

“Had the petitions been granted, the trial could have been put in doubt and a constitutional stand-off created. The Senate is quite protective of its prerogatives in impeachment, and unlike last year, this trial is well under way. So as in the last time the Supreme Court stopped an active trial (2011-2012), the Senate would have taken a vote,” Tamase told Rappler.

As of writing, there is a pending third petition against the proceedings of the House committee on justice, filed on April 20 by lawyer Hue Jyro Go and companions. The SC has yet to act on this, but it’s likely that this will be declared moot too, given the ruling in the first two petitions.

Meanwhile, impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero’s position is still under question at the SC after Torreon and companions filed a petition on July 7 with the High Court. But for Tamase, this legal question should not affect the trial and its validity.

“The power to try is vested by the Constitution on the Senate, not the presiding officer or any single officer. The presiding officer’s rulings are impliedly supported by the rest of the Senate — otherwise they would have called a vote and overturned the call. So any defect in his election by his colleagues will not change the legal bottomline that the Senate is running the show, according to and aided by its own rules,” the UP law associate dean explained. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala, Venus Williams reunion ends in early Canadian Open exit
World.content:
PARTNERS. Alex Eala and Venus Williams in action in the 2026 Bad Homburg Open in Germany.

Filipino star Alex Eala and American icon Venus Williams absorb a straight-sets loss in the opening round of doubles action in the Canadian Open

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala’s keenly awaited reunion with tennis icon Venus Williams ended quickly.

The Filipino and American duo dropped their opening match in the Canadian Open in Toronto as they absorbed a 6-4, 6-3 loss to Japan’s Miyu Kato and Russia’s Liudmila Samsonova in the round of 32 of women’s doubles action on Thursday, August 6 (Friday, August 7, Manila time).

Eala and Williams suffered their second straight defeat as partners after their first team-up in the Bad Homburg Open in Germany in June culminated in a quarterfinal exit.

After pulling level at 4-4 in the opening set, Eala and Williams lost the next six games as their chances of winning slowly slipped away, with Kato and Samsonova wrapping up the match in 1 hour and 15 minutes.

Eala and Williams fought back from a 0-4 hole in the second set, clinching three of the next four games to close the gap to 3-5. However, their comeback ultimately fell short after they were broken in the ensuing game.

The loss marked Williams’ exit from Toronto as she also lost her first match in singles play, falling to Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova in straight sets in the round of 128.

In contrast, Eala — who received a first-round bye as the 25th seed — advanced to the third round after a 6-1, 4-6, 6-2 victory over the USA’s Alycia Parks in the round of 64.

After Bad Homburg, Eala, 21, and Williams, 46, were supposed to link up again in the Washington Open, but the Filipina dropped out at the last minute and the American found another partner in Russia’s Diana Shnaider.

That turned out for the better as Eala went on to capture her first-ever WTA Tour singles title in Washington, where she beat the top three seeds, including American world No. 30 Jessica Pegula in the final.

Now that her doubles stint in Toronto has concluded, Eala can focus on her singles bid as she battles a third consecutive American in Caty McNally in the round of 32 on Friday (Saturday, August 8, Manila time). – Rappler.com

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

World.title: Kazakhstan Takes First Step Toward Air Taxi Era With Passenger eVTOL Flight
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has taken its first practical step toward urban air mobility after a passenger completed the country’s first flight aboard an autonomous electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, signaling that the country’s air taxi ambitions are beginning to move beyond government plans into real-world testing.

According to the Committee of Civil Aviation (CCA), the EH216-S, a two-seat autonomous aircraft developed by Chinese manufacturer EHang for short-distance passenger transport, carried a passenger during a demonstration flight over a specially designated area in Astana as part of the Games of the Future 2026 on Aug. 6, marking Kazakhstan’s first-ever passenger eVTOL flight.

The electric aircraft can travel up to 35 kilometers at speeds of up to 130 kilometers per hour and is designed to operate without a pilot onboard.

The demonstration follows a series of policy announcements made earlier this year. In May, the government outlined plans to develop an urban air mobility ecosystem, including regulations for eVTOL aircraft, vertiports and unmanned air traffic management, while targeting the launch of pilot air taxi routes between Alatau, Almaty and Konayev as early as 2027.

The CCA said the first phase could include demonstration and sightseeing routes lasting between five and 30 minutes over Kazakhstan’s natural, cultural and historical landmarks. In the longer term, authorities see autonomous aircraft supporting emergency medical response, medicine deliveries, firefighting and logistics—applications where speed and rapid deployment are critical—alongside passenger transportation.

Beyond operations, Kazakhstan also plans to localize production of passenger eVTOL aircraft through an international partnership. If implemented, the initiative could position the country not only as an early adopter of advanced air mobility technologies but also as a regional manufacturing hub for an industry that

remains in its early stages globally.

The Ministry of Transport, with other government agencies, is developing the legal and infrastructure framework needed to introduce urban air mobility. Legislative amendments have already been adopted to regulate the operation of eVTOL aircraft, vertiports and unmanned air traffic management systems, laying the groundwork for the safe integration of these technologies into Kazakhstan’s transport network.

Unlike helicopters, eVTOL aircraft rely on electric propulsion, making them quieter and potentially less expensive to operate over short distances. Industry experts view the technology as part of a broader shift toward Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) — a new transportation system intended to complement rather than replace conventional road and air transport.

Several countries, including the United Arab Emirates, China and the United States, are already conducting pilot programs or preparing for commercial eVTOL services, although widespread deployment remains several years away. Initial applications worldwide are expected to focus on airport transfers, tourism, emergency medical services and connecting remote communities before broader urban deployment.

While commercial passenger services remain several years away and will require further testing and regulatory development, the demonstration marks Kazakhstan’s transition from planning to practical experimentation with technologies that could eventually reshape short-distance transportation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Sustainable Aviation Fuel Industry With Alatau Pilot Project
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan took a step toward entering the emerging market for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) after signing a memorandum with Hong Kong-based Full Vision Capital to explore building an integrated production ecosystem in Alatau, a project that could position the country within the global aviation industry’s decarbonization efforts.

The memorandum, signed on Aug.4 following a meeting between Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Full Vision Capital founder Dr. Peter Lee, outlines plans to study the creation of a complete SAF value chain from cultivating agricultural feedstock to processing and producing aviation fuel. The partners will also assess opportunities to deploy smart energy technologies and nickel-hydrogen energy storage systems to support renewable energy integration.

The agreement brings together the Alatau City Authority, Kazakhstan’s Ministries of Energy, Agriculture and Transport, and Full Vision Capital under the Green Kazakhstan initiative.

Speaking during the meeting, Bektenov said Alatau’s special legal regime creates favorable conditions for international investors.

“The Constitutional Law on the Special Legal Regime of Alatau City provides legal certainty, stable tax conditions and a one-stop-shop mechanism for investors. Alatau can become a pilot platform for localizing technologies and your development expertise,” he said.

Lee described the initiative as the beginning of a long-term partnership focused on sustainable urban development.

“We hope to introduce innovative technologies that will help Alatau and Kazakhstan more broadly establish a new international benchmark for sustainable urban development,” he said.

Why sustainable aviation fuel matters

The project reflects a broader global shift as aviation seeks to reduce carbon emissions. Unlike electric aircraft, which remain impractical for most commercial flights, sustainable aviation fuel is widely viewed as one of the few near-term solutions capable of significantly lowering emissions from existing aircraft without requiring major changes to airport infrastructure or airline fleets.

International airlines are also facing growing regulatory pressure to increase SAF use, particularly in Europe, where blending mandates are gradually taking effect. Those requirements are expected to drive long-term demand for new fuel suppliers outside traditional markets.

For Kazakhstan, which possesses extensive agricultural resources and is seeking to diversify its economy beyond conventional energy exports, SAF represents an opportunity to move further up the value chain by producing higher-value, low-carbon fuels rather than exporting raw materials alone.

Alatau as a testbed for green technologies

The project also reinforces Alatau’s role as Kazakhstan’s flagship innovation city. Established under a special legal framework offering tax incentives and simplified administrative procedures, Alatau has been positioned as a testing ground for advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and clean energy solutions.

Rather than focusing solely on fuel production, the memorandum envisions a broader ecosystem combining renewable energy, energy storage and industrial processing, suggesting Kazakhstan aims to integrate green manufacturing with wider urban development.

The memorandum does not commit the parties to immediate construction, but it signals Kazakhstan’s intention to explore participation in a sector expected to expand rapidly over the coming decades. It also reflects a broader shift in the country’s investment strategy from attracting capital for traditional energy projects toward developing industries linked to the global energy transition.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Launches New World Tour
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen has announced a new world tour titled DiMENSIONS, presenting the project as his most personal stage production to date and the latest step in an international career that has steadily expanded beyond music.

According to the artist’s official website, the new program is designed not as a journey through time and space, but as an exploration of the person behind the performer, revealing the different dimensions of Qudaibergen as a singer, composer, producer and individual.

“The world has long known him for his unique voice. This concert is intended to reveal the person behind that voice, presenting a deeper and more complete portrait of the artist,” reads the statement.

Organizers describe the production as a narrative built around emotions, memories and defining moments in Qudaibergen’s life. Rather than presenting isolated episodes, the performance seeks to unite them into a single story shaped by his connection to Kazakhstan, personal values, artistic ambitions and ongoing search for self-understanding.

The announcement comes as Qudaibergen continues to expand his international presence through performances and cultural initiatives. Last October, he performed to a sold-out audience of 15,000 at Mexico City’s Palacio de los Deportes following his first solo concert at the Auditorio Nacional, further strengthening his popularity across Latin America.

His international recognition has also extended beyond the stage. In December, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) appointed Qudaibergen as a Global Goodwill Ambassador in recognition of his humanitarian engagement. Earlier this year, he received the Ambassador of Turkic World Culture order, TURKSOY’s highest distinction, honoring his contribution to promoting Turkic cultural heritage. He was also named Cultural Figure of the Year at Kazakhstan’s People’s Favorite awards.

The announcement also reflects Qudaibergen’s evolving position in Kazakhstan’s cultural diplomacy. While his vocal performances first brought him international recognition, recent years have seen his role expand through humanitarian initiatives, international cultural awards and appearances across new markets. As his audience continues to grow across Asia, Europe and Latin America, Qudaibergen has become one of Kazakhstan’s most visible cultural representatives abroad.

World.title: What Ancient Kazakh Traditions Can Teach Us About Surviving Extreme Heat
World.content:
ASTANA – As climate change fuels increasingly intense heat waves, staying safe in extreme temperatures has become a growing concern across Kazakhstan. This summer, temperatures have climbed above 40 degrees Celsius in several regions, testing both people’s endurance and public health systems.

While modern households rely on air conditioners and fans, Kazakhstan’s nomadic ancestors developed practical ways to stay cool long before electricity. According to a candidate of historical sciences Saltanat Asanova, many of these centuries-old practices remain relevant today.

“Traditional culture, livelihoods and daily life were always closely connected to the natural environment and its changes. People were prepared for both cold and heat,” Asanova told The Astana Times.

For nomadic herders, extreme summer heat was rarely a major problem because they moved with the seasons.

“Nomads who migrated year-round spent summers in cooler areas, either farther north or in high mountain pastures. Moving livestock to alpine grazing lands was the primary way to escape the summer heat. Even on the hottest days, temperatures in the mountains remain significantly lower than in the steppe,” Asanova said.

Daily routines also followed the rhythm of the sun. Work began at dawn, paused during the hottest midday hours and resumed in the evening as temperatures dropped.

“Most household and pastoral work was completed after sunset, when the heat subsided,” she said.

The science behind a cooler yurt

The yurt, the traditional portable dwelling of Kazakh nomads, played a crucial role in keeping families cool.

According to Asanova, the yurt’s design created constant natural airflow. The shanyrak, the circular opening at the top of the roof, was left open during the day, allowing hot air to rise and escape while cooler air remained inside.

To maximize ventilation, yurts were carefully positioned according to prevailing winds. Although entrances traditionally faced southeast, their orientation could be adjusted depending on local wind conditions. Lifting the edges of the felt covering allowed air to circulate freely through the structure.

“When temperatures became especially high, the side felt coverings were removed entirely, leaving only the wooden lattice frame and reed mats. The small gaps between the reeds created excellent ventilation, helping maintain a comfortable indoor temperature without any additional cooling devices,” Asanova said.

Historical accounts by travelers who visited the Kazakh steppe during the summer describe yurts as being noticeably cooler than the outside air.

The felt roof continued to protect residents from direct sunlight.

“Felt has unique insulating properties. It retains warmth in winter while preventing solar heat from penetrating the dwelling during summer,” Asanova said.

Dressing for the heat

Despite the high temperatures, Kazakhs traditionally wore long, loose-fitting clothing rather than exposing their skin.

“It may seem paradoxical, but the hotter it became, the more layers people wore. Quilted robes provided better protection from the sun than lightweight clothing or bare skin. Like felt, multiple layers acted as insulation against overheating,” Asanova said.

She noted that headwear was equally essential.

“Felt hats effectively protected the head from the scorching sun while preventing excessive heat exposure,” she said.

Summer diet

Seasonal eating also helped people cope with the heat.

“During summer, meat was consumed only rarely. The diet consisted primarily of dairy products such as kymyz, airan, shubat, and milk-based kozhe, a traditional grain-and-milk soup,” Asanova said.

Drinks were stored in leather containers known as burdyuks, whose natural materials allowed air circulation while keeping liquids cool. Wooden tubs and clay vessels were also commonly used.

“Natural materials help maintain a relatively stable temperature regardless of the weather. For the same reason, water was traditionally stored in clay containers or leather bags,” she said.

Asanova noted that although tea remained an expensive imported commodity, both nomadic and settled communities embraced an unusual practice: drinking hot tea during hot weather.

“They followed one principle: the hotter the weather, the hotter the drink. People avoided cold water because they believed it disrupted the body’s natural heat regulation and made the heat feel even more intense. Instead, they drank hot green tea, which helps the body adapt to high temperatures and promotes natural cooling,” she said.

Modern medical advice

As heat waves become more frequent across Kazakhstan, general practitioner Malika Muratbekova said traditional advice on coping with extreme temperatures remains relevant, including avoiding excessive consumption of ice-cold water, especially during meals.

“Very cold liquids can slow digestion. The body has to expend extra energy warming the stomach, which can leave a person feeling even more fatigued,” Muratbekova said in an interview with The Astana Times.

She recommends drinking water in small amounts throughout the day, avoiding sugary soft drinks, and wearing loose-fitting, light-colored clothing made from natural or cooling fabrics with ultraviolet protection.

Muratbekova also advised protecting the head with a hat and cooling the body gradually.

“You can place a cooling towel or damp cloth around your neck. Portable fans are also becoming increasingly common. Taking a cool shower, using a spray bottle or damp cloth to moisten the skin can help lower body temperature. However, avoid ice-cold showers because a sudden drop in temperature can place unnecessary stress on the body,” she said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Completes Key Stage of Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable Project
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has completed the most technically challenging stage of the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable project after an undersea cable reached the country’s Caspian coast on Aug. 5, marking a milestone in efforts to establish a new high-speed digital corridor linking Asia and Europe.

The submarine cable, laid along the Caspian Sea floor between Aktau and Sumgait, will directly connect the digital infrastructure of Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, providing an alternative international data transmission route designed to improve connectivity, strengthen network resilience and expand the two countries’ role in Eurasian digital transit.

The project is being implemented by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom International, while the joint venture CaspiLink B.V. will oversee both construction and future operation of the network.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhtelecom Chairman Bagdat Mussin and AzerTelecom International Chief Executive Ana Nakashidze inspected the completion of the marine installation phase aboard the cable-laying vessel.

“We have completed the most difficult stage of the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable project – laying the cable along the Caspian Sea floor. The new route will strengthen Kazakhstan’s digital connectivity with global data networks and create the foundation for the further development of artificial intelligence, cloud technologies and modern data centers,” Madiyev said.

According to the ministry, the government completed the regulatory, customs and organizational procedures required to begin construction without administrative delays.

The project began in 2025 with engineering surveys, route selection and factory testing of a specially armored submarine cable manufactured in China. Engineers designed the route to avoid anchorage zones and military training areas while securing the necessary environmental approvals in Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region.

Construction at sea began in July 2026 using a specialized cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons. Around 70 specialists participated in the round-the-clock operation.

The cable had previously been transported from China to the port of Kuryk before being shipped to Baku, where it was transferred to the cable-laying vessel for installation across the Caspian Sea.

Work is now focused on connecting the cable to coastal infrastructure. Ground infrastructure, commissioning and system testing are expected to be completed this autumn. Unlike many strategic infrastructure projects, the Trans-Caspian cable is being financed entirely by the participating telecommunications operators without state budget funding.

Part of a broader digital corridor

The project forms part of Kazakhstan’s broader strategy to position itself as a regional digital hub alongside its expanding transport and logistics ambitions.

For years, Kazakhstan has sought to strengthen the Middle Corridor connecting China and Europe through the Caspian Sea. While much of that effort has focused on railways, ports and highways, officials increasingly argue that digital infrastructure will become equally important for regional connectivity.

The new fiber-optic route is expected to provide lower-latency and more resilient international data transmission while reducing dependence on existing communication routes. It also complements Kazakhstan’s wider digital agenda, which includes investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure, cloud computing and data centers intended to serve regional markets.

By creating an additional high-capacity data corridor across the Caspian, the project illustrates how Kazakhstan’s concept of connectivity is expanding beyond physical trade routes to include digital infrastructure.

World.title: Kazakhstan Moves to Build Nationwide Flood and Drought Early Warning System
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan signed an agreement on Aug. 4 to develop a nationwide flood and drought early warning system, signaling a broader shift from responding to water emergencies toward anticipating them. The project, developed jointly by the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation’s Information and Analytical Center and Agip Karachaganak, will integrate data on the country’s water infrastructure into a unified forecasting system.

The agreement was signed during the third meeting of the Development Partners Coordination Council under the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, which brought together government agencies, international organizations, financial institutions, development partners, diplomats and private-sector representatives to review progress on Kazakhstan’s Water Partnership Initiative 2024–2030.

The early warning system is expected to combine hydrological data with information on water infrastructure to improve monitoring of flood and drought risks nationwide. Rather than focusing solely on responding to emergencies after they occur, the initiative aims to strengthen preparedness by providing authorities with better forecasting and decision-making tools.

The project reflects a broader evolution in Kazakhstan’s water policy as the country faces increasing pressure from climate variability, recurring droughts and floods, growing demand for water resources and the need to modernize aging infrastructure.

Alongside the forecasting initiative, the ministry signed additional agreements to establish AquaLab, a national center for water innovation, STEM education and environmental awareness. The Water Resources Information and Analytical Center signed cooperation agreements with the Caravan of Knowledge Corporate Foundation, while a separate trilateral agreement involving the Association of Environmental Organizations of Kazakhstan and the Central Asia and Caucasus representative office of The Coca-Cola Company will finance and implement the project.

According to Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov, water conservation has become a new model for managing Kazakhstan’s water resources rather than a standalone policy direction.

“Water conservation is no longer a separate area of work but a new model of water resources management,” he said.

According to him, infrastructure solutions must be accompanied by modern management technologies. Digital tools should create a unified information space, while the introduction of new technologies must be supported by specialist training and the development of a culture of responsible water use.

The initiatives were presented within the framework of the Development Partners Coordination Council, established jointly by the ministry and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Kazakhstan in September 2024. The platform now brings together more than 40 international partners working on water-sector development.

UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan Katarzyna Wawiernia said the council has evolved beyond a forum for discussion into a mechanism that translates cooperation into concrete projects.

“The real value of this work is measured not by the number of meetings but by the joint solutions that are already being transformed into investment projects and improvements in public policy,” she said.

Taken together, the agreements suggest Kazakhstan’s water reforms are entering a new phase. While investment in reservoirs, canals and irrigation systems remains essential, policymakers are increasingly pairing physical infrastructure with digital technologies, forecasting capabilities and research. By integrating data, innovation and international partnerships into a single strategy, Kazakhstan is seeking to build a water management system that is better equipped to anticipate future risks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Leads Central Asia in 2026 Legatum Prosperity Index
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan ranked first among Central Asian countries in the 2026 Legatum Prosperity Index, placing 66th out of 161 economies worldwide, according to the latest report published by the Prosperity Institute.

The annual index assesses countries across more than 130 indicators grouped into three broad pillars: prosperity, freedom and society. The 2026 edition introduced an updated methodology that places greater emphasis on balanced performance across all categories, rather than allowing strong results in one area to offset weaknesses in another.

Kazakhstan ranked 52nd globally in the Development pillar, 45th in Society, and 47th in Integrity of Society. The country recorded its strongest results in education, where it placed 32nd worldwide, and in Integrity of Families, ranking 30th. Kazakhstan also placed 53rd globally for living conditions.

Among Central Asian countries, Kazakhstan outperformed the Kyrgyz Republic (87th), Uzbekistan (94th), Tajikistan (129th), and Turkmenistan (150th). It also ranked ahead of Russia, which placed 103rd overall.

The report identifies Switzerland as the world’s most prosperous country in 2026, followed by Norway, Ireland, Denmark and Finland. According to the institute, Switzerland topped the ranking due to consistently strong performance across all major dimensions without significant weaknesses.

The Legatum Prosperity Index is an annual global assessment that measures long-term prosperity by evaluating economic performance alongside institutional quality, governance, education, health, social capital, personal freedom and other factors affecting quality of life.

World.title: Armenia begins shift from Russia towards EU – but finish line remains distant
World.content:
Armenia between Europe and Russia

Against this backdrop, the European Union pledged to “stand by Armenia”. EU leaders have already announced tens of millions of dollars in financial assistance and opened the bloc’s markets to Armenian goods that had suddenly ceased to meet Russian quality standards. More importantly, Brussels has expressed interest in further deepening ties with Yerevan, while Armenia’s re-elected leadership says the election results demonstrate the public’s desire to continue along the country’s European path.

Parliamentary elections in Armenia are over, but the political—and geopolitical—debate continues. Many viewed the vote as a de facto referendum on the country’s future orientation: Russia or the European Union.During the election campaign, Moscow imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian food products, a move widely interpreted in Armenia as an attempt to influence public opinion. Contrary to some expectations, Russia not only kept those trade restrictions in place after the election but tightened them.

JAMnews reviewed the latest developments and spoke to analysts with opposing views. Residents of Armenia also shared their opinions on how they believe the country should shape its future.

Yerevan residents rush to work in the morning. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

How Armenia’s pivot took shape

Few people remember now, but immediately after the 2018 “Velvet Revolution”, led by then-opposition figure and now Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, he insisted that his government would not pursue any geopolitical realignment. At the time, Armenia was already a member of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Years later, speaking from podiums in both Europe and Yerevan, the same Pashinyan has declared Armenia’s aspiration to join the European Union.

So what happened in between? Over the past several years, the entire security architecture of the South Caucasus has unraveled, triggering a snowball effect. Initially, relations between Yerevan and Moscow developed without major friction. Then came the 2020 Karabakh war. Armenia was defeated and ceased to be the guarantor of Nagorno-Karabakh’s security. Formally, Yerevan had no grounds to hold Moscow responsible in 2020. Nagorno-Karabakh was not part of Armenia, and the agreements signed between the two countries applied only to Armenia itself, not to the unrecognised entity.

However, events then took an unexpected turn.

Over the following two years, Azerbaijan launched several military operations on Armenia’s internationally recognised territory. Yerevan appealed to its allies in the CSTO for assistance, but received neither military support nor even a political assessment of the situation.

The allies responded that it was first necessary to establish where exactly the escalation had taken place, arguing that the Armenia-Azerbaijan border had not been formally delimited. Pashinyan replied sharply:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to claim that the Collective Security Treaty Organization has no area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

Since then, Yerevan, finding itself alone in the face of what it viewed as an external security threat, has frozen its participation in the CSTO and turned increasingly towards Europe. According to some analysts, the price of that shift was Armenia’s official recognition of Nagorno-Karabakh as part of Azerbaijan. In return, the European Union deployed a civilian monitoring mission to Armenia, which helped stabilise the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. Armenia also secured the EU’s political backing.

Retiree Andrey Karapetyan shares his views on European integration. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Shift gathered pace

These developments on the ground were inevitably followed by political change. The entire Armenia-Azerbaijan negotiation process shifted to Western platforms—an outcome few had anticipated. Since the conflict began in the 1990s, Moscow had served as the principal mediator and facilitator of the peace talks.

Following the events of September 2023, when Azerbaijan’s one-day military operation prompted the entire Armenian population to flee Nagorno-Karabakh, Russia effectively lost its influence in the region.

At the same time, Russia also lost its standing among much of Armenia’s population, no longer being viewed as a friendly state.

A park in Yerevan, where locals gather to play backgammon and discuss politics. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Although Russia formally remains Armenia’s strategic ally, many Armenians have not forgotten that Russian peacekeepers effectively acted as bystanders, failing to fulfil their mission of protecting the Armenian population of Nagorno-Karabakh. Following the CSTO’s refusal to defend Armenia’s territorial integrity, relations between Moscow and Yerevan cooled even further. The Armenian leadership also adopted a more outspoken tone towards Russia, both in its rhetoric and in its actions.

At the same time, contacts between the Armenian government and its European partners intensified. Brussels allocated hundreds of millions of dollars to support political and economic reforms in Armenia, as well as strengthen the country’s borders. France also began supplying Armenia with military equipment. The culmination of these developments came on 17 October 2023, when speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared:

“The Republic of Armenia is ready to be as close to the European Union as the European Union considers possible. Our joint statement with President von der Leyen says: ‘In these difficult times, the EU and Armenia stand shoulder to shoulder.'”

In the years that followed, Pashinyan repeatedly stated that Armenia would seek EU membership. The parliamentary elections held in June and their outcome only reinforced the government’s determination.

“Last year, we adopted a law launching the process of accession to the European Union, which, I would remind you, was initiated by civil society. I believe this provides an additional incentive to give new momentum to our democratic and institutional reforms so that we can achieve EU standards as quickly as possible.

This is our main intermediate goal because we understand that no country can become a full member of the European Union without meeting its standards. Therefore, our primary task is first and foremost to comply with EU standards. […]If we are admitted to the European Union, we will be happy. If we are not, we will still benefit, because Armenia will have become a country that meets European standards, with all the positive consequences that entails,” Pashinyan said at the time.

System administrator Artak Gaboyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Russia pushes back

At the start of the crisis in Armenian-Russian relations, Moscow responded relatively cautiously to Yerevan’s efforts to move closer to Europe. The Kremlin sought to avoid further destabilising the situation, citing Armenia’s difficult historical circumstances. Even Armenia’s effective suspension of its participation in the CSTO did not result in a fundamental reassessment of bilateral relations.

However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: ‘There are signs Armenia is heading for ‘divorce’ from the Russian-led EAEU,’ says Armenian political analyst
World.content:
Possible developments in Armenia-EAEU relations

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has travelled to Kyrgyzstan for a two-day working visit to attend a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council. The agenda includes economic cooperation, trade, transport, customs regulation and integration within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

Pashinyan’s visit comes amid Russian restrictions on Armenian goods and growing tensions between the two countries.

Before the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council convened, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk said trade between Armenia and Russia had fallen by two-thirds. He described the decline as “dramatic”.

Armenia’s prime minister has urged people to see the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify the country’s economy.

At the same time, Armenian analysts say there are signs of a “divorce” from the EAEU. Some believe Yerevan may now decide to make a sharp and irreversible break.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk said:

“We expected the situation now unfolding between the EAEU and Armenia. Over the past three to four years, we repeatedly warned our Armenian colleagues about these risks, including the risk of a decline in trade.

“In 2024, trade between Russia and Armenia reached a record high of around $12bn. That was a huge figure. Last year, it fell to about $8bn.

“This year, however, trade has dropped dramatically. It is down by around two-thirds compared with 2025. The current trend suggests it will continue to decline.”

Pashinyan: “The EAEU is de facto paralysed”

The Armenian prime minister says Russian restrictions on Armenian goods are not only Armenia’s problem but also a problem for the EAEU itself.

“In effect, the Eurasian Economic Union is paralysed and no longer functioning. If this issue is not resolved quickly, let me predict that it will mark the beginning of the end for the EAEU,” Nikol Pashinyan said recently.

Russia leads the Eurasian Economic Union. Armenia has been a full member of the bloc since 2015. Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are also members.

Pashinyan also said the EAEU was facing a deepening crisis.

“If this issue is not resolved quickly, I am 100% certain that Armenia will overcome this problem, not the EAEU,” he said.

He added that he intended to raise and discuss all outstanding issues within the EAEU itself.

Comment

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan says:

“If Russia’s pressure on Armenia before the elections was mainly aimed at supporting pro-Russian political forces, its increased pressure now is directed primarily at Armenia’s foreign policy and its efforts to diversify its international partnerships.

“Pashinyan openly hinted at this when he said Armenia could not give up its right to have alternatives. The prime minister also warned that continued economic pressure from Russia could trigger the ‘collapse of the EAEU’. Armenia sees the greatest problems within this multilateral framework and is responding through the same framework.

“On 30 July, for example, Armenia banned imports of tomato paste for six months not only from Russia but also from other EAEU member states. This was clearly a signal to its partners that they should not treat Armenia unfairly.

“The situation closely resembles the events of autumn 2022. Azerbaijan attacked Armenia’s sovereign territory and later occupied parts of it. Armenia then called on the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) to fulfil its obligations under the alliance’s rules, but the bloc refused. That refusal ultimately led Armenia to effectively leave the CSTO.

“Four years later, Armenia has virtually no ties with the CSTO. It no longer takes part in the bloc’s activities, funding or meetings. The relationship can be described as a ‘de facto divorce’ between Armenia and the CSTO.

“The situation is harder to imagine in the case of the EAEU because the bloc is far more integrated. It has a common customs regime, a shared pool of financial transfers, and over the past decade Armenia’s economy has adapted to the logic of the EAEU.

“That means a split between Armenia and the EAEU could happen suddenly and completely.

“The first signs of the mutual disappointment that usually precedes a ‘divorce’ are already clear.”

Context

Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian fruit and vegetables ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary elections. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products, citing quality concerns.

Armenian officials and analysts, however, viewed the measures through the prism of the election campaign. Most analysts expected Russia to ease the pressure after the vote. Instead, Moscow not only kept the restrictions in place but introduced new ones.

In response, the Armenian government launched support programmes for businesses. Exporters began redirecting shipments to the Middle East and the European Union. The EU is also expected to approve a scheme granting autonomous trade measures for Armenian products. The plan would provide significant trade preferences for Armenian exports. Armenia would become the first country without EU candidate status or a free trade agreement with the bloc to benefit from the mechanism.

At the same time, Moscow has urged Armenia to decide quickly whether it wants to move towards the EU or remain in the EAEU. It has also called for a referendum on the issue.

Yerevan says there are currently no grounds for holding such a referendum. Armenian officials argue that the country should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, formally place the issue on the political agenda.

The issue of a referendum also came up during a phone call between Pashinyan and Putin on 27 July, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

However, the Kremlin’s readout of the conversation omitted Pashinyan’s response that it was too early to hold a referendum. It also made no mention of the prime minister raising Russia’s restrictions on Armenian imports. Pashinyan later said the measures “contradict the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and the regulations of the Eurasian Economic Union”. He called for urgent steps to resolve the issue.

Possible developments in Armenia-EAEU relations

World.title: Attack on Georgian comedian accompanied by coordinated information campaign
World.content:
A smear campaign against Georgian comedian Onise Okriashvili involving pro-government media, politicians and coordinated online accounts began before he was attacked, before shifting afterwards to justify the violence and express support for the alleged attacker.

That is the main finding of a study by the Myth Detector project, which says the campaign unfolded systematically across multiple channels, including media outlets and social media.

On 23 July 2026, three men ambushed and brutally assaulted pro-European protest participant, comedian and stand-up performer Onise Okriashvili in Tbilisi over a joke he made about renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze. The suspects were arrested but later released on bail. One of their friends, professional wrestler Giorgi Kartvelishvili, subsequently announced the creation of the “People’s Movement” together with like-minded supporters, saying its aim was to “protect Georgian values, ideals and traditions.”

According to the Myth Detector study, pro-government media outlets and Facebook pages began circulating old videos and public statements by Onise Okriashvili several days before the attack. The material was taken out of context and presented in a way that portrayed the comedian as someone who insulted Georgia’s national, cultural and religious values.

The study says that after the attack, social media and pro-government media promoted narratives claiming the assault had been triggered by Okriashvili’s joke about Nodar Dumbadze. It found that posts and graphics shared from 24 July onwards sought to downplay the attackers’ responsibility and portray them as “defenders of the nation’s honour”.

Identical graphics were circulated simultaneously by supporters of the ruling Georgian Dream party, anti-opposition Facebook pages and pro-government commentators. The central message was that the main suspect, Nikoloz Khurtsilava, did not deserve punishment because he had “defended the national honour of Georgians.”

According to the study, these narratives were also echoed by members of the ruling party. Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili focused not on the assault itself but on the inadmissibility of insulting Nodar Dumbadze. MP Dimitri Samkharadze said he was prepared to act as a guarantor for the defendant, while another lawmaker, Irakli Zarkua, condemned the violence but added that public outrage over jokes targeting the church, the patriarch and prominent writers had been predictable. Levan Kochloshvili, a representative of the pro-government People’s Power party, said he disagreed with the moral condemnation of the accused.

The Myth Detector study also says the campaign to discredit Okriashvili continued after the attack using new material. Pro-government platforms again circulated old videos of the comedian, including clips related to religious issues, as well as a previously shared video in which they claimed he mocked elderly women selling sunflower seeds. According to the study’s authors, this shifted attention away from the assault itself and onto the victim’s remarks.

The report also highlights signs of coordinated online activity. Researchers identified fake accounts that expressed support for both the man accused of carrying out the attack and the movement later announced by Giorgi Kartvelishvili. Some of the accounts posted identical comments, complete with the same grammatical mistakes, beneath stories published by pro-government media, while others used other people’s names and photographs to conceal their identities.

One of the study’s main findings concerns a case in which pro-government media presented a Facebook post by a previously identified troll as the opinion of a real person. According to the authors, the post, which attacked Onise Okriashvili and defended the alleged attacker, was then simultaneously amplified by 13 pro-government online outlets and the Facebook pages of two television channels.

Myth Detector also says part of the campaign relied on paid promotion through sponsored posts. These portrayed Okriashvili and his supporters as “anti-Georgian forces”, while the alleged attacker’s statements were promoted in a way that justified the violence.

Attack on comedian in Georgia

World.title: Returning Abkhaz citizenship to ethnic Georgians: integration or a security threat?
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s parliament is set to consider restoring Abkhaz nationality status to residents of the Gali district. The opposition is firmly against the move, arguing that it would pose a threat to national security.

The parliamentary committee on state and legal policy has approved amendments to the law on civil status acts that would extend the right to restore Abkhaz nationality status and surnames to foreign nationals permanently residing in Abkhazia who are ethnic Abkhazians, as well as “direct descendants of people who lost their Abkhaz nationality as a result of anti-Abkhaz national policies pursued in the 19th and 20th centuries.”

Behind this lengthy wording lies one specific group: ethnic Georgians living in Abkhazia’s Gali district. In 2011, the overwhelming majority of them – around 30,000 people – were stripped of their Abkhaz citizenship on the grounds that they also held Georgian citizenship.

In place of Abkhaz passports, they were issued permanent residence permits allowing them to live indefinitely in the breakaway republic.

Calls to allow residents of the Gali district to regain Abkhaz citizenship have periodically resurfaced in debates over the full integration of the area’s population.

One proposal has been to allow them to change their recorded ethnicity in official documents from Georgian to Abkhaz. Supporters argue there is a historical basis for this, as some Gali residents have surnames of Abkhaz origin, and their ancestors are believed to have been assimilated into the Georgian population at the turn of the 20th century.

Under Abkhazia’s current citizenship law, such a change in official records would automatically entitle Gali residents to regain Abkhaz citizenship, even if they also hold Georgian citizenship.

The proposed amendments to the law on civil status acts are due to be debated at the next parliamentary session, and judging by the opposition’s reaction, the discussion is likely to be heated.

“Pushing this bill through under the current foreign policy circumstances creates additional and extremely dangerous risks that could be exploited by external forces to undermine stability and national security,” five opposition groups said in a joint statement.

They argue that if Gali residents regain Abkhaz passports while retaining Georgian citizenship, they could play a much greater role in the republic’s political life by running for parliament or the presidency, initiating referendums and influencing key political decisions.

According to the opposition, “such a prospect poses a direct threat to the national interests and fundamental rights of the Abkhaz people, secured at the cost of enormous sacrifice.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhaz citizenship for ethnic Georgians

World.title: Head of US-based TRIPP+ foundation holds talks in Armenia: Key takeaways
World.content:
TRIPP+ Foundation chief visits Yerevan

Konstantin Sokolov, head of the TRIPP+ foundation, is visiting Armenia. Armenia’s Foreign Ministry disclosed the visit in a statement identifying Sokolov as president of the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Foundation.

The ministry said Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan met Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to the US special envoy for peace missions. Konstantin Sokolov also attended the meeting.

“The participants discussed ongoing efforts to implement the TRIPP programme. Both sides emphasised their commitment to launching the programme on the ground as quickly as possible.”

A day earlier, reports said the US authorities had doubled funding for TRIPP+, increasing it from an initial $201m to $402m.

The TRIPP+ Foundation was established as a separate investment fund. Its primary role is to finance the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project. The project centres on a road linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The Armenian government views the route as part of its Crossroads of Peace initiative to reopen regional transport links. According to a US State Department representative, TRIPP+ has the authority to provide loans, make equity investments and award grants to support strategic private-sector development.
