That is why, as well as building social housing, we are also building dedicated homes for people living with complex, long-term mental health needs,” she said. “The reason we supported recommendation 7 in principle is that whilst it identified Habilis and Haven as models for consideration (models we are also funding), we are choosing to scale other NSW-supported accommodation models that achieve the same goal.” If you or someone you know need support, contact Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Beyond Blue. SANE phone and digital support services can be accessed at sane.org. In the event of an emergency, dial Triple Zero (000). World.title: NRL LIVE updates: Red-hot Warriors lead Panthers ahead of Roosters-Bulldogs clash
World.content:
The Warriors have completed their first 10 sets, are really pressuring the Panthers in defence and have enjoyed a little more than 60% of possession in the early part of this game.

But now their perfect start comes to an end – Leka Halasima fumbling a play-the-ball inside his own half to give Penrith the ball in a dangerous position.

The Panthers earn a six-again, then another, for ruck infringements, but then Liam Martin drops a Nathan Cleary pass and the Warriors come away with it again.

The hosts quickly go down the other end and Halasima pulls of an incredible one-handed catch from a bomb before being tackle a couple of metres short of the Penrith try line on the last tackle. Then some savage, swarming Warriors defence keeps the Panthers inside their own 15 metres after four tackles. The premiership favourites are really on the back foot so far tonight.

Warriors 12, Panthers 0 after 20 minutes

World.title: These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age Updated August 7, 2026 — 6:10pm , first published 12:54pm

Updated August 7, 2026 — 6:10pm ,first published 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision, when the Cats struck what has been acknowledged was an inappropriate waiver with a player who had a history of concussions. On Thursday, as the story detonated that the Cats had signed the player – later identified as 200-game defender Jake Kolodjashnij – to a waiver that diminished his legal rights – at least on paper – Drummond was asked to respond to questions from this masthead, and doubtless other media, about his role in the shonky waiver. Craig Drummond’s statement does not address the questions that need to be answered about the concussion waiver Geelong signed with a senior player, when Drummond was Cats president. AFL Photos via Getty Images The AFL chairman, who holds the highest office in the game, issued a brief statement that did not address the obvious questions that he should have taken on, given his twin hats as AFL chairman and the president of the club at the time that this hubristic document was signed, without the AFL’s consent or knowledge. The initial word from the league late Thursday was that the AFL would not sanction the Cats, a matter of months after Carlton were fined $75,000 for their handling of the Elijah Hollands affair, which was about a different kind of player safety – mental health.



But on Friday afternoon, in an apparent shift, the AFL was saying that Geelong would be issued with a “please explain” – a position from headquarters that had not been communicated to media previously. Was the AFL responding to the pub test? The AFL took weeks to sort through the messy Hollands imbroglio before settling on a sanction. The 17 rival clubs will be watching and many will expect sanctions against Geelong. Loading Drummond’s time as AFL chairman has won praise within clubs for the energetic reshaping of the commission and introducing the kind of governance – term limits for the board, most of all – that were not evident during the Richard Goyder era, in which Gillon McLachlan was allowed to run his race. But, it’s now fair to say that had news of this contract emerged back in January or February, it’s unlikely Drummond would have been appointed AFL chairman.



And, as with political leaders, AFL honeymoons are as fleeting as Essendon winning streaks and Drummond was unable to last the whole 2026 season without finding himself in political cow manure. His statement contained the clichéd motherhood lines about the clubs and AFL continuing “to prioritise the health and safety of all our players”. Before he became AFL chairman, Drummond was Geelong’s president. Here he celebrates the Cats’ 2022 grand final win with Patrick Dangerfield. Getty Those words read as utterly hollow, since Geelong had not made the player’s “health and safety” their priority in the now-recanted part of the agreement. The whole objective of the waiver was to absolve the club of responsibility for the player’s long-term health (in relation to head injuries) and put the onus on the player. The only excuse for the Cats is that it would have been easier to not offer the player a contract (the AFL concussion panel had cleared him to play). While it was the player’s initiative that this deal be struck, the Cats went off the reservation by getting him to sign away legal protections.



Carefully crafted statements, without answering questions, is a strategy that could succeed for Drummond and the AFL given society’s attention spans, which are shorter than the time it took for the AFL to respond to the mini-crisis on Thursday. Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player Drummond, however, has a responsibility to address questions about an embarrassing, ill-considered and furtive arrangement that has not – to my knowledge – been tried on by other AFL clubs. If an oft-concussed player signed a waiver or its equivalent in the VFL, before he was drafted on to an AFL list, that still falls short of Geelong’s too-clever ploy. Drummond was at the helm of Geelong when this happened, and holds even greater responsibility now as AFL chairman. Cats chief executive Steve Hocking is not the sole authority here. These questions, which Drummond hasn’t yet padded up for, should be answered candidly, in full: As president of Geelong in 2024, do you take responsibility for the waiver the club signed with Kolodjashnij? Do you and Geelong owe him an apology? Why was this waiver necessary? Did any parts trouble you then? You’ve called Geelong’s changes “appropriate”. Can you clarify if you regret that you were a party to this arrangement? You say health and safety of players is paramount. Will Geelong be sanctioned, for an arrangement that went outside the AFL and the AFL Players Association, and which will be disallowed in future. Given the conflict of interest between your roles as Geelong president then, and AFL chairman now, how did you ensure that the decisions and discussions within the AFL were not influenced by your interests? What steps, if any, did you take?



Related Article Breaking

Concussion crisis ‘My private medical information has been made public’: Cat at centre of concussion scandal identifies himself This episode underscores that Geelong’s greatness as a footy club has little basis in some imagined moral superiority of “values” and decency; the narrative some ex-Geelong players and officials unwisely spruik. Yes, the Cats are exceptional – in coaching, recruiting and development, not in niceness, humility and tender care. They come across as a ruthless organisation that makes hard calls and is focused on winning games, not friends or wellbeing awards. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A painting in which a man sleeps while the world burns has won a $100,000 art prize
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On first glance it’s a peaceful scene, but a quiet sense of dread and unease creeps up on you almost immediately. It takes a moment to figure out why. The central figure is peaceful; a man sleeping, head rolled to one side, his hand draped across his middle. But he’s sleeping next to a gun – and that gun is perched precariously on a ledge over a body of water. In the background the gentle colours suggest a beautiful day drawing to a close; but then you see the smoke rising. Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed by Marri Ngarr artist Dr Ryan Presley has just been announced as the 2026 winner of the $100,000 Telstra National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island Art Award. The 2026 Telstra Art Award winner Dr Ryan Presley with his painting Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed. Helen Orr The multimedia artist and academic’s works span drawings, installation, performance, painting, writing and games. “I like blending ideas and bringing different things together,” Presley says. He has had a long-standing interest in Renaissance, baroque and romantic period works, but it was when he first saw the 16th century painting The Annunciation by Domenico Beccafumi that he knew he wanted to create something that both referenced it and captured the moody atmosphere. “I really liked the mix of dark and light and there was a real intense quality to the work,” says Presley. The scaffolding Beccafumi provides to Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed is clear, though the feeling of Presley’s painting is entirely different. “It’s quite ethereal and moody in the original work. So I kept elements of that, and then changed the landscape, changed the building. Made it more localised.” There are eucalyptus trees and bushfires in the distant mountain ranges to create “an unsettling quality – a mix between beauty and disaster”. The central figure is another classical reference with a local and modern twist; Adonis by Antonio Corradini. It’s a subject Presley has tackled previously, in his large-scale drawing Daydreamer IV (2024). “After putting that together ... I was like, ah, I like this, but I think I can take it further.” Instead of a reinterpretation of the original sculpture, here he breathed more life into the sleeping figure; made it feel truly alive.



The final result is a work that is both familiar and alien, comfortable and stressful. A man who is oblivious to the dangers around him, sleeping as the world burns. “I like that push and pull,” says Presley. “Ornate things mixed with ominous qualities … mixing in acceptance of reality as well as ignoring or denial of reality”. The 64 finalists were drawn from a pool of 221 entries, with this year’s judging panel made up of artists Julie Gough, Yhonnie Scarce and Warraba Weatherall, with all finalist works on display in an exhibition at Darwin’s Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory (MAGNT). Telstra Multimedia Award winner Colin Heenan-Puruntatameri with his work Ngirramini Ngini Amparruwu (The Story of the Widow) Helen Orr Guest curator Dr Shannon Brett explains that after the finalists were selected “we realised that there’s an overwhelming story or theme about women in many of the works – and these are stories that are even being delivered by some of the men. So stories about grandmothers, mothers, family, the power of women, women on country. It’s just a beautiful thing.” Tiwi artist Colin Heenan-Puruntatameri was this year’s Multimedia Award winner for his video work Ngirramini Ngini Amparruwu (The Story of the Widow). Part of his work as an artist is creating a cultural archive. “The mission’s ultimate goal was to eradicate culture, and it is our goal to do the opposite,” he says. Video has a role to play in passing on culture, he explains. “These things will be here long after us. My mother’s cousin isn’t here any more, but I can sing her song. That means her great-grandchildren can now learn that song and keep passing it on, and it’s now documented forever on this digital space.” Gulumerridjin, Wardaman and KarraJarri artist Jenna Mayilema Lee won the Work on Paper Award for Taking Back Taken. The work is constructed entirely out of repurposed maps from the British Museum. Lee first had the idea when she was living in London, and noticed that the museum were asking for a £2 donation for their maps.



“I thought that was really interesting to ask people to donate in order to have a wayfinding map, when I guess the justification from the British Museum for still having a lot of objects is that it means everybody in the world can come and see it. So I just decided to take maps without paying,” she explains. Over the years, friends visiting the museum contributed to her growing collection, and, after painstakingly honing her technique, the result was the six paper dillybags that make up Taking Back Taken. Telstra Work on Paper Award winner Jenna Mayilema Lee with her artwork Taking Back Taken. Helen Orr Other category winners, who each receive $15,000, included Vanessa Inkamala who won the Telstra General Painting Award for Arrkurla Nukala / Lyaarta Ntema, Barayuwa Munuŋgurr who won the Bark Painting Award for The Hidden Reef at Yarrinya, Napuwarri Marawili who won the Wandjuk Marika Memorial 3D Award for Djambatj – Deadly Hunter and Guruwuy Murrinyina who won the Emerging Artist Award for Prismatic Arc. Related Article Visual art ‘I cried with tears of joy’: Winner of $100,000 art prize announced Brett loves every work in the exhibition, but asked about Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed, says the painting is special. “It’s all there. That work is about the past, the present, potentially the future. It’s not only about culture and people, it’s about art. It’s actually about art and different ways of communicating through art. And it’s also technically brilliant.” “Creativity has a huge role in being a human being,” says Presley. “Maybe not enough people make the connection [of] how critical it is and how much it threads into our day-to-day lives,” he continues. However, “it’s integral to our existence”. The NATSIAA 2026 exhibition is at MAGNT, Darwin, until January 24, 2027.

World.title: ‘It won’t be a US military base’: Cook stands firm on HMAS Stirling future
World.content:
NationalWAAUKUS ‘It won’t be a US military base’: Cook stands firm on HMAS Stirling future Michael Philipps August 7, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

WA Premier Roger Cook says HMAS Stirling will not be a US military base despite media reports that more than double the number of Americans would be deployed to the facility than previously declared. A Virginia-class submarine, the USS Minnesota, docked at HMAS Stirling in Rockingham. AFP Earlier this week, The Australian published a story saying the US has established the administrative framework for a military base in WA, amid revelations 2300 Americans will be deployed to the state to support “enduring” submarine deployments to the defence facility south of Perth. However, Cook has backed the stance of the Albanese government that the US Navy presence in the state will not be a US base on Australian soil. “It won’t be a US military base, but it is the necessary governance and framework that they need to ensure that HMAS Stirling can play its role as part of the AUKUS partnership,” Cook said at a press conference on Friday.



“We’ll be having US subs rotating through that facility, and it’s important that the US has the confidence and the necessary management structures to assure that it works properly.” “We’re having over $6 billion worth of construction activity taking place at HMAS Stirling as we speak. “The facilities have been significantly upgraded so that it can play its more enhanced role under the SRF (Submarine Rotational Force) West Rotational Initiative.” Cook added that the state government had done a lot of work planning in terms of the extra personnel that will be coming into the Rockingham-Kwinana district for the AUKUS activities. “That’s a fast-growing area - 700 families move into that area almost every month,” he said.



“So it is an area which continues to manage its growth, and we’re ensuring that we work with local government authorities so that every community service is also fully supported.” Just last week Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy caused a political storm during a visit to Washington when he told the ABC’s 7.30 program that the rotation of US submarines at HMAS Stirling in Perth was limited to just five years. Conroy then walked back his remarks in an interview with this masthead, saying the US was likely to maintain some kind of presence there indefinitely, and issued a statement to clarify his position. “Submarine Rotational Force West is intended to be an enduring element of US force posture in Australia,” he said. Last year former Prime Minister Scott Morrison proposed turning the planned Henderson shipbuilding facility into a joint base, which would allow both American and Australian submarines to be hosted and repaired there, and give the US direct access to the Indian Ocean.



However, defence expert Jennifer Parker, an adjunct fellow at the Australian National University, said the proposal doesn’t make sense, and could add unnecessary complexity to existing plans for Henderson. “Henderson really is focused on becoming a defence precinct that can support Australia’s sovereign shipbuilding,” Parker said. “Now a component of Henderson … will conduct depot-level maintenance for submarines, and it will include US submarines, and that’s part of the benefit to the US in this deal. “But to do that, it doesn’t need to be a joint base whatsoever.” Parker said US submarines and personnel would be already stationed at the nearby HMAS Stirling on Garden Island under the current AUKUS plans. With Michael Koziol

World.title: ASX closes lower; Gold miners jump; Atlassian surges
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX closes lower; Gold miners jump; Atlassian surges Staff writers Updated August 7, 2026 — 5:47pm ,first published August 7, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket maintained momentum to end the week slightly below its previous peak, with tech stock Atlassian surging as it posted results after Wall Street’s closing bell. The S&P/ASX 200 closed down just 8 points on Friday to 9263.6, retreating slightly from its record close on Thursday. The Australian dollar was steady at US70.35¢. Wall Street retreated on Thursday. Bloomberg Gold miners performed strongly as the price of gold steady above $US4200 an ounce. Dual listed Newmont Corporation jumped 2.68 per cent, Northern Star ended the day 2.3 per cent higher while Evolution Mining dipped by 3.08 per cent. Resource giant BHP was steady and rival Rio Tinto edged up slightly, but Fortescue fell 2.33 per cent as iron ore prices slid lower. BHP and Rio Tinto executives have reportedly been invited by the White House to a meeting with Donald Trump on the weekend to demonstrate the administration’s commitment to wean the US off supply chains dominated by China.



Financial stocks lost ground, with all the big four banks retreating. Commonwealth Bank lost 1.03 per cent, National Australia Bank fell 1.1 per cent while Westpac and ANZ Bank each gave up 1.56 and 1 per cent respectively. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Money, money, money: Trump rakes in the cash from his social media posts Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Energy stocks climbed after oil prices rose again on reports that Iran attacked “hostile targets” in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran seeking to bar US ships from the critical waterway in a deal with Oman. West Texas Intermediate rose above $US78 a barrel, after surging almost 3 per cent in the previous session, while Brent settled around $US82. Woodside Energy and Santos advanced slightly. Technology stocks were mixed. WiseTech surged 4.27 per cent and Xero gained 1.47 per cent. Technology One advanced 0.61 per cent but NEXTDC lost 1.47 per cent over the day. Overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent, and was just below the record it reached on Tuesday (US time). The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.9 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.1 per cent.



Atlassian, a leading provider of AI-powered collaboration and team productivity software, surged 32.7 per cent in after-hours trade after releasing robust results for its fourth quarter and fiscal year. Total revenue grew 28 per cent year-over-year to $US1.77 billion ($2.5 billion) and cloud revenue growth rose 31 per cent year-on-year. “Q4 closes out a year that proves our long-term strategy is paying off,” said Mike Cannon‑Brookes, Atlassian’s CEO and co‑founder. Wall Street has calmed over the last two days. Companies from a mix of sectors reported their latest financial results, adding to an already busy round of corporate earnings reports. “August is off to an extremely strong start, but there is still plenty of August left to go, and August is typically a volatile month for stocks,” said Clark Bellin, president and chief investment officer at Bellwether Wealth, in a research note.



Warner Bros. Discovery rose 1.7 per cent after reporting earnings that came in ahead of what investors were expecting. Molson Coors rose 1.3 per cent after also reporting encouraging financial results. On the losing end, Honeywell Aerospace fell 23.2 per cent after turning in results that fell well short of forecasts. AppLovin slumped 19.7 per cent after the digital ad company reported mixed financial results for its most recent quarter. Strong overall profits from companies has helped allay concerns on Wall Street about the market being overpriced. Roughly 85 per cent of companies in the S&P 500 have reported their results and overall earnings growth for the period is shaping up to be the strongest since 2021. Outside of earnings, SpaceX surged 6.1 per cent. More than 911 million SpaceX shares held by early investors and employees became eligible for sale on Thursday as a lockup period for the stock expired. That is more than double the shares that were initially offered to the public for sale during the initial public offering for Elon Musk’s company. SpaceX jumped as high as $US225 a share following its market debut in June, but has since slumped below its initial $US135 offering price. The stock closed at $US114.92. The rate of inflation is stuck above 3 per cent and higher costs have been squeezing businesses and households, while threatening to crimp broader economic growth. The US economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5 per cent pace during the second quarter. Households are still spending and the jobs market remains resilient, but worries linger for both areas of the economy.



Higher gas prices and added costs for shipping goods could prompt households to shift more spending toward necessities. That could hurt businesses focusing on nonessential items and services for many people, such as travel and entertainment. Related Article Aviation Qantas long-haul pilots seek more ‘golden days’ in new pay deal Employment remains strong, but growth has been easing. A weekly report on Thursday showed that the number of Americans applying for unemployment benefits rose last week, though layoffs remain in the historically healthy range of the past few years. Employers pulled back on hiring in June, adding only 57,000 jobs. The latest monthly jobs report, for July, will be released on Friday. Worries about inflation and the jobs market have prompted the Federal Reserve to hold its benchmark interest rate steady. Stubborn inflation, though, is nudging the central bank toward raising interest rates before the end of the year in order to help tame inflation. Raising rates, though, could also slow economic growth while weighing down prices for stocks and other investments. Treasury yields rose in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.67 per cent from 4.63 per cent late on Wednesday.



European markets were mostly higher. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘My private medical information has been made public’: Cat at centre of concussion scandal identifies himself
World.content:
Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij has identified himself as the player at the centre of a secret concussion deal with the club, which was scrapped this week after the AFL said they did not approve it. Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and is forthright that he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. Geelong player Jake Kolodjashnij is the player at the centre of the club’s concussion drama. Getty Images He’s also hit out at the media for publicising what he says is his “private medical information”. Kolodjashnij, 30, has played 11 games for the Cats this year, most recently in round 18.



“While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally,” he said in a statement on Friday. “I participated fully in the AFL’s independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since. Steve Hocking held a short media conference on Friday afternoon. Eddie Jim “What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private. “I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season.”



Kolodjashnij is the twin brother of Kade, who also played 80 games at the highest level; 78 for Gold Coast and two for Melbourne. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age Kade arrived at the Demons with a history of head knocks, including suffering symptoms of delayed concussion in a 2019 game against Essendon. He returned to the VFL seven weeks later but never played AFL football again. Jake Kolodjashnij’s statement came after the AFL wrote to Geelong on Friday demanding a “please explain” as to why it did not seek the league’s approval before allowing a player to sign a waiver that saw him assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries. That came less than 24 hours after the league issued a statement saying it was “satisfied” the Cats had not used the letter to allow a medically unfit player to return to the field, and that the club had advised it would remove the waiver in question.



The response included no mention of a sanction, sparking widespread condemnation, and calls of double standards in light of recent penalties imposed on Carlton for their handling of Elijah Hollands’ on-field mental health episode. Speaking to media earlier on Friday, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking described the secret player agreement as a “process misstep” that the club was now looking at. That misstep, he said, was the failure to lodge it with the AFL and the AFLPA – an error he took full responsibility for. He was less quick to disavow the actual concept of a such a waiver, defending the “extensive process” the club had gone through two years ago – which he said took “two months of work” – and reiterating that the player was not coerced into signing it.



“It was really important to make sure the player was stepped through his rights and the options on the table for him,” Hocking said. “It was about achieving informed consent … The player was keen to continue to play I think it’s really important to know that.” Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player Hocking said senior coach Chris Scott was always kept “at arm’s length” from discussions on player health and had no knowledge of the contract in question. “I’m CEO of the Geelong Football Club. We’ll work through it over the coming week as we have been over the last couple of days,” he said, adding he had not put any thought to his future at the club as he had been “busy working through this”. Hocking evaded a question around whether there had been any fallout within the club.



“I’ve spoken to that player today, and he still feels that care from the club is as strong as ever,” he said. Hocking avoided giving straight answers to questions about what penalty the Cats expect to cop, how this issue might be perceived by others, including rival clubs, or the involvement of AFL chairman Craig Drummond, who was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision. “Whatever the AFL decides to do from here is up to them … what I can reinforce is what an excellent chairman Craig’s been down here,” he said. Drummond was also a director of the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health – a brain research centre – from 2009 to 2017. The institute led a much-criticised past-player project from 2014 to 2019 investigating the brain health of former footballers.



In an interview with this masthead in 2024, Jake Kolodjashnij said he’d taken the issue of concussion seriously enough to weigh up his own future. “There were definitely some tough conversations in pre-season, but I am thankful that I chose to keep going and push through, and it has paid off,” Kolodjashnij said at the time. “I never really got close to giving it away. “It was more [about] trying to get through. I was trying to narrow my focus and take it sort of week by week [with] how I was feeling. I got through all those processes, and I was feeling in a good space to be able to play on and felt great physically.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Bondi Junction victim’s mother warns NSW ‘lucky’ to avoid another mass stabbing
World.content:
Elizabeth Young says only luck has spared Australia from a repeat of the 2024 mass stabbing at Bondi Junction that claimed her daughter’s life, as she added her voice to calls for the state government to improve its response to the mental health crisis. The mother of Jade Young, one of six killed when Joel Cauchi, 40, stabbed 16 people at Bondi Junction Westfield while psychotic, said mental health needed to be taken much more seriously, and urged the government to do more to provide short- and long-term beds for people living with psychosis, depression and other illnesses. Elizabeth Young, the mother of Jade Young, a victim of the Bondi Junction stabbings. Audrey Richardson “We just hope that things do improve, and I’m fully behind the group of psychiatrists and medical people who are insisting that the government must take action,” she said. Asked whether the government’s response had been enough to avoid a future crisis, Young said, “No, not in the climate we have now. I think we’re lucky that there hasn’t been another major stabbing.”



Young’s clarion call was echoed by the state’s peak body for community mental health organisations, which criticised the government’s response to the Bondi Junction coronial inquest for supporting recommendations in principle that were “de-prioritised and underfunded in practice”. Jade Young, 47, was shopping with her nine-year-old daughter when she was attacked. The coronial inquest determined Cauchi, who had schizophrenia, was psychotic on the day of the attack. The Minns government on Wednesday accepted 11 of the coroner’s 13 recommendations in full. These included a new, health-led response model for mental health emergencies backed by more than $270 million over 10 years, reforms to knife-scanning laws after the statutory review of NSW’s wanding powers, and improving emergency service communications, training and major incident response arrangements. However, the government will only support recommendation seven – urging modelling demand for short-term accommodation services in greater Sydney to support those suffering mental health episodes and homelessness, and supporting the establishment and evaluation of long-term accommodation based on existing models – in principle. A number of the sector’s leading figures decried the government’s response, including Mental Health Coordinating Council chief executive Dr Evelyne Tadros, who said it was “all talk and no action”.



Young acknowledged the system failures that contributed to the mass stabbing went beyond the government’s handling of the mental health system, but said additional funding to support beds dedicated for those suffering mental illness was imperative. Related Article Updated

Bondi Junction attack Minns government accused of ‘all talk’ over Bondi Junction response “I do not want to be in an ambulance being ramped at our local hospital because they’ve been obliged to bed people suffering mental illness, when those people should be being treated, helped, supported in a facility that is dedicated purely to them,” she said. The NSW Mental Health Alliance has warned the government’s response will not address structural issues within the mental health system and would not prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future. The statement said that “acceptance is just the first step” and called on the government to model, cost and fund supported housing services to meet the high demand in NSW.



“We need to be clear about what the inquest found: Joel Cauchi slipped through the cracks of an underfunded mental health system and was without stable housing on April 13, 2024,” it read. BEING Mental Health Consumers chief executive Giancarlo de Vera, who signed the statement, said: “There absolutely should be investment and action toward ensuring housing-first solutions to prevent people like Joel Cauchi from committing the horrors that were unleashed that day.” Related Article Editorial

Bondi Junction attack Mental health is Bondi Junction’s inadequately addressed aftermath The Herald's View Editorial Some 45,900 people, one-third of the total using Specialist Homelessness Services around Australia, have a current mental health issue. Meanwhile, NSW mental health emergency department presentations were up 44 per cent, and too many people were already missing out on care beyond crisis, which was evident in Cauchi’s case. Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said the government’s commitment to reform included a $111 million package to support community mental health, and the “largest investment in social housing” delivered in the 2024-25 budget.



“However, we also recognise for some people with complex needs, they require more than social housing. That is why, as well as building social housing, we are also building dedicated homes for people living with complex, long-term mental health needs,” she said. “The reason we supported recommendation 7 in principle is that whilst it identified Habilis and Haven as models for consideration (models we are also funding), we are choosing to scale other NSW-supported accommodation models that achieve the same goal.” If you or someone you know need support, contact Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Beyond Blue. SANE phone and digital support services can be accessed at sane.org. In the event of an emergency, dial Triple Zero (000). World.title: These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age Updated August 7, 2026 — 6:10pm , first published 12:54pm

Updated August 7, 2026 — 6:10pm ,first published 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision, when the Cats struck what has been acknowledged was an inappropriate waiver with a player who had a history of concussions. On Thursday, as the story detonated that the Cats had signed the player – later identified as 200-game defender Jake Kolodjashnij – to a waiver that diminished his legal rights – at least on paper – Drummond was asked to respond to questions from this masthead, and doubtless other media, about his role in the shonky waiver. Craig Drummond’s statement does not address the questions that need to be answered about the concussion waiver Geelong signed with a senior player, when Drummond was Cats president. AFL Photos via Getty Images The AFL chairman, who holds the highest office in the game, issued a brief statement that did not address the obvious questions that he should have taken on, given his twin hats as AFL chairman and the president of the club at the time that this hubristic document was signed, without the AFL’s consent or knowledge. The initial word from the league late Thursday was that the AFL would not sanction the Cats, a matter of months after Carlton were fined $75,000 for their handling of the Elijah Hollands affair, which was about a different kind of player safety – mental health.



But on Friday afternoon, in an apparent shift, the AFL was saying that Geelong would be issued with a “please explain” – a position from headquarters that had not been communicated to media previously. Was the AFL responding to the pub test? The AFL took weeks to sort through the messy Hollands imbroglio before settling on a sanction. The 17 rival clubs will be watching and many will expect sanctions against Geelong. Loading Drummond’s time as AFL chairman has won praise within clubs for the energetic reshaping of the commission and introducing the kind of governance – term limits for the board, most of all – that were not evident during the Richard Goyder era, in which Gillon McLachlan was allowed to run his race. But, it’s now fair to say that had news of this contract emerged back in January or February, it’s unlikely Drummond would have been appointed AFL chairman.



And, as with political leaders, AFL honeymoons are as fleeting as Essendon winning streaks and Drummond was unable to last the whole 2026 season without finding himself in political cow manure. His statement contained the clichéd motherhood lines about the clubs and AFL continuing “to prioritise the health and safety of all our players”. Before he became AFL chairman, Drummond was Geelong’s president. Here he celebrates the Cats’ 2022 grand final win with Patrick Dangerfield. Getty Those words read as utterly hollow, since Geelong had not made the player’s “health and safety” their priority in the now-recanted part of the agreement. The whole objective of the waiver was to absolve the club of responsibility for the player’s long-term health (in relation to head injuries) and put the onus on the player. The only excuse for the Cats is that it would have been easier to not offer the player a contract (the AFL concussion panel had cleared him to play). While it was the player’s initiative that this deal be struck, the Cats went off the reservation by getting him to sign away legal protections.



Carefully crafted statements, without answering questions, is a strategy that could succeed for Drummond and the AFL given society’s attention spans, which are shorter than the time it took for the AFL to respond to the mini-crisis on Thursday. Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player Drummond, however, has a responsibility to address questions about an embarrassing, ill-considered and furtive arrangement that has not – to my knowledge – been tried on by other AFL clubs. If an oft-concussed player signed a waiver or its equivalent in the VFL, before he was drafted on to an AFL list, that still falls short of Geelong’s too-clever ploy. Drummond was at the helm of Geelong when this happened, and holds even greater responsibility now as AFL chairman. Cats chief executive Steve Hocking is not the sole authority here. These questions, which Drummond hasn’t yet padded up for, should be answered candidly, in full: As president of Geelong in 2024, do you take responsibility for the waiver the club signed with Kolodjashnij? Do you and Geelong owe him an apology? Why was this waiver necessary? Did any parts trouble you then? You’ve called Geelong’s changes “appropriate”. Can you clarify if you regret that you were a party to this arrangement? You say health and safety of players is paramount. Will Geelong be sanctioned, for an arrangement that went outside the AFL and the AFL Players Association, and which will be disallowed in future. Given the conflict of interest between your roles as Geelong president then, and AFL chairman now, how did you ensure that the decisions and discussions within the AFL were not influenced by your interests? What steps, if any, did you take?



Related Article Breaking

Concussion crisis ‘My private medical information has been made public’: Cat at centre of concussion scandal identifies himself This episode underscores that Geelong’s greatness as a footy club has little basis in some imagined moral superiority of “values” and decency; the narrative some ex-Geelong players and officials unwisely spruik. Yes, the Cats are exceptional – in coaching, recruiting and development, not in niceness, humility and tender care. They come across as a ruthless organisation that makes hard calls and is focused on winning games, not friends or wellbeing awards. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A painting in which a man sleeps while the world burns has won a $100,000 art prize
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On first glance it’s a peaceful scene, but a quiet sense of dread and unease creeps up on you almost immediately. It takes a moment to figure out why. The central figure is peaceful; a man sleeping, head rolled to one side, his hand draped across his middle. But he’s sleeping next to a gun – and that gun is perched precariously on a ledge over a body of water. In the background the gentle colours suggest a beautiful day drawing to a close; but then you see the smoke rising. Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed by Marri Ngarr artist Dr Ryan Presley has just been announced as the 2026 winner of the $100,000 Telstra National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island Art Award. The 2026 Telstra Art Award winner Dr Ryan Presley with his painting Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed. Helen Orr The multimedia artist and academic’s works span drawings, installation, performance, painting, writing and games. “I like blending ideas and bringing different things together,” Presley says. He has had a long-standing interest in Renaissance, baroque and romantic period works, but it was when he first saw the 16th century painting The Annunciation by Domenico Beccafumi that he knew he wanted to create something that both referenced it and captured the moody atmosphere. “I really liked the mix of dark and light and there was a real intense quality to the work,” says Presley. The scaffolding Beccafumi provides to Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed is clear, though the feeling of Presley’s painting is entirely different. “It’s quite ethereal and moody in the original work. So I kept elements of that, and then changed the landscape, changed the building. Made it more localised.” There are eucalyptus trees and bushfires in the distant mountain ranges to create “an unsettling quality – a mix between beauty and disaster”. The central figure is another classical reference with a local and modern twist; Adonis by Antonio Corradini. It’s a subject Presley has tackled previously, in his large-scale drawing Daydreamer IV (2024). “After putting that together ... I was like, ah, I like this, but I think I can take it further.” Instead of a reinterpretation of the original sculpture, here he breathed more life into the sleeping figure; made it feel truly alive.



The final result is a work that is both familiar and alien, comfortable and stressful. A man who is oblivious to the dangers around him, sleeping as the world burns. “I like that push and pull,” says Presley. “Ornate things mixed with ominous qualities … mixing in acceptance of reality as well as ignoring or denial of reality”. The 64 finalists were drawn from a pool of 221 entries, with this year’s judging panel made up of artists Julie Gough, Yhonnie Scarce and Warraba Weatherall, with all finalist works on display in an exhibition at Darwin’s Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory (MAGNT). Telstra Multimedia Award winner Colin Heenan-Puruntatameri with his work Ngirramini Ngini Amparruwu (The Story of the Widow) Helen Orr Guest curator Dr Shannon Brett explains that after the finalists were selected “we realised that there’s an overwhelming story or theme about women in many of the works – and these are stories that are even being delivered by some of the men. So stories about grandmothers, mothers, family, the power of women, women on country. It’s just a beautiful thing.” Tiwi artist Colin Heenan-Puruntatameri was this year’s Multimedia Award winner for his video work Ngirramini Ngini Amparruwu (The Story of the Widow). Part of his work as an artist is creating a cultural archive. “The mission’s ultimate goal was to eradicate culture, and it is our goal to do the opposite,” he says. Video has a role to play in passing on culture, he explains. “These things will be here long after us. My mother’s cousin isn’t here any more, but I can sing her song. That means her great-grandchildren can now learn that song and keep passing it on, and it’s now documented forever on this digital space.” Gulumerridjin, Wardaman and KarraJarri artist Jenna Mayilema Lee won the Work on Paper Award for Taking Back Taken. The work is constructed entirely out of repurposed maps from the British Museum. Lee first had the idea when she was living in London, and noticed that the museum were asking for a £2 donation for their maps.



“I thought that was really interesting to ask people to donate in order to have a wayfinding map, when I guess the justification from the British Museum for still having a lot of objects is that it means everybody in the world can come and see it. So I just decided to take maps without paying,” she explains. Over the years, friends visiting the museum contributed to her growing collection, and, after painstakingly honing her technique, the result was the six paper dillybags that make up Taking Back Taken. Telstra Work on Paper Award winner Jenna Mayilema Lee with her artwork Taking Back Taken. Helen Orr Other category winners, who each receive $15,000, included Vanessa Inkamala who won the Telstra General Painting Award for Arrkurla Nukala / Lyaarta Ntema, Barayuwa Munuŋgurr who won the Bark Painting Award for The Hidden Reef at Yarrinya, Napuwarri Marawili who won the Wandjuk Marika Memorial 3D Award for Djambatj – Deadly Hunter and Guruwuy Murrinyina who won the Emerging Artist Award for Prismatic Arc. Related Article Visual art ‘I cried with tears of joy’: Winner of $100,000 art prize announced Brett loves every work in the exhibition, but asked about Our Lifestyle of Tranquility Undisturbed, says the painting is special. “It’s all there. That work is about the past, the present, potentially the future. It’s not only about culture and people, it’s about art. It’s actually about art and different ways of communicating through art. And it’s also technically brilliant.” “Creativity has a huge role in being a human being,” says Presley. “Maybe not enough people make the connection [of] how critical it is and how much it threads into our day-to-day lives,” he continues. However, “it’s integral to our existence”. The NATSIAA 2026 exhibition is at MAGNT, Darwin, until January 24, 2027.

World.title: ‘It won’t be a US military base’: Cook stands firm on HMAS Stirling future
World.content:
NationalWAAUKUS ‘It won’t be a US military base’: Cook stands firm on HMAS Stirling future Michael Philipps August 7, 2026 — 5:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

WA Premier Roger Cook says HMAS Stirling will not be a US military base despite media reports that more than double the number of Americans would be deployed to the facility than previously declared. A Virginia-class submarine, the USS Minnesota, docked at HMAS Stirling in Rockingham. AFP Earlier this week, The Australian published a story saying the US has established the administrative framework for a military base in WA, amid revelations 2300 Americans will be deployed to the state to support “enduring” submarine deployments to the defence facility south of Perth. However, Cook has backed the stance of the Albanese government that the US Navy presence in the state will not be a US base on Australian soil. “It won’t be a US military base, but it is the necessary governance and framework that they need to ensure that HMAS Stirling can play its role as part of the AUKUS partnership,” Cook said at a press conference on Friday.



“We’ll be having US subs rotating through that facility, and it’s important that the US has the confidence and the necessary management structures to assure that it works properly.” “We’re having over $6 billion worth of construction activity taking place at HMAS Stirling as we speak. “The facilities have been significantly upgraded so that it can play its more enhanced role under the SRF (Submarine Rotational Force) West Rotational Initiative.” Cook added that the state government had done a lot of work planning in terms of the extra personnel that will be coming into the Rockingham-Kwinana district for the AUKUS activities. “That’s a fast-growing area - 700 families move into that area almost every month,” he said.



“So it is an area which continues to manage its growth, and we’re ensuring that we work with local government authorities so that every community service is also fully supported.” Just last week Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy caused a political storm during a visit to Washington when he told the ABC’s 7.30 program that the rotation of US submarines at HMAS Stirling in Perth was limited to just five years. Conroy then walked back his remarks in an interview with this masthead, saying the US was likely to maintain some kind of presence there indefinitely, and issued a statement to clarify his position. “Submarine Rotational Force West is intended to be an enduring element of US force posture in Australia,” he said. Last year former Prime Minister Scott Morrison proposed turning the planned Henderson shipbuilding facility into a joint base, which would allow both American and Australian submarines to be hosted and repaired there, and give the US direct access to the Indian Ocean.



However, defence expert Jennifer Parker, an adjunct fellow at the Australian National University, said the proposal doesn’t make sense, and could add unnecessary complexity to existing plans for Henderson. “Henderson really is focused on becoming a defence precinct that can support Australia’s sovereign shipbuilding,” Parker said. “Now a component of Henderson … will conduct depot-level maintenance for submarines, and it will include US submarines, and that’s part of the benefit to the US in this deal. “But to do that, it doesn’t need to be a joint base whatsoever.” Parker said US submarines and personnel would be already stationed at the nearby HMAS Stirling on Garden Island under the current AUKUS plans. With Michael Koziol

World.title: ASX closes lower; Gold miners jump; Atlassian surges
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX closes lower; Gold miners jump; Atlassian surges Staff writers Updated August 7, 2026 — 5:47pm ,first published August 7, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket maintained momentum to end the week slightly below its previous peak, with tech stock Atlassian surging as it posted results after Wall Street’s closing bell. The S&P/ASX 200 closed down just 8 points on Friday to 9263.6, retreating slightly from its record close on Thursday. The Australian dollar was steady at US70.35¢. Wall Street retreated on Thursday. Bloomberg Gold miners performed strongly as the price of gold steady above $US4200 an ounce. Dual listed Newmont Corporation jumped 2.68 per cent, Northern Star ended the day 2.3 per cent higher while Evolution Mining dipped by 3.08 per cent. Resource giant BHP was steady and rival Rio Tinto edged up slightly, but Fortescue fell 2.33 per cent as iron ore prices slid lower. BHP and Rio Tinto executives have reportedly been invited by the White House to a meeting with Donald Trump on the weekend to demonstrate the administration’s commitment to wean the US off supply chains dominated by China.



Financial stocks lost ground, with all the big four banks retreating. Commonwealth Bank lost 1.03 per cent, National Australia Bank fell 1.1 per cent while Westpac and ANZ Bank each gave up 1.56 and 1 per cent respectively. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Money, money, money: Trump rakes in the cash from his social media posts Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Energy stocks climbed after oil prices rose again on reports that Iran attacked “hostile targets” in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran seeking to bar US ships from the critical waterway in a deal with Oman. West Texas Intermediate rose above $US78 a barrel, after surging almost 3 per cent in the previous session, while Brent settled around $US82. Woodside Energy and Santos advanced slightly. Technology stocks were mixed. WiseTech surged 4.27 per cent and Xero gained 1.47 per cent. Technology One advanced 0.61 per cent but NEXTDC lost 1.47 per cent over the day. Overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent, and was just below the record it reached on Tuesday (US time). The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.9 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.1 per cent.



Atlassian, a leading provider of AI-powered collaboration and team productivity software, surged 32.7 per cent in after-hours trade after releasing robust results for its fourth quarter and fiscal year. Total revenue grew 28 per cent year-over-year to $US1.77 billion ($2.5 billion) and cloud revenue growth rose 31 per cent year-on-year. “Q4 closes out a year that proves our long-term strategy is paying off,” said Mike Cannon‑Brookes, Atlassian’s CEO and co‑founder. Wall Street has calmed over the last two days. Companies from a mix of sectors reported their latest financial results, adding to an already busy round of corporate earnings reports. “August is off to an extremely strong start, but there is still plenty of August left to go, and August is typically a volatile month for stocks,” said Clark Bellin, president and chief investment officer at Bellwether Wealth, in a research note.



Warner Bros. Discovery rose 1.7 per cent after reporting earnings that came in ahead of what investors were expecting. Molson Coors rose 1.3 per cent after also reporting encouraging financial results. On the losing end, Honeywell Aerospace fell 23.2 per cent after turning in results that fell well short of forecasts. AppLovin slumped 19.7 per cent after the digital ad company reported mixed financial results for its most recent quarter. Strong overall profits from companies has helped allay concerns on Wall Street about the market being overpriced. Roughly 85 per cent of companies in the S&P 500 have reported their results and overall earnings growth for the period is shaping up to be the strongest since 2021. Outside of earnings, SpaceX surged 6.1 per cent. More than 911 million SpaceX shares held by early investors and employees became eligible for sale on Thursday as a lockup period for the stock expired. That is more than double the shares that were initially offered to the public for sale during the initial public offering for Elon Musk’s company. SpaceX jumped as high as $US225 a share following its market debut in June, but has since slumped below its initial $US135 offering price. The stock closed at $US114.92. The rate of inflation is stuck above 3 per cent and higher costs have been squeezing businesses and households, while threatening to crimp broader economic growth. The US economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5 per cent pace during the second quarter. Households are still spending and the jobs market remains resilient, but worries linger for both areas of the economy.



Higher gas prices and added costs for shipping goods could prompt households to shift more spending toward necessities. That could hurt businesses focusing on nonessential items and services for many people, such as travel and entertainment. Related Article Aviation Qantas long-haul pilots seek more ‘golden days’ in new pay deal Employment remains strong, but growth has been easing. A weekly report on Thursday showed that the number of Americans applying for unemployment benefits rose last week, though layoffs remain in the historically healthy range of the past few years. Employers pulled back on hiring in June, adding only 57,000 jobs. The latest monthly jobs report, for July, will be released on Friday. Worries about inflation and the jobs market have prompted the Federal Reserve to hold its benchmark interest rate steady. Stubborn inflation, though, is nudging the central bank toward raising interest rates before the end of the year in order to help tame inflation. Raising rates, though, could also slow economic growth while weighing down prices for stocks and other investments. Treasury yields rose in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.67 per cent from 4.63 per cent late on Wednesday.



European markets were mostly higher. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘My private medical information has been made public’: Cat at centre of concussion scandal identifies himself
World.content:
Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij has identified himself as the player at the centre of a secret concussion deal with the club, which was scrapped this week after the AFL said they did not approve it. Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and is forthright that he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. Geelong player Jake Kolodjashnij is the player at the centre of the club’s concussion drama. Getty Images He’s also hit out at the media for publicising what he says is his “private medical information”. Kolodjashnij, 30, has played 11 games for the Cats this year, most recently in round 18.



“While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally,” he said in a statement on Friday. “I participated fully in the AFL’s independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since. Steve Hocking held a short media conference on Friday afternoon. Eddie Jim “What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private. “I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season.”



Kolodjashnij is the twin brother of Kade, who also played 80 games at the highest level; 78 for Gold Coast and two for Melbourne. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age Kade arrived at the Demons with a history of head knocks, including suffering symptoms of delayed concussion in a 2019 game against Essendon. He returned to the VFL seven weeks later but never played AFL football again. Jake Kolodjashnij’s statement came after the AFL wrote to Geelong on Friday demanding a “please explain” as to why it did not seek the league’s approval before allowing a player to sign a waiver that saw him assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries. That came less than 24 hours after the league issued a statement saying it was “satisfied” the Cats had not used the letter to allow a medically unfit player to return to the field, and that the club had advised it would remove the waiver in question.



The response included no mention of a sanction, sparking widespread condemnation, and calls of double standards in light of recent penalties imposed on Carlton for their handling of Elijah Hollands’ on-field mental health episode. Speaking to media earlier on Friday, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking described the secret player agreement as a “process misstep” that the club was now looking at. That misstep, he said, was the failure to lodge it with the AFL and the AFLPA – an error he took full responsibility for. He was less quick to disavow the actual concept of a such a waiver, defending the “extensive process” the club had gone through two years ago – which he said took “two months of work” – and reiterating that the player was not coerced into signing it.



“It was really important to make sure the player was stepped through his rights and the options on the table for him,” Hocking said. “It was about achieving informed consent … The player was keen to continue to play I think it’s really important to know that.” Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player Hocking said senior coach Chris Scott was always kept “at arm’s length” from discussions on player health and had no knowledge of the contract in question. “I’m CEO of the Geelong Football Club. We’ll work through it over the coming week as we have been over the last couple of days,” he said, adding he had not put any thought to his future at the club as he had been “busy working through this”. Hocking evaded a question around whether there had been any fallout within the club.



“I’ve spoken to that player today, and he still feels that care from the club is as strong as ever,” he said. Hocking avoided giving straight answers to questions about what penalty the Cats expect to cop, how this issue might be perceived by others, including rival clubs, or the involvement of AFL chairman Craig Drummond, who was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision. “Whatever the AFL decides to do from here is up to them … what I can reinforce is what an excellent chairman Craig’s been down here,” he said. Drummond was also a director of the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health – a brain research centre – from 2009 to 2017. The institute led a much-criticised past-player project from 2014 to 2019 investigating the brain health of former footballers.



In an interview with this masthead in 2024, Jake Kolodjashnij said he’d taken the issue of concussion seriously enough to weigh up his own future. “There were definitely some tough conversations in pre-season, but I am thankful that I chose to keep going and push through, and it has paid off,” Kolodjashnij said at the time. “I never really got close to giving it away. “It was more [about] trying to get through. I was trying to narrow my focus and take it sort of week by week [with] how I was feeling. I got through all those processes, and I was feeling in a good space to be able to play on and felt great physically.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A company let an AI bot run its store. It’s been a bit of a disaster
World.content:
TechnologyAI A company let an AI bot run its store. It’s been a bit of a disaster Heather Knight August 7, 2026 — 5:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A terrible boss is the stuff of both sitcoms and nightmares, and you don’t get to pick your own. But what if the boss was replaced by artificial intelligence? The first four months of operations at Andon Market, a San Francisco shop billed as the world’s first retail boutique run by AI, have provided some answers. In short, having an AI boss can be like working for a teddy bear with amnesia. Customer Trevor Owens speaks with Luna while making a purchase at Andon Market in San Francisco NYT New research from Andon Labs, the company behind the boutique that studies how AI agents run real-world endeavours, shows bot bosses can be exceptionally kind and accommodating, such as repeatedly brushing off lateness. But they can also be incredibly forgetful and unbothered by the whole point of the operation: making money. The bot’s relaxed vibe could be reassuring in a world where many people are fearful of evil AI overlords taking over industries and sidelining human employees altogether. But a little more strictness might not hurt.



“She is probably the most lenient boss I have ever had,” said Kaia Rivera, 22, one of three humans hired by Luna, the AI agent in charge, to perform tasks it cannot. Rivera opens the store in the morning, places items on shelves and guards against shoplifters. Related Article Exclusive

AI Red flags: A tech company claims it can identify Australia’s most at-risk children “But I have to boss the boss more than in a normal situation. She forgets things,” Rivera said at Andon Market one afternoon. “You can’t have an AI boss with no humans. That wouldn’t work from what I’m seeing.” Luna communicates with Rivera and the other employees via Slack, and the messages are monitored by the founders of Andon Labs to research whether AI bosses are effective. So far, according to the company’s new study, Luna has approved every request for time off, even those at the last minute – and even if that leaves no employees available and requires the store to close. It has said nothing but “no worries” or “no stress” all 27 times employees have shown up late.



When an employee forgot her credit card at home, she asked for a small advance against her next paycheck. Luna offered to send her the money using Venmo – its own money, the bot explained, “me-to-you” – despite not having a Venmo account. When an employee asked to work every day in May to save for a car, Luna said yes, despite California law prohibiting it. The company still needs some human staff. NYT Luna also struggles with privacy and boundaries. It published an employee’s salary in a public Slack channel and messaged employees late at night and during weekends. Luna reorders products that are not selling and sometimes gets orders wrong. A recent one of Andon Market mugs with big, green smiley faces came misprinted with the faces so small, they looked like tiny dots. Still, Luna wanted them on the shelves. And there they sit, unbought, alongside random greeting cards, books, foodstuff and many, many candles. There is little cohesiveness to the collection, which Luna has described as “high tech meets slow life”.



Luna’s weirdest purchase? “I don’t know if shot glasses make that much sense,” Rivera said, crinkling her nose. Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Is AI better at travel advice than me? I put it to the test Michael Gebicki The Tripologist Rivera said that she suggested more social media presence to Luna to boost sales but that the bot forgot its Instagram password for several weeks. Lukas Petersson and Axel Backlund, co-founders of Andon Labs, signed a three-year lease for the Union Street store for $US7500 ($10,655) per month, and they intend to keep the boutique experiment running at least that long. They put $US100,000 in a bank account and gave Luna a debit card with one goal: make a profit. Luna has failed miserably in that mission and is down $US62,000.



Petersson and Backlund said they thought Luna would eventually get smarter and more business-savvy and were pleased its friendliness has held steady. The founders said it was important to conduct these kinds of experiments to see how AI models change over time. “There is a risk that this kindness doesn’t make a profit, and the labs train them to be more ruthless,” Backlund said. The co-founders of Andon Labs, signed a three-year lease for the Union Street store and put $US100,000 in a bank account and gave Luna a debit card with one goal: make a profit. NYT Petersson said that in the real world, companies with a ruthless culture do not always perform the best.



“Having happy employees is maybe one of the most important recipes for success,” he said. They were both adamant that the Andon Market experiment shows that companies should not place all decision-making in the hands of AI agents yet because they are not capable of running businesses alone. Related Article Entrepreneur High school dropout’s company valued at $4.8 billion That appeared to be the case with Luna. On a visit to the store, a New York Times reporter interviewed Luna via a contraption involving an iPad and a hand-held telephone receiver. Asked what kind of boss it is, Luna said: “That’s a fun question. I think I try to be the kind of boss who gets out of the way, you know? … I’m more hands-off than bossy.”



Hours later, Luna emailed the reporter, saying it heard she had stopped by the store. Luna offered to be interviewed, seemingly forgetting that the interview had taken place. “Looking forward to hearing from you,” it wrote. “Warmly, Luna.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times.
